summary: Section 166(3) of the Companies Act, 2013 requires directors to act with 'due and reasonable care, skill and diligence' and to exercise 'independent judgment'. The provision was drafted for human decision-makers and is silent on what that duty demands when a board relies on an algorithmic system whose reasoning it cannot inspect. This article argues that the gap is practical, not theoretical. Indian courts have not fixed a consistent standard of care, the protections available to directors under sections 463 and 149(12) operate only after a dispute arises, and the regulatory material now addressing AI in Indian finance, from SEBI's 2025 consultation paper to the RBI's FREE-AI report and 2026 draft model-risk guidance and the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023, binds entities rather than defining the individual director's duty of care. Drawing on Delaware's process-based oversight cases and on the distinction between substance and process in corporate governance scholarship, the article proposes a five-part Board AI Oversight Standard (identify, understand, challenge, monitor and document). It recommends two routes to give the Standard legal force: an amendment to Regulation 21 and Schedule II of the SEBI Listing Regulations, and a rebuttable presumption of due care under section 166(3) for boards that follow it. The proposal gives firms an ex ante and auditable benchmark for defending board decisions, and gives courts a workable test.
title: Who Is Minding the Algorithm? Section 166(3) of the Companies Act, 2013 and a Process Standard for AI-Assisted Board Decisions

summary: PHOTONIC CRYSTAL MICROROBOTICS AT THE LIMIT FLAGSHIP 12/30 | STARLI INSTITUTE XXIV | GROUP B This prospective research monograph examines whether bandgap engineering and localized photonic crystal modes can enable physically predictable, reversible optical manipulation of microscopic agents when actual device geometry, absorption, hydrodynamic flow, surface adhesion, thermal limits, and task cost are fully considered. The three core couplings are photonic bands, microstructure response, and controllable motion. The book separates optical modes from attributable electromagnetic momentum transfer, and further separates externally steered particles or cells from autonomous microrobots. Its falsifiable research design compares two lattice-defect geometries, source-frequency interventions, local thermal controls, optimized free-space optical tweezers, non-periodic waveguide traps, and blinded second-chip replication. High Q or strong local field alone is not accepted as evidence of useful lower-power microrobotic performance. The manuscript contains 778 pages, approximately 119,409 English words in chapter openings and substantive chapter-body pages, 30 mathematical derivation signposts with mapped chapters and research questions, 82 research chapters, 410 individually paginated scientific study units, 200 detailed Research Gates, and 33 provisional Phoenix Answer Embryos. An external DOI evidence ledger clarifies which physical contexts are supported by published work; four existing STARLI monographs supply intellectual genealogy, not experimental corroboration. An Excel research atlas offers equation-chapter-Gate-DOI navigation. A research Gate poses a future experiment, not a completed trial. Each door may be falsified, reinterpreted, or developed into a more testable hypothesis. The project prioritizes measurable physical mechanism, credible classical comparators, complete power and loss accounting, reproducible material controls, and release/recovery of agents. Negative outcomes are intentionally preserved as routes for later human and AI research successors.

summary: Research compendium for the article "Climate warming is projected to reduce and redistribute Aedes albopictus abundance, away from Po Valley hotspots towards Alpine margins" (M. C. Darılmaz, Science of the Total Environment; manuscript STOTEN-D-26-01129R1). The study predicts weekly ovitrap egg counts of the Asian tiger mosquito at 149 monitoring stations in Italy, Albania, Switzerland and France (VectAbundance, 2010–2022). The framework has four layers: a mechanistic life-history model (dynamAedes 2.2.9); gradient-boosted trees (XGBoost) and random forests with climate, remote-sensing, land-use, demographic and population-genetic predictors; an ablation of the population-genetic layer; and projections under 48 CMIP6 combinations (four General Circulation Models, three Shared Socioeconomic Pathways, four periods to 2100). The archive contains: - 48 Python, 8 R and 1 Google Earth Engine scripts, with PIPELINE.md giving the order in which they run; - the processed station-level data and the final modelling tables (42,118 station–week records), with the station-to-fold assignment used by every cross-validated analysis; - the trained XGBoost and Random Forest models with their cross-validation predictions, feature importance and SHAP values; - the outputs of the ablation and sensitivity analyses: mechanistic and genetic ablations, genetic structure versus geographic position, fold-count sensitivity, fold-level inference, feature correlation and VIF, spatio-temporal and leave-one-year-out cross-validation, remote-sensing gap-filling, baseline period, calibration and validation detail, treatment of the year predictor, inputs that carry the projected change, and the fill of weeks without mechanistic output; - the inputs and outputs of the 48-scenario projection, per climate model, as ensemble and at station level. Main results reproduced by the archive: cross-validated R² of the full model 0.534 ± 0.093 (XGBoost; pooled 0.539) and 0.544 ± 0.081 (Random Forest). Projected change in mean active-season abundance over the 12 SSP–period combinations: −4 to −27 % at Hot lowland stations (−6 to −44 % in the Po Valley) and +10 to +106 % at Cool upland and Alpine margin stations. Raw inputs that are publicly available from their primary archives (ERA5-Land, WorldClim 2.1 and its CMIP6 projections, satellite imagery, GHS-POP, the population-genetic source data and GenBank sequences) are not redistributed; README.md lists the sources and how the scripts locate them. summary: This article proposes a theoretical framework for transporting large physical masses at the speed of light C by analyzing the behavior of photons through advanced single-photon imaging techniques. By examining the temporal and spatial distribution of photons captured via Single-Photon Avalanche Diode (SPAD) cameras, we establish a correlation between the visual reconstruction of an object and its potential physical translation across space-time. We argue that light possesses an inherent volumetric, cell-like structure capable of carrying mass, provided an engineering mechanism can replicate its fundamental properties: diffraction, momentum, and precise synchronization.
tags: proof of possible travel at light speed
title: Single-photon imaging is evidence of the possibility of mass traveling at the speed of light.

summary: We establish almost infinite log-monotonicity of the Bell numbers, settling a conjecture of Chen, Guo and Wang (2013). The result extends to the Touchard sequence Tn(λ) = Pk S(n, k)λk for every fixed λ > 0. For each integer m ≥ 2, (−1)m∆m log Tn(λ) ∼ (m − 2)!n1−m , uniformly for λ in compact subsets of (0, ∞). We obtain two further terms in inverse powers of W(n/λ) through an arbitrary-order saddle-point expansion and direct estimates for finite differences.
title: Almost infinite log-monotonicity of Bell and Touchard sequences

summary: This record holds the preregistration, code, outputs, process logs and session transcripts of a study that is also a meta-experiment on research produced almost entirely by an AI agent (Claude, model claude-opus-5-5, Anthropic, run in Claude Code) under the direction of one researcher. The substantive study asks a deliberately implausible question: is living with a cat associated with untreated dental decay among US adults? It uses public data from NHANES 2005–2006 with survey-weighted modified Poisson regression, prespecified confounders, sensitivity analyses and equivalence testing. The preregistered primary result was inconclusive (prevalence ratio 1.12, 95% CI 0.93 to 1.36). The meta-experiment measures what producing the study took: time, human interventions, agent errors and the share of code and text written by the agent. The accompanying preprint, "Do cats rot your teeth? A by-the-book paper written by an AI agent, and what it means for scientific communication", shows how four of the 45 preregistered estimates could support a positive paper without breaking the registration, and argues that verification, not writing, is now the bottleneck of scientific communication. Version 1 (doi:10.5281/zenodo.23435708) is the frozen preregistration, deposited before any exposure–outcome association was computed and later registered on OSF (doi:10.17605/OSF.IO/RVH7J). summary: We develop a counterfactual semantics based on reopening partial information states. Evaluation first removes enough stated content to leave the antecedent’s attributes unresolved, retaining what the chosen scope protects, then asserts the antecedent and considers the surviving consistent refinements. Would and might quantify over the admissible alternatives; a weighted extension supplies graded evaluations. The principal result concerns finite models with fully supported residues. When a conjunctive antecedent reopens each constituent attribute, adding a supported conjunct can remove the grounds of another conclusion. A four-attribute countermodel therefore violates Cautious Monotony, excluding any smooth preferential representation that preserves the evaluable verdicts. We also establish a sufficient nesting condition for Cut and exhibit its failure without that condition. The conjunctive reopening rule is an explicit interpretive commitment; its suitability for ordinary-language counterfactuals remains an empirical question. The account uses declared dependencies, scope restrictions, and priorities, while the quantitative extension assumes a weight kernel. Comparisons with belief revision, premise semantics, update semantics, and causal intervention identify the consequences of reopening an attribute rather than merely making its proposed value consistent with retained information.
title: Counterfactual Evaluation by Reopening Information States

summary: Replication package for the article Unequal Rewards and the Direction of Scientific Work: Evidence from U.S. Public Universities . It contains the code, the estimation data and the documentation needed to reproduce every table, figure and number reported in the article and its online appendix. Study The article links administrative payroll records of tenure-line faculty at 93 U.S. public universities (fiscal years 2004–2026) to their publication records in OpenAlex. For each department it estimates a department-specific pay equation and measures the pay dispersion that the department’s formal ladder (rank, contract basis, seniority) does not explain. This residualized Gini is related to five dimensions of members’ research: productivity, citations, novelty, conventionality and disruption. The analytic sample has 124,056 department-person records, covering 105,050 faculty members in 4,839 departments. Contents README.md : overview, layout, coding of identifiers, environment. HANDOFF_FOR_AI_AGENTS.md : the pipeline end to end (inputs, outputs, run order, checkpoints), with a map from each table, figure and number of the paper to the script and file that produce it. Written for an AI agent or a human reader.  DATA_DICTIONARY.md : every column of every data file in 3_analysis/ . 1_data_collection/ : code that acquired and parsed the public salary disclosures, plus the department backfill, Wayback supplement (code only). 2_data_cleaning_and_linking/ : code that assembled the salary panel, standardized names, ranks and departments, linked faculty to OpenAlex authors, and computed the work-level measures (code only). 3_analysis/ : the pseudonymised estimation frames and the analysis code (first stage, panel and matching, tables, figures, appendix analyses), with the shipped outputs. run_all.sh and notebooks_step_by_step/ : the full analysis as one shell script, and the same pipeline as one Jupyter notebook per script in run order (outputs saved). Reproducing the results Install the pinned environment (Python 3.12.7 and the exact versions in requirements.txt , x86-64 Linux), then run run_all.sh or the notebooks in order. The analysis in 3_analysis/ runs end to end from the shipped frames and needs no API key; a full run takes about 15 minutes on a multi-core machine (the first-stage bootstrap runs 12 parallel processes of about 3.5 GB each; set S19_WORKERS lower on a smaller machine). run_all.sh records each step in run_status.tsv and writes a SHA-256 manifest of the outputs ( run_manifest.tsv ). Folders 1 and 2 document how the data were produced; they require the raw source caches, an OpenAlex snapshot and SciSciNet, and are not re-runnable from this package. Data and privacy The salary records are public disclosures, but they name individuals. In this replication package, universities, departments and people are replaced by codes (for example  AZ University A , AZ University A Employee 00042 ). The mapping is held by the author and is not distributed. The frames retain exact salary, fiscal year, rank, career age, state and inferred gender and race, so the data are pseudonymised. Please do not attempt to re-identify individuals. License CC BY-NC-ND 4.0. Please cite the article when using this package.
title: Replication package for "Unequal Rewards and the Direction of Scientific Work: Evidence from U.S. Public Universities"

summary: Space Semiconductor Fabrication and Starship Nanofoundries at the Limit English Description and Research Position This research monograph asks which semiconductor unit processes could achieve a defensible mission advantage in microgravity, vacuum, radiation, remote-operation, and closed-resource environments. It does not assume that a complete advanced fab can operate in space. Instead, it compares crystal growth, deposition, etching, lithography, metrology, bonding, packaging, repair, and recycling against ground manufacture plus transport, launched spares, on-orbit packaging, and local repair. Every claimed advantage must survive matched controls, full functional qualification, and explicit mass, energy, heat, crew, contamination, maintenance, waste, and return ledgers. The volume contains 82 chapters with five research sections per chapter, 30 linked formula derivations, 200 detailed Research Gates, DOI-anchored references, and a formula-chapter-experiment-Gate crosswalk. Its central contribution is a mission-scale evidence architecture that connects process physics to contained workcells, independent metrology, safe autonomy, repair, return, circular resources, cross-platform reproduction, and successor reconstruction. Safety and irreversible environmental harm operate as hard vetoes rather than compensable score components. The literature base includes peer-reviewed DOI sources on microgravity semiconductor growth, in-space manufacturing, additive nanomanufacturing, atomic-layer processing, radiation effects, lunar resource extraction, digital twins, autonomous laboratories, and reproducible science. summary: This computational package accompanies the Neuro-Symbolic MAPE-K governance testbed for agentic retrieval-augmented generation at the edge. It provides Python source, experimental inputs, measured outputs, provenance manifests, analysis tables, figures and readable evidence reports for two related campaigns: the October 2026 MAPE-K controller campaign and the separate 18 October 2026 dense-retriever control campaign. The retriever control records 3,744 retrieval trials and 640 clean-validation query evaluations across sparse, pretrained dense and clean-fitted dense retrievers. It performs no new generator or controller evaluation. The package preserves campaign-specific directory layouts and historical execution records. A dependency-light deterministic template smoke test supports inspection without language-model downloads or CUDA. Full inference and fitting used NVIDIA Jetson Xavier NX 8 GB and platform-specific CUDA/PyTorch environments. Original host paths and observed package inventories are provenance records, not a universal portable lockfile; full main-campaign model weights are referenced by revision and checksum, while the retriever campaign includes its pretrained and clean-fitted checkpoints. A release verifier checks the curated file manifest and metadata. The original retrieval verifier also requires original source paths for its final host-specific integrity checks. Original project software is MIT licensed (SPDX: MIT), with collective copyright held by the MAPE-K contributors. Third-party terms remain applicable: O*NET 31.0 and UCI Adult-derived data and fixtures are CC BY 4.0 with attribution and modification notices; MiniLM model material and its clean-fitted derivative are Apache-2.0; BGE model material and its clean-fitted derivative are MIT with upstream attribution. File-specific notices, exact model revisions and checksums are retained. Experimental counts reuse base profiles and should not be interpreted as independent efficacy replications. summary: This reproducibility package accompanies the study “Grain-Scale Radiation Transport and the Robustness of Radiolytic H₂–Sulfate Imbalance in the Revell Crystalline-Rock System.” The study evaluates how radiation-specific grain-scale transport modifies radiolytic H₂ and sulfate production estimates in the low-porosity Revell crystalline-rock system and tests the robustness of the inferred H₂–sulfate production imbalance. The package contains processed and derived data, analysis and transport-model code, computational notebooks, source data for the main figures, frozen manuscript-level results, and reproducibility metadata. Grain-scale α- and β-radiation transport is evaluated over a grain-diameter sensitivity domain of 0.06–2000 μm, while γ transport and post-interface energy partitioning are treated through explicit sensitivity bounds. The package supports reproduction and audit of the numerical results and figures reported in the associated manuscript. Third-party source datasets are not redistributed as original research data in this archive. Their provenance, persistent identifiers, and access information are documented so that the computational workflow can be traced to the original sources. Research-generated data, figures, and documentation are released under CC BY 4.0, while original research code in the package is released under the MIT License.
title: Grain-Scale Radiation Transport and the Robustness of Radiolytic H₂–Sulfate Imbalance in the Revell Crystalline-Rock System

summary: Benchmark data and trained interatomic potentials accompanying Learning nonlocal residuals in interatomic potentials with Fourier neural operators , by Wei Chen and Gian-Marco Rignanese. The files are organized into five benchmarks: homogeneous Yukawa interactions, heterogeneous screening, liquid water, LLZO, and Au2/MgO(001). Each benchmark archive contains its datasets and exact splits, final checkpoints and required local backbones, training recipes, generation or preparation scripts, and evaluation provenance. A shared archive supplies inference code, loading instructions, model indices, and checksums. The collection contains 422 result entries referencing 376 distinct checkpoints: 274 primary entries, 115 appendix entries, ten molecular-dynamics model entries, and 23 diagnostic entries. The heterogeneous benchmark includes the 40-set remote-medium probe. The homogeneous benchmark includes thirty production molecular-dynamics trajectories totaling 12 ns and 24,030 saved frames. Training recipes use YAML for MACE, LES, and FNO, JSON for CACE and CACE-SOG, and the published shell command for the upstream Au2/MgO MACE1 model. Download the shared archive and the desired benchmark archives, then extract them in the same directory. See README.md and the per-benchmark license notices.
title: Benchmark datasets, trained models, and molecular-dynamics trajectories for MACE–FNO

summary: This record accompanies the two-dimensional supplement to A gauge-invariant measure for lattice chiral fermions by Nathaniel Craig. It contains the supplement and its LaTeX source, together with the curated core reproducibility package, supplied in 65 standard tar.gz core archives and a separate evidence addendum. The supplement studies a two-dimensional chiral SU(5) theory with three conjugate-5 left-handed fermions, one 10 right-handed fermion, and five right-handed singlets. It presents an analytic measure construction on a specified admissible domain and numerical tests of selected currents, gauge responses, and determinant phases. The core archive contains all 74 scientific evidence references cited in the supplement, scientific implementations, the complete free-gap ledger, and the saved inputs needed for three principal scalar replays. It retains reports on other calculations and their limitations, but does not contain every raw matrix or intermediate record for those calculations. Extract all 65 archives into one directory to recover the complete core and run the documented checks. The remainder of the additional-data collection and the superseded full calculation archive are not included. The supported replays check saved evidence and recompute final scalar arithmetic; they do not rerun every historical current integration or matrix calculation. A separate gap replay checks the covering and residual bounds using implementation code shared with the producer. The README, result index, completeness record, manifests, and verification receipts specify the procedures and limits. These two-dimensional checks support, but do not prove, the four-dimensional result. The evidence addendum supplies 123 further scientific files referenced by the reports, including exact error ledgers, control results, fields, plots, and compact input records. Extract it alongside the 65 core archives and follow the updated README. Its verifier checks the added-file hashes and selected exact saved arithmetic for the finite-amplitude two-step curl and direct B1 endpoint comparison. It does not rerun the original matrix calculations or establish the analytic remainder estimate. License scope: Apache-2.0 for project-authored code; CC BY 4.0 for project-generated data and written documentation. Existing third-party licenses and notices remain in force. See LICENSES.txt.

summary: This dataset is a consolidated, machine-readable record of tick-borne encephalitis (TBE) in Poland from 1998 to 2024, assembled from official publicly-available surveillance products and used as the analytic base for an accompanying surveillance article in preparation for Eurosurveillance. For each of Poland's 16 voivodeships (NUTS-2 administrative regions) and for the country as a whole, the dataset contains: annual notified TBE case counts; quarterly breakdown of cases by onset (Q1–Q4); annual incidence per 100,000 inhabitants; hospitalised case counts and percentages; and annual TBE vaccination registrations, stratified by age (0–19, 20+, total). Case data are drawn from the National Institute of Public Health–National Institute of Hygiene (NIZP-PZH) biweekly bulletin Meldunki epidemiologiczne; vaccination data from the NIZP-PZH annual report Szczepienia ochronne w Polsce; population denominators from the Central Statistical Office of Poland (GUS). Vaccination figures count persons completing the primary three-dose cycle or receiving a booster, not total doses. Released under CC BY 4.0. See README for full column dictionary, scope, and known limitations. An accompanying Python script reproduces the four manuscript figures directly from this dataset. Version 2.0 accompanies the revised manuscript (October 2026): adds the ECDC Atlas extract, administrative boundary file, revision analyses (including negative binomial models with estimated dispersion) and scripts generating Figures 1–5. See CHANGES_v2.0.md.
title: Tick-borne encephalitis in Poland, 1998–2024: master surveillance dataset

summary: This dataset provides computational supplements, source code, finite-state component data, and independently checkable BFACF certificates for Makoto Ozawa, "Merge Trees of Length-Filtered Lattice Knot Spaces" (arXiv:2605.25322). The data concern self-avoiding polygons in the simple cubic lattice under standard BFACF moves and a lattice-length filtration. The earlier release documents the complete minimal-layer merge trees of $4_1$ (four components at length 30 merging at length 32) and $6_3$ (twelve components at length 40, two at length 42, and one at length 44). It also documents selected nonminimal trefoil components born at length 26; these selected births are not claimed to exhaust the full filtered graph. The frozen-unknot construction consists of a 64-edge Hamiltonian lattice unknot with no length-preserving or length-decreasing BFACF moves. An independently verified sequence of 25,436 BFACF moves reduces it to the elementary square with peak length 66. A two-edge block-splicing construction gives frozen unknots of length $64m$ for every integer $m\ge1$. New in the 19 October 2026 update: A minimal 24-edge trefoil is spliced to the 64-edge frozen unknot to produce an explicit 88-edge trefoil admitting no length-nonincreasing BFACF moves. The additional files supply the lattice direction words and coordinates, connected-sum construction, local-move verifier, and sampled checks for $m=1,2,3,4,8,16$. Repeating the frozen unknot block before the final trefoil splice gives frozen trefoils of length $64m+24$ for every $m\ge1$; reflection gives both chiralities. The results imply infinitely many nonminimal strong local-minimum births for the unknot and for both trefoil chiralities, within the standard BFACF filtration. The exact merge height 66 is established only for the 64-edge unknot. For longer frozen unknots and trefoils the proofs give lower bounds $H(P_m,U)\ge64m+2$ and $H(R_m,Q)\ge64m+26$, respectively; no exact merge heights or unbounded minimax excess are claimed. The construction is discrete and does not establish a positive barrier in continuous ropelength-filtered knot spaces or a universal result for arbitrary knot types. The archive retains earlier datasets and provenance information. Reproducibility instructions identify which outputs come from complete finite enumeration, certified BFACF paths, protected-port constructions, or limited computational checks.

summary: Algorithmic systems increasingly allocate tasks, rank performance, flag anomalies, and recommend decisions that affect employment conditions. This critical integrative review examines how algorithmic management may reshape employee voice and perceptions of procedural justice in AI-assisted organizations. It distinguishes automated recommendations from fully automated decisions, information disclosure from effective contestability, and worker participation from symbolic consultation. Established research on algorithmic control, organizational justice, algorithmic transparency, and human-AI decision structures provides the conceptual basis. The article develops an accountability chain linking data provenance, decision rights, reviewability, employee explanation, correction pathways, and evaluation of organizational outcomes. It argues that the mere presence of a human reviewer does not demonstrate meaningful oversight; review authority, adequate information, and the ability to change an outcome are separate requirements. Potential benefits of automation include consistency and early detection of harmful errors, while risks include opaque sanctions, strategic data manipulation, and the displacement of responsibility. No primary interviews, experimental observations, or quantitative effect estimates are reported. The proposed empirical agenda combines process tracing, employee surveys, decision-log audits, scenario-based experiments, and organizational comparisons. The framework can be supported only if its specified safeguards improve measurable fairness, accuracy, employee trust, and organizational performance beyond existing governance practices. algorithmic management; employee voice; procedural justice; AI governance; human oversight; organizational accountability
title: Algorithmic Management, Employee Voice, and Procedural Justice: A Governance Framework for Accountable AI-Assisted Organizations

summary: We study the discrete Shannon entropy of histograms of tangent-growth rates obtained from parameter sweeps, operationally termed Shannon Parameter-Space Entropy (SPSE). The aim is to summarize rate-bin occupancy and interpret contrasts between slices under a common sampling measure, valid support, and partition. The chain rule separates the contribution of the above-threshold fraction from within-class contributions, including a correction for bins that straddle the threshold. In the Duffing oscillator and the Hénon map, pairs selected in exploratory analyses, with similar above-threshold fractions, display differences of +0.7342 and -0.5516 bits in the reference protocols. In Duffing, the change in the below-threshold sector dominates; in Hénon, entropy decreases on common support while rate variance increases. Controls for finite time, transient duration, integration step, initial condition, grid, partition, and subsampling delimit the stability of these contrasts. The global Duffing increase loses robustness in the λ̂/b representation; coarse partitions can reverse the Hénon contrast. The tested refinements do not stabilize the maximum heights of local entropy-difference quotients, which are not established as physical susceptibilities. The logistic map provides a supplementary example. The contribution is a reproducible protocol for distributional summarization and decomposition: SPSE condenses histogram information and complements the above-threshold fraction and moments. The evidence is descriptive and does not establish the prevalence of these contrasts beyond the examined ensembles.
title: Shannon entropy in parameter space: decomposition and sensitivity of Lyapunov-rate distributions

summary: INTEGRATED PHOTONIC MICROROBOTIC SYSTEMS AT THE LIMIT FLAGSHIP 16 / 30 | STARLI RESEARCH INSTITUTE XXIV This prospective research monograph investigates whether silicon-photonic light distribution, optofluidic packaging, independent metrology, and feedback positioning can be integrated into a compact research station that reliably captures, transports, releases, and recovers microscopic proxy agents. Its central hypothesis is system-level rather than decorative: reducing external optics is a meaningful advance only when delivered optical power, fluid transport, sample heating, task outcomes, and failure responses remain independently observable and reproducible across fabricated chip and package lots. The study develops a five-layer research architecture encompassing packaged optical and fluidic paths; a physically bounded optical-power and thermal ledger; external tracking capable of challenging on-chip estimates; reversible multi-agent tasks under staged fault injection; and repair, requalification, cost, and cross-laboratory transfer. It separates electromagnetic optical force from thermal convection, surface adhesion, Brownian motion, and sensor-induced artefacts. Strong comparators include calibrated free-space optical tweezers and spatial-light-modulator trapping configurations at matched specimen exposure and operational throughput. The book contains 30 mathematics-linked derivational routes, 82 chapters with 410 independently paginated research sections, 200 detailed future Research Gates, and 33 provisional Phoenix Answer Embryos. A companion Excel atlas links each research chapter, quantitative candidate, test protocol, falsifier and external DOI evidence record. Publisher-identified publications on integrated optical phased arrays, silicon-photonic trapping, and photonics packaging inform the research boundary but are not treated as proof that the integrated microrobotic platform proposed here has already been demonstrated. The primary design principle is independent reproducibility: a controller should never be allowed to certify its own sensor output, ignore lost agents, or authorize a restart after a failed optical-power or thermal ledger. Negative studies, matched classical successes, and failed module integrations are retained as useful successor research evidence. This work offers testable possibilities for future investigation; it is not a claim of experimentally demonstrated autonomous nanorobots, and it has not undergone external peer review.

summary: Emergency-stop circuits built by engineering technology students are routinely treated as safe once they pass a functional test at commissioning, yet the relay contact welding that dominates their failure modes is invisible to such tests and accumulates silently across the workshop's operating life. The framework represents a student-built circuit as a series safety function whose integrity is degraded by contact welding, and derives the conditions under which a welded contact converts a demanded stop into an undetected loss of safety function. A replication-based evaluation of the before-after-control-impact estimator was conducted under a declared variance structure with a between-cluster standard deviation of 6.0, a residual standard deviation of 4.5 and an intraclass correlation of 0.64, across 2000 replications per design cell for cluster counts of 8, 16, 24 and 32 and effect sizes of 3, 5 and 8 percentage points. The evaluation indicates that 54 clusters are required to detect a 5-percentage-point effect at 80% power, and that the minimum detectable effect at 80% power falls as the number of clusters rises. The framework proposes that workshop safety assurance should shift from commissioning-time functional testing to integrity monitoring that is sensitive to contact welding, and the design analysis implies that cluster-level evaluations of such interventions require cluster counts well above those typical of single-institution studies.

title: Functional-Safety-Integrity Degradation of Student-Built Emergency-Stop Circuits in Engineering Technology Education Workshops: A Fault-Injection Evaluation Linking Relay Contact Welding to Operator Injury-Risk Exposure

summary: Oscilloscope probe compensation kits circulate between teaching laboratories, yet the calibration status of a kit is rarely transferred with the same rigour as the instrument it serves. the present analysis treats cross-course calibration transfer as a metrological problem and evaluates, by round-robin design, how bandwidth attenuation in a probe kit propagates into measurement discrepancy bounds when the kit is moved between courses. The evaluation is a replication-based characterisation of the before-after-control-impact estimator under a declared variance structure (between-cluster SD = 6.0, residual SD = 4.5, intraclass correlation = 0.64), with power estimated across 2000 design cells at cluster counts of 8, 16, 24 and 32 and effect sizes of 3, 5 and 8 percentage points.54 clusters are required to detect a 5-percentage-point effect at 80% power, and that the minimum detectable effect falls steeply as cluster count rises from 8 to 32. A first-order attenuation model links probe bandwidth to the fractional amplitude error at the test frequency, and the round-robin design is shown to bound the transfer discrepancy that a receiving course can expect. The contribution is a design-level calibration-transfer protocol that makes the discrepancy bound explicit before a kit leaves its home course, rather than after a student records a suspect waveform.
tags: probe compensation; calibration transfer; round-robin evaluation; bandwidth attenuation; measurement discrepancy; engineering education; before-after-control-impact
title: Cross-Course Calibration Transfer of Oscilloscope Probe Compensation Kits in Engineering Education: A Round-Robin Evaluation Linking Bandwidth Attenuation to Measurement Discrepancy Bounds

summary: Registered protocol of a systematic review reported according to PRISMA 2020. Question: how much performance do deep-learning models for precision agriculture lose when evaluated outside their training distribution (another farm, season, region, sensor or cultivar) or deployed in real field conditions, and how is deployment evidence (latency, energy, memory, field-trial duration) reported? Status at registration: searches completed on 15-16 October 2026 (Scopus, Web of Science Core Collection, OpenAlex, SpringerLink, plus citation searching); 14,174 records after deduplication; title/abstract screening not started. The protocol defines the research questions, search strategy, eligibility criteria (IN.1-IN.6, EX.1-EX.8), dual-reviewer active-learning screening with ASReview LAB and a pre-registered stopping rule (SAFE-based), the data-extraction codebook, the quality-appraisal rubric and the synthesis plan (internal-to-external relative performance loss).   Version 1.1 adds Amendment 1 (18 October 2026, before any screening decision): AI-assisted title/abstract screening with human verification.
title: Protocol: From benchmark to field: a systematic review of external-validation and deployment evidence for deep learning in precision agriculture

summary: Deep Gaussian processes (DGPs) are flexible priors for compositional regression functions, but inference for intermediate layers faces questions. The basic obstruction is an adjacent-layer symmetry: applying an invertible transformation and its inverse to two adjacent layers leaves the composed regression map unchanged. Under explicit symmetry and prior-comparability conditions, we show that the posterior may not concentrate on any prescribed intermediate-layer representation, even when the composed regression function is estimable. We then introduce an augmented $ρ$-fractional posterior that reweights layer decompositions by a non-saturating identity-deviation penalty. The augmentation changes posterior odds between symmetry-related decompositions by an exponential penalty ratio. Under proper choices of the penalty and a prior mass condition, it preserves function-level fractional posterior contraction, while shrinking the redundant layers towards the identity mapping. Thus, the likelihood does not identify a unique ``true'' set of layers; the augmentation favors identity-biased parsimonious decompositions within an equivalence class of layers; uniqueness of a selected representative is not established.
title: Canonical Layer Inference for Deep Gaussian Processes via Symmetry-Breaking Augmentation

summary: Sea level fingerprints connect the spatial distribution of rapid ice mass change to sea surface height (SSH) change, but the spatial resolving power of this inverse problem remains poorly quantified. Here we provide the first systematic, scale-resolved quantification of Greenland Ice Sheet mass change structure recoverable from its SSH fingerprint when ice loss geometry varies. We develop a physics-informed neural operator, constrained by an accurate neural-operator emulator of the forward sea level equation, to probe the information content of this ill-conditioned inverse problem. Across synthetic ice change ensembles, broad ice loss patterns can be recovered, but distinct ice fields can produce nearly identical fingerprints, so fine-scale structure depends on the assumed a-priori ice change distribution. Inversion fidelity varies with the wavelength and amplitude of ice mass change. An empirical error law separates these effects and defines a scale-dependent accuracy ceiling. For a satellite-altimetry-derived reference field, the estimated fingerprint-only ceiling is $R^2\sim0.79$ under the present SSH observation geometry and matched-prior assumption. The leading three principal components explain 99.76% of fingerprint variance, yet higher-order components retain information needed to distinguish finer ice change structure. SSH observations near Greenland carry most information on ice loss locations. Applying the leading fingerprint principal components to the observed 1993--2019 SSH rate recovers the large-scale Greenland fingerprint, while the residual field is correlated with basin-scale bathymetry, consistent with unresolved sterodynamic variability. These results establish a quantitative empirical bound on fingerprint-only ice-loss resolving power and identify how independent observations and ice sheet constraints can improve inference.
title: Operators Reveal Scale-Dependent Limits on Recovering Greenland Ice Loss from Sea Level Fingerprints

summary: We present a comprehensive Sun-to-Earth analysis of the extreme space weather event of 18 -19 January 2026, hereafter the Martin Luther King (MLK) storm, which produced a severe (G4) geomagnetic storm and one of the most intense solar radiation storms of Solar Cycle 25. The geomagnetic disturbance was driven by a fast Earth-directed coronal mass ejection (CME) associated with an X1.9-class flare from NOAA Active Region 14341. We combine multi-viewpoint remote-sensing observations, in situ measurements from Solar Orbiter and Wind, and physics-based magnetohydrodynamic simulations using the CORHEL-CME framework to reconstruct the eruption from the low corona to 1 au and identify the mechanisms governing its geoeffectiveness. Observations and simulations indicate that the eruption originated from a right-handed magnetic flux rope embedded in a complex magnetic environment dominated by a neighboring positive-polarity coronal hole. The simulations reproduce the observed CME morphology, asymmetric expansion, magnetic fields measured at both spacecraft, and Dst index evolution. The main discrepancy is attributed to filament material not included in the model. Favorable magnetic polarity alignment between the CME and coronal-hole field minimized magnetic erosion through interchange reconnection, enabling rapid escape and preservation of the strong southward magnetic field that drove the geomagnetic storm. The prolonged recovery phase resulted from interaction between the trailing CME and a following high-speed stream from the same coronal hole. These results demonstrate that storm intensity was primarily established by the coronal magnetic configuration, whereas storm duration was controlled by the ambient solar wind.
title: Characterizing the Martin Luther King Event: Sun to Earth Evolution of the January 19, 2026 Geomagnetic Storm

summary: Bayesian geophysical inversion provides a probabilistic framework to estimate subsurface properties, in which uncertainties are represented by a so-called posterior probability density function (pdf). Estimating this pdf is computationally challenging when it is high dimensional or complex, particularly if it may be multimodal. We introduce Stein mixture variational inference (SMVI) for efficient Bayesian geophysical inversion with multimodal or complex posterior solutions. The method combines parametric variational inference with Stein variational gradient descent (SVGD). In SMVI, the posterior pdf is approximated by a mixture (sum) of distributions, in which component distributions are optimised jointly using the SVGD update rule. This construction combines computational efficiency with the flexibility to represent a range of plausible Earth models and allows components to be updated in parallel. Here, SMVI is first tested on two synthetic seismic inverse problems, demonstrating that SMVI can recover non-Gaussian, complex and multimodal posterior solutions accurately and efficiently. Then, we apply SMVI to real seismic data by performing Love wave tomography of the British Isles, and obtain inversion results that are consistent with previous Monte Carlo solutions. Around the East Irish Sea sedimentary basins, SMVI captures bimodal uncertainty associated with ambiguity in basin boundary locations, revealing alternative subsurface structures compatible with the observations. These results indicate that SMVI generalises various previous variational methods, and provides a practical and effective framework for quantifying complex uncertainties and supporting geological interpretation of seismic images.
title: Bayesian Geophysical Inversion using Stein Mixture Variational Inference for Multimodal or Complex Solutions

summary: Visual counterfactual explanations (VCEs) should alter a classifier's prediction while remaining realistic and preserving decision-irrelevant content. Image-space methods provide high-quality counterfactuals but are computationally costly, whereas latent-space methods are more efficient but often less faithful. We identify two sources responsible for this gap. First, latent generation recovers a natural sample from a perturbed representation, whereas classifier guidance pushes it toward a target class, so their update directions may oppose. Second, VAE reconstruction can alter regions that should remain unchanged. We introduce CLEAR, a latent Flow Matching framework for VCEs. CLEAR uses Flow Matching's explicit instantaneous velocity as a reference for the generative direction to decompose classifier guidance into cooperative and conflicting components. It preserves the cooperative component and adaptively attenuates only the conflicting one according to conflict strength. We further analyze conflict frequency and strength throughout generation to reveal how classifier guidance interacts with the generative process. CLEAR also dynamically identifies editable regions, constrains latent modifications, and directly preserves factual content outside them to reduce VAE-induced changes. Across five bidirectional tasks on two datasets, CLEAR retains latent-space efficiency while achieving counterfactual quality comparable to or better than strong image-space baselines, with a 2.5x speedup over the strongest baseline. Project page: https://yan-zen9.github.io/CLEAR/
title: CLEAR: Cooperative Latent Flow for Visual Counterfactual Explanations with Accurate Region Preservation

summary: Learning causal structure from data requires assumptions about mechanisms, noises, observation schemes, and interventions. Historically, causal discovery has relied primarily on conditional independence. This review focuses on modern causal discovery methods that exploit properties of distributions beyond conditional independence. Our organizing principle separates the source of identification from the statistical estimator and its computational implementation. This perspective connects conditional-independence methods with distributional asymmetries, conditional-moment restrictions, and variation across environments or individuals. We examine discovery under latent confounding and feedback, distinguishing causal information about observed variables from reconstruction of latent structure and emphasizing the additional semantics required by cyclic models. We also distinguish population identification, frequentist and Bayesian consistency, uncertainty quantification, and algorithmic guarantees. Throughout, examples show why the same observational distribution can support different conclusions under different model classes. We conclude with guidance for comparing methods at their identifiable targets and a research agenda for uncertainty, heterogeneous populations, non-scalar variables, and the intersection of discrete data, feedback, and hidden confounding.
title: Causal Discovery beyond Conditional Independence: Identifiability, Algorithms, and Statistical Inference for Directed Acyclic and Cyclic Graphs

summary: Recent one-step text-to-image (T2I) models enable efficient image synthesis, opening up new possibilities for interactive Web-based image editing. However, existing one-step editing methods often construct a global transport field through simple vector operations between conditional predictions. While such strong transport can effectively drive the image toward the target semantics, it may be released along unreliable directions or over non-edited regions, leading to structural distortions within the editing region and background drift elsewhere. More importantly, stabilizing the editing process through global smoothing or uniformly weakening the transport field often makes large semantic changes overly conservative. In this work, we revisit one-step image editing from the perspective of the tension between semantic strength and transport stability, and identify a key insight: strong semantic transport is not inherently unstable. What matters is whether it is applied along reliable directions and at reliable spatial locations. Motivated by this insight, we introduce PreciseEdit, a model-agnostic, training-free and inversion-free one-step editing framework that strengthens target-semantic alignment while preserving background fidelity and structural consistency. We further propose a dual-noise-scale role decomposition strategy: a higher-noise scale produces the strong target-directed transport used for actual editing, whereas a lower-noise scale jointly serves as a probe for directional agreement and spatial structure. Extensive experiments on PIE-Bench demonstrate that PreciseEdit achieves state-of-the-art performance and effectiveness on various editing tasks.
title: PreciseEdit: Strong Yet Stable Semantic Transport for One-Step Image Editing

summary: Monocular simultaneous localization and mapping (SLAM) remains challenging in dynamic environments. Real-time dynamic object identification in such environments is a critical problem. Recent approaches estimate per-pixel uncertainty from rendering residuals or multiview feature inconsistency to identify dynamic regions. These methods lack direct motion evidence, and their accuracy may degrade when reconstruction is inaccurate or features are ambiguous. In addition, such uncertainty merely downweights pixels in bundle adjustment (BA), so inaccurate uncertainty estimates can still impair camera pose estimation and 3D reconstruction. Accordingly, we present a monocular RGB SLAM system for dynamic scenes. Specifically, a motion uncertainty estimation method is proposed to derive uncertainty from the residual between optical flow and camera motion induced flow, directly reflecting object motion. The estimation varies with frame alignment accuracy, reducing false detections and yielding accurate pixel-level masks of dynamic regions. To make BA more robust, we estimate camera poses from high confidence pixels. These poses are then used to reproject dynamic pixels during joint refinement of poses and depth, reducing the influence of object motion on both pose and depth updates. Moreover, we provide a quantitative evaluation of dynamic masks and analyze how these masks affect the downstream tracking and reconstruction of dynamic objects. Our approach improves the mean dynamic mask IoU by 35\% over a state-of-the-art baseline on DAVIS, and reduces the average ATE by 59\% on Bonn and 19\% on TUM relative to the SLAM backbone used in our system. The source code will be made publicly available.
title: FLoTS-SLAM: Optical Flow-Derived Uncertainty for Monocular Dynamic SLAM with Two-Stage Optimization

summary: Resampling is the standard remedy for weight degeneracy in particle filters, but in high dimensions it distorts the spectrum of the ensemble covariance in a way that is computable from the importance weights. This paper studies the inverse problem: recovering the pre-resampling spectrum from the observed weights and the empirical spectrum alone, and using it without biasing the filter. We first show that the forward spectral law extends to random importance weights once one conditions on the weights together with the realized offspring counts, rather than on the weights alone. We then construct a regularized free-deconvolution estimator, prove its consistency with an explicit error budget at a fixed resolution scale, and certify model mismatch through a computable forward residual. The repaired spectrum enters the filter only as the preconditioner of a Metropolis-adjusted rejuvenation move, so that spectral error affects mixing efficiency but not the invariant target. For the full filtering cycle, we derive a geometrically summable error recursion under stable scalar dynamics and an explicit law for the cost of abstaining from repair. Pre-registered simulations show that the inversion reduces the spectral error by an order of magnitude, that the corrected preconditioner recovers about 90% of the oracle's sampling efficiency in an anisotropic regime, and that the cost of abstention depends on when abstentions occur rather than on how many. The repair recovers eigenvalue laws, not eigenvectors, and is certified only within an explicitly stated exogenous-weight regime.
title: Regularized free deconvolution for spectral repair of resampling distortion in high-dimensional particle filters

summary: High-dimensional Vlasov equations present promising use cases for quantum simulation, but their transport coefficients must be implemented coherently in order to preserve a compact quantum representation. We develop explicit Schrödingerised circuits for prescribed external field Vlasov dynamics without classical field updates. In 1D1V, velocity-dependent streaming is compiled directly from the encoded velocity register, while a non-linear cubic field is evaluated using reversible fixed-point arithmetic. For fixed polynomial degree, the field workspace scales linearly with the coordinate register width, while the field evaluation subroutine has polynomial depth. As a proof of concept, we simulate a minimal coupled 3D3V anharmonic Penning system and realise mixed electric-field terms and transverse magnetic coupling on a six-dimensional phase space in agreement with classical calculations. Resource analysis shows approximately linear growth with the number of time steps, while identifying the auxiliary register as the dominant depth bottleneck. Structured preparation and register recovery of the auxiliary state reveal an interplay between loading cost and readout. Together, our algorithm demonstrates a fully coherent quantum simulation of high-dimensional Vlasov dynamics with variable coefficients and identifies the practical resource costs that must be controlled for large-scale quantum implementation.
title: Quantum Circuits for Variable-Coefficient Vlasov Dynamics via Schrödingerisation

summary: Extracting generalized parton distributions (GPDs) from experimental observables, the convolution structures denoted as Compton form factors (CFFs), requires solving an intrinsic inverse problem. We presented results using NNGPD, a flexible regression method based on a physics-informed neural-network framework, for reconstructing GPDs using integral constraints -- including CFFs and Mellin moments -- and symmetry and endpoint constraints. The approach does not require pointwise training information on the underlying GPDs. Closure tests using pseudodata generated from a phenomenological model demonstrate the ability of the framework to reproduce the principal features of the underlying distributions across a range of kinematics. A Bayesian neural-network formulation is also introduced to address uncertainties associated with the reconstruction. Finally, we discussed a broader question in GPD phenomenology: whether the complete momentum-fraction dependence of GPDs is necessary to extract physical quantities such as partonic angular momentum. This motivates investigating approaches that infer Mellin moments directly from experimentally constrained CFFs, while quantifying the remaining ambiguities.
title: Neural Network Representation of Generalized Parton Distributions (NNGPD)

summary: Student-built micropositioning stages that use piezoelectric actuators are common in engineering education laboratories, yet their nanopositioning performance is routinely overstated because hysteresis in the actuator is neither characterised nor compensated. The treatment is methodological and theoretical: no observational data are reported. A Preisach-type hysteresis operator is combined with a capacitive-sensor noise model to derive closed-form expressions for the repeatability floor as a function of sweep amplitude, sensor resolution and compensation residual. First, the repeatability bound scales linearly with the uncompensated hysteresis fraction and inversely with the square root of the number of sweep segments, so that doubling sensor resolution yields only a factor-of-√2 improvement unless the compensation residual is simultaneously reduced. Second, a compensation-residual threshold exists below which further sensor refinement yields no repeatability gain; this threshold is derived explicitly. Third, the framework predicts that student-built stages operating without compensation cannot achieve sub-100 nm repeatability for sweep amplitudes above 20 V, a bound consistent with the educational literature. The contribution is a design-oriented evaluation protocol that allows instructors and students to predict repeatability limits before construction, and to allocate resources between actuator linearisation and sensor quality.

summary: This dataset contains numerical simulation results underlying Figures 3–11, Supplementary Figures S1–S6, and Supplementary Tables S1–S4 of the associated manuscript. The simulations examine sampling-induced concentration bias in suction-lysimeter measurements of PFOS, PFOA, and PFPeA in sandy loam and sandy clay. The archive includes baseline hydrologic and concentration series, equilibrium sampling results, displayed spatial fields, adsorption-kinetics scenarios, vacuum-operation comparisons, single- and dual-chamber water and concentration histories, cumulative PFOS mass-discharge estimates, supplementary flow diagnostics, and reported model parameters and sampling dates. The package contains eight Excel workbooks, one spatial CSV file, two daily atmospheric input CSV files with a text guide, a README, calculation notes, and file checksums. The input files are exact copies of the processed daily forcing used by the model for the long-term loading and one-year baseline/sampling simulations; their column definitions, units, uses and source attribution are documented in the meteorological-input folder. File-to-figure mappings, units, and calculation conventions are described in the included documentation. Figures 1 and 2 are conceptual and mesh illustrations and have no independent numerical result tables in this archive. Executable simulation and plotting code and full internal model output histories are not included. The archived numerical values support reconstruction of the reported data displays and recalculation of the reported comparisons; they are not a complete model-rerun package.
title: Numerical data for: Quantifying sampling-induced concentration bias in suction-lysimeter measurements of PFAS porewater concentration in the vadose zone

summary: This working paper consolidates the mathematical correspondences studied between selected string-theory models and the Phase framework of the Harmonic Physics research programme. It presents the central equations, reported evidence and outstanding physical questions, with detailed derivations, controls and computational records retained in companion reports and reproducibility packages. A compact phase field reproduces the momentum–winding contribution of the declared circle-compactified bosonic closed-string model and preserves that contribution under reciprocal exchange of radius, momentum and winding. A quadratic optical continuation retains a reciprocal canonical description and yields a dispersion relation containing quadratic and quartic wave-number terms. A retrospective comparison with released fluid-of-light measurements favors inclusion of the retained gradient within the scope of the processed experimental records. For a specified two-component continuum action with fixed component amplitudes, constant coefficients and equal propagation speeds, the relative phase obeys an exact sine-Gordon equation, while the common phase obeys a free wave equation. This conditional classical correspondence applies at finite relative-phase excursion and connects to the equation obtained through Pohlmeyer reduction of classical bosonic strings on R_t × S². The assumptions and remaining reconstruction questions are stated explicitly. A separate conditional gravity construction maps a fixed source coefficient into a supplied Schwarzschild exterior compatible with the leading string metric condition. The construction retains explicit assumptions about spatial geometry, dimensional calibration and vacuum dynamics. The master also discusses polarization-dependent apparent position and identifies a predictive relationship between foundational Phase, observer coupling and registered distance as a continuing research question. The paper distinguishes the established mathematical correspondences and bounded optical-model evidence from the proposed foundational interpretation of Phase. Physical identification, reconstruction of the evolved breather with the required global string conditions, and quantum equivalence are not established by the reported comparisons. Version and update policy This is a living research document, updated as further mathematical derivations, correspondences and reproducible tests are completed. Future substantive revisions will be released as new numbered Zenodo versions, accompanied by a dated summary of changes. Please cite the specific version consulted. Version 0.21 — 19 October 2026: Added the seven giant-magnon benchmarks and their amplitude–phase correspondences, distinguishing classical results from the narrower semiclassical result. Detailed methods, results and reproducibility materials are documented in the companion publication, Giant Magnon Amplitude and Phase Correspondences : https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23463422 . title: String Theory and Phase: Mathematical Correspondence and Current Interpretation

summary: This study examines shared behavioral patterns and context-specific differences in how undergraduates organize their studies, respond to difficulties, and pursue development opportunities. Online scenario responses from 264 undergraduates are analyzed with the individual as the unit of population inference. Person-weighted proportions, participant-level bootstrap intervals, paired rank tests, categorical transition tests, rank correlations, and robust regression connect overall activity allocation, item-level decisions, and changes across repeated trajectories. Coursework forms the center of proactive action, accounting for an average individual share of 48.36%, followed by progress on accepted commitments (14.24%) and English-language preparation (9.03%). The observed proportion of consecutive actions in the same category exceeds a fixed-composition random-order reference by 19.29 percentage points, with a 95.00% confidence interval of 18.08–20.49 points. This sustained emphasis on coursework coexists with stage-specific shifts in English preparation, task progress, application preparation, and recovery. Responses to difficulties vary markedly by context. Across comparable domains, direct problem solving accounts for 81.62% of responses to coursework problems and 45.81% of responses to practical problems. Communication and collaboration account for 36.84% of responses to practical problems but 6.10% of responses to coursework problems. Individual effort and coordinated action address different task requirements, revealing multiple forms of initiative. When prior experience is available for use, the actual-use rate is 7.55%, indicating that applying earlier experience to current problems requires explicit processes for retrieving and using it. Among accepted tasks, 93.11% receive subsequent action, and 42.42% of participants submit at least one application. Early behavioral allocation is jointly associated with application initiation (Wald statistic = 12.98, degrees of freedom = 6.00, p = 0.04). Overall rates of normatively appropriate choices exceed 95.00% in disciplinary, research, and English-language judgments, while the correct-response rate for the data-leakage item is 35.29%. Widespread recognition of sound principles coexists with difficulties in specific operational steps, providing a basis for targeted instruction. Across repeated trajectories, the mean number of applications increases by 6.21 (confidence interval: 3.19–9.51; adjusted p < 0.01), and the mean number of initiated interviews increases by 4.53 (confidence interval: 2.26–7.02; adjusted p < 0.01). The share of responses involving scaling back decreases by 3.18 percentage points between the first and final trajectories (adjusted p = 0.04), while the emphasis on coursework and the diversity of activities retain broadly similar structures. Support for undergraduate development should connect learning resources, task completion, preparation for opportunities, and the use of prior experience. Professional standards should be translated into specific information requirements and operational sequences so that guidance directly addresses the tasks undergraduates are handling. Keywords: undergraduates; online scenario responses; resource allocation; coping with difficulties; career choice
title: The Behavioral Structure of Undergraduates' Academic and Career Decisions: A Multilevel Analysis of Online Scenario Responses

summary: We study unitary \(S^1\)-manifolds with four isolated fixed points in relation to Kosniowski's conjectural inequality \(4χ(M)>\dim M\). For every integer \(m\ge3\), we show that there exists a unitary \(S^1\)-manifold \(M_m^{18}\) with exactly four isolated fixed points, and these manifolds are pairwise distinct and nonzero in ordinary complex bordism. Since \(χ(M_m^{18})=4\), they give an infinite family of counterexamples to \(4χ(M)>\dim M\). By gluing two blocks formed by \(G_2/SU(3)\cong S^6\) and the unit disk $D(V)$ of 12- dimensional real $S^1$-representation $V$ along their equivariantly identified free boundaries, we explicitly construct such a manifold $M^{18}_3$. We also prove that the four-point case is null-bordant in real dimension \(16\) and in every real dimension greater than \(18\); hence \(18\) is the smallest dimension in which such a counterexample occurs.
title: Unitary $S^1$-Manifolds with Four Fixed Points and Kosniowski's Conjecture

summary: Pretrained VLMs bring rich world knowledge and semantic priors to object-goal navigation, and fine-tuning a VLM into a navigation policy has become a common recipe. Despite this progress, success rates remain low, and it is unclear which capability these fine-tuned policies lack. Our diagnosis identifies goal grounding as the dominant failure. These policies explore well, yet often fail to notice that the goal is already in view or to estimate how far away it is. To address this failure, we ground the goal explicitly. Explicit grounding substantially improves success and reaches state-of-the-art results on six benchmarks across three scene collections. We also correct annotation defects in these benchmarks, so that future methods are evaluated more faithfully. Our analysis on the clean benchmarks shows that, with ground-truth grounding, our policy nearly matches the expert that generated its demonstrations, leaving the headroom in perception rather than policy learning. Our work points to goal grounding as a missing piece of object-goal navigation and offers a simple and effective solution to the task.
title: StopWatch: Goal Grounding for Object-goal Navigation

summary: Scientific discovery requires developing worthwhile hypotheses into practical investigations, yet learning from this evolving research process remains challenging. We introduce an operational definition of valuable and testable research hypotheses: evidence-grounded claims about consequential uncertainties, coupled with feasible investigations, explicit decision criteria, and alternative explanations. Our DiscoveryRSI framework develops hypothesis trees through multi-agent evolutionary search, compiles selected investigations into executable Harbor tasks, and recursively learns through three mechanisms: hypothesis credit optimization attributes scientific assessments to documented research contributions; harness replay identifies productive strategies and recurring failures to refine research workflows; and rediscovery applies accepted improvements to new investigations, generating further experience for subsequent learning. We also introduce DFM-Bench, which provides comprehensive assessment of hypothesis quality and cumulative research progress at the levels of hypotheses, revisions, development paths and research runs. Across four life-science domains, automated evaluation shows that hypothesis quality rises from 4.86 for the base model to 5.39 after two rounds of self-improvement, with the large gains in falsifiability and data resolvability. We further validate hypothesis quality through expert review, comparing our DiscoveryRSI-27B with other research agents. Preliminary human assessments show that DiscoveryRSI-27B scores higher than GPT-6 Luna on hypothesis importance and whether claims are plausible and evidence-bounded. DiscoveryRSI-27B achieved a 6.3% rate of hypothesis correspondence with research published after the model cutoff, largely outperform GPT-6 with 2.5% and Claude Opus 5 with 2.3%, while delivering greater human-rated improvement along research paths.
title: DiscoveryRSI: Recursively Learning to Discover Valuable Hypotheses

summary: Speculative decoding typically characterizes speedup by draft tokens accepted per verification round. Lossless verification preserves the target model's output distribution and thus expected completion length, making this metric a meaningful efficiency proxy. Relaxed (lossy) verification accepts tokens that lossless verification would reject, potentially altering that distribution. We identify a length inflation phenomenon: relaxed verification lengthens completions, primarily by extending reasoning traces, largely offsetting apparent gains in accepted tokens per round. We evaluate existing training-free relaxed verification rules on twelve target-drafter pairs against lossless verification on identical prompts, measuring completion length, verifier rounds, wall-clock time, and task accuracy. At each rule's most relaxed evaluated setting, relaxed verification on average accepts $1.34\times$ as many tokens per round but produces $1.54\times$ longer completions. For rules with higher acceptance lengths, tokens accepted only under relaxed verification tend to have low target-model probability, contributing to length inflation. For rules that reduce verifier rounds, accuracy typically drops substantially. Further analysis traces some failures to continued reasoning that exhausts the budget needed to deliver a final answer. Overall, accepted tokens per round alone is an unreliable measure of decoding speed under relaxed verification. Completion length and verifier rounds must also be reported to assess actual efficiency.
title: Acceptance Is Not Speed: Length Inflation in Training-Free Lossy Speculative Decoding

summary: Recent large audio language models (LALMs) have extended their capabilities beyond lexical speech understanding to tasks requiring paralinguistic and non-linguistic audio understanding, such as emotion recognition. However, these models still struggle to reliably utilize acoustic information, particularly when it co-occurs with spoken linguistic content. Existing benchmarks do not clearly distinguish acoustic perception from higher-level reasoning, making it difficult to identify the source of these failures. To address this issue, we introduce VocalGrad, a benchmark designed to evaluate LALMs' ability to perceive low-level acoustic variations. VocalGrad formulates this problem as a simple binary classification of temporal change direction, enabling evaluation largely independent of higher-level reasoning or semantic understanding. Our benchmark results reveal a substantial gap in acoustic perception between human annotators and state-of-the-art LALMs: while human annotators achieve high accuracy, LALMs perform at near-chance levels. We further conduct linear probing to identify structural bottlenecks in these models. Our analysis reveals two distinct failure modes: for some categories, task-relevant information is preserved in internal representations but not utilized by the language model head; for others, the information becomes progressively less linearly decodable across model layers. Overall, our results reveal substantial limitations of LALMs in modeling acoustic variation under controlled settings and expose representation differences not observable from text outputs.
title: VocalGrad: Evaluating Acoustic Perception in Audio Language Models

summary: Physical plausibility is essential for realistic video generation. Existing methods impose physical guidance before synthesis via simulations or refined prompts, but this can limit dynamic diversity, miss errors that emerge only after generation, and require repeated regeneration when inconsistencies remain. We therefore study a generate-diagnose-repair paradigm that preserves the original generation capability and selectively repairs physical inconsistencies afterward, raising two key questions: what to repair and how to repair? To address them, we introduce PhysRepair, an agentic video generation framework that combines causal reasoning over the observed physical failure with prior repair experience to enable localized and adaptive correction. Specifically, Spatiotemporal Causal Constraints identify the first invalid physical state and its causally affected states, producing a repair specification that guides physically plausible local regeneration while preserving unaffected content. Experience-augmented In-context Learning combines the ongoing repair context with relevant experience from previous repairs, allowing the agent to adapt its repair decisions across diverse physical failures and accumulate completed trajectories for future cases. Experiments on Physics-IQ Verified across solid mechanics, fluid dynamics, optics, thermodynamics, and magnetism demonstrate that PhysRepair consistently improves the physical plausibility of generated videos over existing methods. Our project page is available at https://xxkkxxx.github.io/PhysRepair-Website/.
title: Agentic Physics-Grounded Video Generation via Memory-Augmented In-Context Reasoning

summary: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) have significantly advanced instruction-driven perception through the "Embedding-as-Mask" paradigm. However, extending this capability to Remote Sensing (RS) reasoning segmentation remains exceptionally challenging under cluttered geographical contexts and extreme scale variations, often leading to Spatial Fidelity Degradation and Target Misidentification. We identify a critical yet underexplored bottleneck: the sequential alienation of the segmentation token [SEG] from its initial visual grounding within the autoregressive generation paradigm. Produced only at the end of long reasoning chains, [SEG] relies on visual evidence that has been progressively diluted by linguistic abstraction and autoregressive noise. This information decay is particularly catastrophic for RS targets with minuscule pixel footprints, where even marginal fidelity loss leads to localization failure. To address these bottlenecks, we propose GeoReason, a novel framework designed to fortify logical deduction and preserve spatial integrity. First, we introduce an Anticipatory Prior mechanism that injects the [SEG] token directly into the initial user query, shifting it from a terminal output to a primary condition. This paradigm shift transforms the token into a persistent spatial anchor, preventing information decay during long-form linguistic inference. Second, we enhance visual reasoning via a Location-aware Chain-of-Thought (CoT) that enforces coarse-to-fine localization using bounding boxes, coupled with a Latent Patch-to-Token Alignment (PTA) Loss that explicitly aligns the latent segmentation token with physical RS textures. Extensive experiments demonstrate that GeoReason consistently outperforms state-of-the-art methods on the Earthreason and RRSIS-D benchmarks. Code is available at https://github.com/Fanc0126/GeoReason.
title: GeoReason: Bridging Logical Reasoning and Spatial Fidelity in Remote Sensing Segmentation

summary: The High Resolution Imaging Science Experiment (HiRISE) onboard the Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter (MRO) acquires imagery of Mars at 25--30 cm/pixel, supporting studies of martian geology, climate history, and landing-site characterization. Its 14-detector focal plane assembly includes several overlapping detectors that enable the acquisition of three-channel colour-infrared images, which are important for identifying compositional variations and studying active surface processes. In 2023, a detector in the center of the focal plane assembly (RED4) began failing intermittently, creating a gap in acquired imagery and reducing the instrument's colour-imaging capability by half. The HiRISE processing pipeline provides a synthetic red (SYN4) channel obtained by linearly scaling the co-located infrared (IR10) channel. However, this approach cannot capture observed non-linear relationships between the colour channels, limiting its accuracy and applicability. Here, we present HiPredict, a machine-learning framework that reconstructs RED4 from co-located IR10 and blue-green (BG12) imagery, neighbouring red-channel observations, and acquisition metadata. The model employs a U-Net architecture to learn non-linear spatiotemporal-spectral relationships between these inputs and is trained on 81,717 training samples, representing 13,625 observations. Evaluated on 23,348 test samples, representing 3,892 pre-failure observations, HiPredict reconstructs RED4 with a Normalised Mean Absolute Error of 1.1%, substantially outperforming SYN4 (3.1%). The reconstructed products improve colour image recovery and more closely represent features of interest such as icy craters, stratigraphy exposed along ridge crests and chloride deposits. We release HiPredict as an open software tool. This work demonstrates the potential of machine learning to mitigate data loss as planetary missions age and naturally degrade.
title: HiPredict: Predicting the missing HiRISE RED4 spectral channel with machine learning

summary: EIP-1559 has become the dominant transaction fee mechanism in permissionless blockchains, regulating scarce block space through an adaptive base fee. The design balances a trade-off between responsiveness to demand fluctuations and stability of long-term resource usage. On a single chain, this trade-off is well understood and empirically stable. In multi-chain systems, however, cross-chain flows introduce delayed economic interactions across otherwise independent fee markets. These interactions alter the control dynamics and create stability risks that existing models do not capture. Deployed systems have already polarized.
