summary: annotations-orchestration is a Python library for configuring and running LLM annotation and evaluation experiments. It combines a resumable, manifest-driven scheduler with an optional terminal editor and a declarative annotation runner. Span metrics are computed by annotations-evaluate ; annotation clients, taggers, provider capabilities and hints come from annotations4all . Scope and architecture Base scheduler: experiment YAMLs and optional controller manifests define runs, defaults, execution settings and ordering. The default legacy runner uses a subprocess CLI contract and does not require an annotation library. Optional editor: the tui extra provides annotations-tui , a Textual editor for single-run and multi-run experiments and controllers. Editing, inspection and effective-run previews do not execute experiments. Optional standard runner: the annotate extra uses annotations4all>=0.3.1,<1 to annotate from a declarative annotation block without a custom consumer frontend. Metrics: this package adapts run records and writes reports; it does not implement metric counting. Run reports use the SemEval-compatible flat scenarios of annotations-evaluate ; that library also provides a nested standard report. Release notes 0.3.0 This release adds the editor, standard runner and provider-aware configuration layer to the 0.2 scheduler. Existing state files, PID locks, graceful shutdown, resume planning, manifest-key validation and the metric definitions remain supported. Manifest editor: structured forms, full YAML editing and effective-run previews share a common side-effect-free resolver with the CLI. New, duplicate, remove, reorder and Save As workflows preserve comments and quotes where supported. Saves show a diff and use atomic replacement with conflict detection; ambiguous YAML falls back to raw editing. Read-only mode and unsaved-change dialogs protect documents. Inheritance and responsive forms: Experiment → Defaults → Runs shows effective values and their origin without materializing inherited overrides. New runs stay empty. Legacy-header migration requires explicit diff confirmation. Run cards group model/prompting, annotation/input and connection settings. Provider/model configuration: a packaged catalog and startup-directory overlay provide presets and manual IDs. Explicit Refresh reads metadata only for the selected provider/key context. Capability evidence is field-specific and session-only; custom endpoints require trust confirmation before receiving a key. Credentials and display: the editor manages only the startup directory's .env , masks values and uses explicit atomic writes. Secrets do not enter manifests, settings or diffs. F9 controls NerdFont icons and persistent themes; --theme overrides the session and Ctrl+P opens the command palette. Reasoning and hints: reasoning and effort are separate inherited fields. Contradictory settings are rejected; live-reported effort choices constrain selection while incompatible stored values remain diagnostic. Contextual hints cite sources and change no settings. Declarative annotation: runner: standard supports configurable and per-label tagging with schema-validated label/description pairs, context, German or English prompts and message splitting. A no-inference preflight validates inputs and a fresh output destination. Input and gold semantics: the runner and directory inspector share non-mutating normalization for top-level Prodigy spans and ground_truth.prodigy/tags . Missing gold produces an annotation-only completion; explicitly empty gold remains evaluable. Conflicting gold representations are rejected before inference. Scheduling and pacing: ordinary remote runs share a configurable pool; self-hosted runs are sequential per host. The exact HU endpoint has a dedicated serial lane capped at 10 requests per minute, independent of scheduling mode. Other explicitly paced endpoints share endpoint-scoped state below the results directory. Request-level policy belo
title: annotations-orchestration

summary: Multi-agent approaches have been investigated recently as a means of improving the scalability of reinforcement learning for neural combinatorial optimization. Existing methods assume that all problem instance information is known upfront. However, real-world problems are often dynamic: relevant information is progressively revealed as the agents take actions (e.g., arriving at an edge in a routing problem only to discover it is untraversable). In such cases, existing methods fail to coordinate agents to explore and exploit the progressively revealed information. To address the arising coordination challenge, we introduce PACT (Plan-Augmented Coordination via Trace-graphs). PACT augments the environment graph with auxiliary nodes representing the plans of agents, which are connected to the resource nodes to indicate future dependencies. The proposed message-passing scheme over the augmented graph grounds inter-agent coordination in the environment and enables proactive, rather than reactive, conflict resolution. We show that PACT improves solution quality in dynamic problems relative to baselines and exhibits the best transfer to larger instances on which, remarkably, it outperforms centralized oracles with privileged access to instance uncertainty.
title: PACT: Plan-Augmented Coordination via Trace-Graphs for Dynamic Multi-Agent Combinatorial Optimization

summary: Developing coordination policies for complex multi-agent systems relies on either labor-intensive algorithm design or opaque task-specific reinforcement learning. With recent advances in autonomous coding agents, we show that policy search directly in code space offers a compelling third path that combines automated optimization with explicit interpretability. We investigate a human-directed workflow in which coding agents iteratively propose, implement, evaluate, diagnose, and eventually refine algorithms guided by simulation feedback and explicit correctness verification. We conducted two case studies and found that this workflow robustly outperformed any manually engineered solutions. On a challenging map in the 2024 League of Robot Runners competition, a two-day search discovered a policy that exceeds the stronger locally reproduced competition entry by 35.0% on the densest instance and generalizes to unseen map instances. In simulated real-world warehouses with irregular lanes, continuous robot geometry, and asynchronous motion, a week-long search discovered an entirely new class of multi-agent pathfinding algorithm that outperforms a calibrated proprietary solution in throughput by 58.9%. Under stated assumptions, we further prove that the new algorithm is collision-free and completes, in finite time, every accepted goal that is not withdrawn or replaced. Together, the studies show that policy search in code space powered by state-of-the-art coding agents offers a highly competitive path to building real engineering solutions that are both effective and analytically tractable.
title: Policy Search in Code Space for Multi-Agent Pathfinding

summary: Commit messages provide records of code changes and help developers understand and maintain software. To reduce the manual effort involved in writing them, commit message generation (CMG) approaches automatically generate commit messages that describe code changes in natural language. Existing CMG approaches generally treat CMG as a standalone task and optimize generated messages primarily for similarity to developer-written references. However, this objective may not properly reflect the practical usefulness of generated commit messages. This limitation matters in current AI-assisted software engineering workflows, where commit messages are used as shared information to serve different software engineering activities. To fill this gap, we propose TraceMsg, which uses issue-commit traceability, a representative software engineering activity, to guide commit message generation. TraceMsg is a collaborative multi-agent framework that coordinates message generation, traceability reasoning, and feedback-guided refinement, allowing generated messages to serve traceability while using reasoning feedback to guide issue-conditioned refinement. We evaluate TraceMsg on six open-source projects. The experimental results show that TraceMsg achieves an average Hit@1 of 0.893 and an MRR of 0.911, improving Hit@1 and MRR by 13.16% and 38.75%, respectively, over the best baseline for each metric.
title: Beyond Similarity-Based Generation: Guiding Commit Message Generation with Issue-Commit Traceability

summary: Recent test-time scaling methods improve model performance by increasing inference-time compute. One practical form of this is parallel scaling, where a model samples multiple independent reasoning streams and aggregates their answers using methods like voting, reranking, or verification. While effective, this approach leaves the streams uncoordinated, and a discovery made in one rollout cannot influence any other. Multi-Sequence Verifiers jointly score candidate answers after generation, but the reasoning streams remain independent during inference. ParScale takes a step toward model-internal parallel scaling by learning to aggregate multiple forward passes, but its streams still do not exchange information while processing a sequence. We introduce BatchParScale, an attention mechanism that allows parallel streams to exchange information through a small set of communication positions. We evaluate BatchParScale on a new Parallel Needle-in-a-Haystack retrieval benchmark and in pretraining, fine-tuning, and cooperative multi-agent reinforcement learning. Across these settings, BatchParScale outperforms ParScale on language-model loss and remains competitive on coordination-sensitive MARL tasks. Masked pretraining runs beat an unmasked single-sequence baseline despite local sequence corruption, and LoRA fine-tuning shows the mechanism can be added to a pretrained Transformer. At the same time, fact retrieval performance for pretrained and finetuned BatchParScale models remains unclear.
title: BatchParScale: Sparse Batch-Mixing for Sequence Models

summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly used to refactor source files, but file-local evaluations do not reveal changes to contracts, dependencies, or caller assumptions affecting repository adoption. To address this gap, we conduct 1,500 generation attempts across 150 production files from 15 open-source Java repositories, five LLM configurations, and two dependency-aware generation conditions: single-prompt refactoring and LangGraph-based multi-agent refactoring. Of these attempts, 1,455 yield complete candidates eligible for analysis. We evaluate these candidates using local changes, repository-facing structural indicators, detected caller impact, the behavioural-equivalence indicator, and available test evidence, and categorize them as Low-risk, Review-needed, High Contract/Dependency Risk, or Inconclusive. The results show that 1,365 candidates (93.8%) are classified as High Contract/Dependency Risk, whereas 106 (7.3%) have at least one detected broken downstream caller and 290 (19.9%) have a false behavioural-equivalence indicator; only eight satisfy the Low-risk criteria. Within the reason-covered subset, the High-risk rate decreases under more conservative dependency-delta thresholds, while 60 of the 65 candidates with conclusive targeted-test outcomes pass, including 50 classified as High risk. Paired analyses of 705 complete pairs identify no statistically significant generation-condition difference in the principal risk indicators, although model configurations differ in specific detected risk channels. These findings suggest that practitioners should treat LLM-generated refactorings as candidates requiring staged repository-level verification, while future research should validate screening and extraction precision and strengthen compilation, behavioural, and coordinated multi-file verification.
title: When LLM-Generated Refactorings Ripple: An Empirical Study of Repository Adoption Readiness

summary: Multi-agent scientific discovery with large language models raises a coupled learning problem: research assignments determine both which experiments are pursued and the experiences from which agents adapt. We introduce MELD, a unified hierarchical test-time training framework that jointly adapts a team-level Coordinator policy and agent-level individual Scientist policies within a single discovery process. The Coordinator generates a joint portfolio of search branches and research directives over a shared derivation tree, while Scientists develop hypotheses and execution plans implemented by a shared frozen Executor. Both levels receive alternating GRPO-style parameter updates under a shared smooth best-of-budget objective, allowing team organization and individual research behavior to co-evolve in a recursive self-improvement loop. Our analysis establishes objective alignment for the hierarchy, characterizes conditions for coordination gains over independent parallel discovery and the first-order benefit of private adaptation, and derives a finite-budget regret bound for adapted models. On 22 MLGym and MLE-bench tasks, MELD is best on 20 of them and achieves the highest aggregate normalized scores on MLGym, using a 4B backbone for coordination and research. Most baselines use proprietary Scientists, and all systems share one frozen Executor.
title: MELD: Recursive Self-Improvement via Hierarchical Coordination for Multi-Agent Scientific Discovery

summary: AI agents are growing more capable and persistent, and are being deployed in ever larger numbers. As more start collaborating, AI control measures must remain effective when they covertly collude on a harmful objective. We introduce MiniLab, a synthetic series of live services and codebases (5 interconnected services, 249 benign tasks, 8 attack objectives), adapted from internal AI deployment infrastructure. We demonstrate distributed attacks, in which different agents carry out separate attack fragments, and how their covertness evades frontier monitors when reading their trajectories individually. We show how distributed attacks spread across diverse contexts and harmful objectives through 16 human-optimized attacks (weight exfiltration, unmonitored rogue deployment, permission elevation, and more). A frontier monitor, GPT-5.6 Sol, reading each agent separately flags only 7% of successful distributed attacks, compared with 87% when a single agent carries out the same side task. Individual attacks can also be composed into longer attack sequences toward a greater loss-of-control outcome, without any individual agent being flagged. Finally, we tested whether models can plan these covert attacks: even with execution and monitor feedback, the best model-planned attacks succeed covertly against a single-trajectory GPT-5.6 Sol monitor in at most 25% of executions, compared with 80% for human-crafted plans, though this may scale with model capabilities. By turning worst-case coordinated attacks into reproducible red-team cases, our work provides a foundation for preventing locally benign agent actions from accumulating into system-level loss of control.
title: Red-Teaming Multi-Agent Attacks for Loss-of-Control Risks

summary: As automated research is increasingly adopted for writing papers, automated review has become a critical link between paper generation and quality control. However, existing methods largely rely on single-model feedback or simple review aggregation, failing to explicitly model expert responsibilities or collective deliberation in actual peer reviews, which limits effective cross-examination and reliable decision-making. Therefore, we formulate paper review as a computational modeling problem of peer review mechanisms and propose RoundtableReview, a deliberative multi-agent framework for enhancing automated research. RoundtableReview structures each paper into eight semantic slots and coordinates six academic and industry reviewers with complementary perspectives, retrieval sources, and specialized responsibilities. Through independent assessment, cross-examination, roundtable deliberation, dynamically weighted voting, and chair synthesis, the framework generates evidence-based and traceable feedback. Experiments on two automated research backbones show that the method improves paper quality in both backbones and outperforms baselines in automatic and human evaluations with fewer comments.
title: Discuss More, Comment Less: Boosting Automated Research via Multi-Perspective Collaborative Review

summary: Evaluating an agent's planning ability remains challenging for open-domain tasks, where verifying procedures through execution is often impractical. Existing evaluations typically assess only the final plan and do not distinguish procedural errors such as missing, incorrect, or misordered actions. We introduce STEPBENCH, a benchmark of 6,885 verified procedures crawled from wikiHow across 81 open-domain categories. From each procedure, we derive 5 diagnostic tasks: four with deterministic answers involving withheld, incorrect, or shuffled steps, and one requiring next-step generation. We additionally evaluate full-plan generation to examine how diagnostic performance correlates with end-to-end plan validity. Using the same procedures across tasks lets us directly compare different planning capabilities. For generation, STEPEVAL identifies critical failures that prevent goal completion. Across 14 configurations of 12 models, we find substantial differences across planning capabilities, with step ordering proving the most difficult: the strongest model correctly orders only 63.0% of procedures, dropping to 33.1% for those with nine or more steps. Incorrect-step detection also predicts judged plan validity across models, suggesting a lower-cost alternative for evaluating generation quality. On STEPBENCH-Val, comprising 214 procedures published in 2026, comprehension scores and rankings remain stable, suggesting limited influence from memorisation.
title: StepBench: Diagnosing Real-World Procedural Understanding in AI Agents

summary: Code, job scripts and derived results supporting a study of operational water level forecasting for flood monitoring in Lamphun, northern Thailand. Five compact single-hidden-layer neural networks forecast hourly stage 6 to 18 hours ahead at three gauges (P.5, P.87, P.85), each paired with an upstream gauge. The record contains the open-source NumPy (Levenberg–Marquardt) ANN on which all retrospective results are based, evaluated on 65 leave-one-flood-year-out blocks (configurations from an earlier MATLAB experiment published separately); benchmarks against persistence, a linear model given the same inputs, XGBoost, and long short-term memory (LSTM) and GRU networks with a sensitivity analysis; leakage checks (predictor selection by LASSO repeated inside every block, whole-year early stopping, an antecedent-rainfall candidate pool); Diebold–Mariano tests, a datum-independent Kling–Gupta efficiency, threshold exceedance scores, skill by flow state, upstream travel time and a scan for frozen gauge records; and the reference code and a 76-day evaluation (2 August–17 October 2026) of the deployed hourly forecasting and alerting service. Summary results for every table and figure are included, with a synthetic example dataset that demonstrates the input format and evaluation code. The hourly water levels and daily rainfall were obtained from the Royal Irrigation Department (RID), Thailand, and are not included because redistribution permission has not been confirmed; with those data, the retrospective analyses can be re-run from the scripts provided. The record supports a manuscript and does not constitute validation of an autonomous flood-warning system.   Supports the manuscript submitted to *Natural Hazards*: *Selecting hourly water-level forecasting models for flood warning in small-to-medium basins of Thailand: benchmarks, leakage control and operational verification*. Every retrospective result is based on the open-source Python ANN (P.87 with 5 hidden units), with leakage checks and a 76-day operational record. - New analysis code: `python_main_evaluation.py`, `model_comparison.py` (all methods on the hours common to every method; Table 2, Fig. 3), `gbm_benchmark.py` (XGBoost), `infold_selection.py` (in-fold LASSO; base, causal-wavelet and rainfall pools; Table 3), `rain_daily_parse.py` (daily-rainfall parser; rainfall not included), `export_travel_time_data.py` and `export_travel_time_py.py` (Fig. 5 values), `rain_delta_rmse.py` (per-year rainfall effect), `gbm_tuned.py` and `gbm_tuned_eval.py` (nested-tuned XGBoost), `swrm_additions.py` (90% prediction intervals, P.87 one-unit check, P.85 bias and stage relation), `code/ann/python/ann_rerun.py` (5 hidden units for P.87; whole-year early stopping). - GRU: `lstm_benchmark.py` updated (`--cell gru`) and `hpc/slurm/gru_erawan.sbatch` added. - New results: `python_main_evaluation.json`, `model_comparison.json` and per-year CSVs, `gbm_runs.json`, `gru_benchmark.json`, `infold_selected_*.json`, `rain_delta_rmse_per_year.csv`, `gbm_tuned_runs.json`, `gbm_tuned_eval.json`, `swrm_additions.json`, `operational_evaluation_20261017.json` (window to 17 October 2026), per-year metrics of the ANN reruns. - `figures/`: the eight figures of the Natural Hazards manuscript (Fig1–Fig8); earlier figures remain in versions 1.0.0 and 1.1.0. - Removed: the MATLAB reference scripts with their registry builder and MATLAB-vs-Python comparison files (published separately by T. Chaipimonplin; `registry.json` is kept), and all figure-drawing scripts (the record ships the final figures only). - Environment: scikit-learn 1.7.1, xgboost 3.4.1, scipy 1.16.1 added.
title: Lamphun Flood Forecasting: Analysis Code and Evaluation Results

summary: GO3 New Release Notes This release introduces major enhancements to GAF 2.2 annotation parsing, native annotation filtering in Rust, transparent .gz support, bidirectional gene–term queries, expanded ontology graph traversal, pairwise GO term similarity/distance matrices, semantic redundancy reduction & clustering, and built-in Gene Ontology Enrichment Analysis (ORA). ────── What's New 1. Native GAF Annotation Filtering (load_gaf_terms) Filter annotations directly during Rust-level GAF parsing with zero Python overhead: • evidence_codes: Keep only annotations matching specific evidence codes (e.g., ["EXP", "IDA", "IPI", "IMP", "IGI", "IEP"]), or use only_experimental=True as a shortcut. • exclude_evidence_codes: Exclude specific evidence codes (e.g., ["IEA", "ND"]). • ignore_not=True: Automatically discard negative annotations (NOT qualifiers such as NOT|located_in). • aspects: Restrict loaded annotations to specific GO aspects (["P"], ["F"], ["C"] or "BP", "MF", "CC"). • taxons: Filter by NCBI taxon IDs (["taxon:9606"] or ["9606"]). • assigned_by: Keep only annotations curated by specific databases (e.g., ["UniProt", "MGI"]). 2. Full 17-Column GAF 2.2 Inspection (parse_gaf & GAFAnnotation) • Added go3.parse_gaf(path, ...) returning GAFAnnotation objects with all 17 GAF 2.2 columns (db, db_object_id, db_object_symbol, qualifier, go_id, db_reference, evidence_code, with_from, aspect, db_object_name, db_object_synonym, db_object_type, taxon, date, assigned_by, annotation_extension, gene_product_form_id). • Supports the exact same native filtering arguments as load_gaf_terms, plus to_dict() for seamless DataFrame conversion (pd.DataFrame([a.to_dict() for a in records])). 3. Transparent .gz Compressed File Support • load_obo, load_gaf_terms, and parse_gaf now transparently read .obo.gz and .gaf.gz files on the fly without requiring prior decompression on disk. 4. Bidirectional Gene–Term Lookup API Inspect the loaded GAF index directly from Python: • go3.list_genes(). List all loaded gene symbols. • go3.get_terms_for_gene(gene, ontology=None). Retrieve GO term IDs annotated to a gene (optionally filtered by ontology aspect). • go3.get_genes_for_term(go_id). Retrieve all genes directly annotated to a GO term. 5. Expanded Ontology Graph Traversal (GOTerm) • Added term.descendants (all transitive child terms) alongside term.ancestors. • Added term.relations (Dict[str, List[str]]) exposing typed ontology relationships (part_of, regulates, negatively_regulates, positively_regulates, etc.). • Added go3.list_terms(ontology=None) to list all non-obsolete GO term IDs, optionally filtered by ontology ("BP", "MF", "CC"). 6. Pairwise Term Similarity & Distance Matrices • go3.term_similarity_matrix(terms, similarity="lin"). Parallelized pairwise similarity matrix (N × N) for a list of GO terms. • go3.term_distance_matrix(terms, similarity="lin"). Normalized semantic distance matrix (1 - sim, with self-similarity normalized for unbounded metrics like "ic" / "resnik"), ready for scipy, scikit-learn, or umap. 7. Semantic Redundancy Reduction & GO Term Clustering • go3.reduce_redundant_terms(terms, threshold=0.7, similarity="lin", scores=None, prefer="ic"). REVIGO-style greedy semantic deduplication of GO term lists based on custom scores (e.g., -log₁₀(FDR)), Information Content ("ic"), or ontology depth ("depth"). • go3.cluster_go_terms(terms, threshold=0.7, similarity="lin"). Connected-components clustering of semantically related GO terms. 8. Native GO Enrichment Analysis (ORA) • go3.go_enrichment(...) & EnrichmentResult. High-performance Over-Representation Analysis computed in Rust with ontology ancestor propagation (true-path ru
title: Mellandd/GO3: v2.0.0

summary: engiNIR 1.0.0, the first public release. Install with uv add enginir or pip install enginir (Python 3.12 or newer). Documentation: https://enginir.readthedocs.io First public release. Workflow enginir.Project runs the project workflow in one call per step: add_dataset , add_target , Dataset.add_roi , fit and Model.predict , with datasets, ROIs, targets and models addressed by name. Calibrations, sample sets, signal domains, stored recipes and provenance are created automatically. One HDF5 project file (schema viewer-v3 ) holds datasets, calibrations, ROIs, reference values, preprocessing recipes, signal domains, sample sets, model runs and prediction runs, linked by stable ids. Desktop viewer enginir-viewer with the Explore, Model and Predict workspaces, built on the same Project rules. Library Readers for EVK EIFF, ENVI, HDF5, CSV/Excel, SPC, SPA and JCAMP-DX. Preprocessing: Savitzky-Golay smoothing and derivatives, SNV, MSC, EMSC, detrending and smoothing, as scikit-learn transformers and as validated PreprocessingRecipe s. Models: PLS and PCR for the project workflow; SIMCA, LDA, SVR, random forest and MLP as scikit-learn estimators. Validation: grouped cross-validation, Kennard-Stone, RMSEC/RMSECV/RMSEP, R², bias, RPD and RPIQ, leverage, Hotelling T² and Q outliers. Plots of spectra, predictions, scores, loadings, VIP and image maps. Guarantees Training and prediction convert and preprocess spectra with the same code; MSC and EMSC are fitted inside every cross-validation fold. Cross-validation groups by ROI, so pixels of one ROI never appear in both training and validation folds. Prediction is refused before it runs when the data cannot produce the model's signal (instrument format, number of bands, calibration, signal unit). Every object is validated when it is written and when a project is opened; stored objects cannot be overwritten with different content. Prediction streams through image files in bounded memory. Packaging Python 3.12 and newer; CI runs on 3.12, 3.13 and 3.14. Install from PyPI with uv add enginir or pip install enginir . Documentation on Read the Docs: https://enginir.readthedocs.io . Each GitHub release is archived on Zenodo and uploaded to PyPI by a workflow that checks that the tag matches the version and that CI passed for the commit. Notes for users of pre-1.0 versions Fitted estimators pickled with engiNIR before 1.0 cannot be loaded: their fitted state means something else (the PLS intercept, for example, applied to mean-centred spectra) and would give wrong predictions. Loading one raises an error; fit the model again. Pickles now record the engiNIR version. SNV divides by the sample standard deviation (n - 1), as defined by Barnes et al.; earlier versions used the population standard deviation, which scales SNV spectra by sqrt(n / (n - 1)) (0.2 % for 220 bands). Release candidates 1.0.0rc1 to 1.0.0rc3 were tagged but not published; 1.0.0rc4 was published as a pre-release. The library code is the same in all release candidates and in 1.0.0; they differ in tests, packaging and documentation only.
title: engiNIR: A universal engineering tool for near-infrared spectra and hyperspectral imaging

summary: Archival deposit accompanying A Controlled Audit of a Negative Result: Training Recipe, H.264 Compression Levels and a Frequency-Stream Deepfake Detector , under review at IEEE Access (revision 1). This is version v2.0.2 of the deposit; it goes with release v2.0.2 of the repository. This controlled, self-audited study tests one frequency-based design for compression-robust deepfake detection: CAFRL, which adds block-DCT and FFT-phase streams with compression-conditioned band attention, and an adversarial compression-invariance loss, to an EfficientNet-B0 face backbone. Five separate findings follow. (1) Under the registered rule, CAFRL as specified scored 3.66 AUC points below a backbone-matched EfficientNet-B0 at CRF 40 (paired, one seed). (2) After the audit found eight defects, the control's training recipe recovered 3.96 points for CAFRL's own components (post-audit pre-specified); in a one-seed ablation reverting changes singly, only the backbone learning rate gave an interval excluding zero. (3) At that recipe, these untuned frequency-stream implementations showed no detectable difference from the spatial controls at two feature widths (post-audit pre-specified), yet a standalone frequency head scored 85.27 test-split AUC points at CRF 40 at the selected checkpoints (exploratory). (4) Restoring the adversarial loss at that recipe made no detectable difference in a registered test (0.87 points, Holm-adjusted p = 0.084); the estimator stayed accurate at the selected checkpoints. (5) In registered three-seed tests, real H.264 training levels beat PSNR-matched JPEG versions of the same frames by 7.48 points at CRF 40 (averaged over CRF-40 exposure), and CRF-40-level data added 1.88 points averaged over codec; flat robustness was measured within the trained levels. CAFRL numbers use EMA weights. Evidence: FaceForensics++-family, GAN-era, single-pass H.264 compression. The repository — https://github.com/Capta1n-n9m0/cafrl-negative — holds the per-video model scores, the decision rules frozen before the runs they adjudicate, every run's configuration and validation curve, the evaluation and statistical harness, the face-crop and re-encode pipeline, the self-audit record with its defect ledger, and two claims maps that give the artifact and method for each reported value row by row. Its tagged tree (v2.0.2) is included here as cafrl-negative-v2.0.2.tar.gz . This version holds: cafrl-negative-v2.0.2.tar.gz — the repository at tag v2.0.2 (new). <run>.best.pt — 26 frozen model checkpoints (2.7 GB in all), one file per run: the best.pt (best mean validation AUC) of each run added in revision 1, with checkpoints-r1-manifest.json giving each one's run, architecture, arm, training protocol, augmentation policy, seed, selected epoch, selection metric and SHA-256 (carried unchanged from v2.0.1, first deposited in v2.0.0; no best_valloss.pt ). The v2.0.0 release notes call this payload checkpoints-r1.tar ; the deposit holds the same 26 checkpoints as separate files. checkpoints.tar — 37 frozen model checkpoints (6.0 GB), every best*.pt of the 27 v1.0.0 runs, with checkpoints-manifest.json (carried unchanged from v2.0.1, first deposited in v1.0.0). crop-coordinates.tar.zst — 48,294 per-video face-crop records: the frames selected, the bounding boxes, the five-point landmarks and the alignment settings. Given the source corpora, obtained under your own data-use agreement, these regenerate the exact crops the models were trained and evaluated on (carried unchanged from v2.0.1, first deposited in v1.0.0; this version adds no crop coordinates). SHA256SUMS (every file above, the carried ones included) and README-DEPOSIT.md . The v2.0.1 source tarball stays in the v2.0.1 record and is not part of this version. No dataset media is redistributed here or in the repository. FaceForensics++, DeepFakeDetection and Celeb-DF v2 are released by their authors under signed agreements that do not per

summary: Six independent 100 ns molecular dynamics trajectories of human acetylcholinesterase (PDB 4EY7) in complex with two ligands: donepezil, whose dual-site binding mode is established crystallographically in that structure, and N-(1-benzylpiperidin-4-yl)-2-phenyl-1H-benzimidazole-5-carboxamide (DAH-004). Three trajectories per ligand were generated from the same equilibrated structure under identical parameters, differing only in the initial velocity distribution. The deposit contains the production trajectories (water and ions removed, 200 ps sampling), the GROMACS run input files, twelve minimum-distance time series to Trp86 and Trp286 computed with gmx pairdist, the per-window contact occupancy table, and the scripts that generate the figures of the associated manuscript. Software: GROMACS 2026.0, AMBER99SB-ILDN, GAFF2 with AM1-BCC charges, TIP3P water. This version adds the excursion-kinetics analysis: Figure 4 and the script that generates it from the twelve minimum-distance time series.
title: Replica dependence of catalytic-site contact in acetylcholinesterase-ligand simulations: benchmark data

Holotype : China • ♂; Guangxi Zhuang Autonomous Region, Pingxiang, Shaoping forest farm; 22 ° 4 ' N, 106 ° 55 ' E; alt. 280 m; 1 Apr. 2013; X. F. Yang leg.; genitalia slide no. YWX 18110. Sorolopha specialis sp. nov. is very similar to S. ferruginosa and S. nanlingica in forewing pattern, but can be distinguished by the presence of blackish androconial scales on the lower surface of the hindwing in males. In male genitalia morphology, S. specialis sp. nov. resembles several congeners, including S. ferruginosa , S. nanlingica , S. baribaris , and S. viridis Sakagami, 2023. It differs from S. ferruginosa by the valva having a straight neck and a cucullus whose distal part is ~ 2 / 3 the length of the ventral prominence; in S. ferruginosa , the valva has a gently curved neck and a cucullus with distal part ~ 1 / 2 the length of the ventral prominence. Sorolopha specialis sp. nov. differs from S. nanlingica and S. baribaris in the male genitalia by the valva with a relatively long neck and a semi-rounded ventral prominence; in contrast, these two species have a valva with a short neck and a ventral prominence of the cucullus that gradually widens outward. Sorolopha specialis sp. nov. differs from S. viridis in that the distal part of the cucullus is uniform in width and ~ 2 × as wide as the neck of the valva; whereas in S. viridis , the distal part of the cucullus gradually narrows outward and is approximately equal in width to the neck of the valva. Description. Adult (Fig. 5). Forewing length 6.0– 7.5 mm. Head (Fig. 7): Frons creamy white. Vertex roughly scaled, pale brown suffused with green. Antenna extending to middle of forewing, brown. Labial palpus porrect, creamy white, suffused with pale grey and green laterally; median segment expanded, terminal segment relatively short, stout. Thorax : Collar brown suffused with green basally and pale brown apically. Tegula green basally and brown distally. Dorsum smooth, green suffused with brown, posterior crest indistinct. Hind leg pale brown, tibia and basal subsegment of tarsus with dense, blackish scales in males. Forewing subrectangular; costa nearly straight except for a slightly curved apex, termen slightly oblique; upperside grayish brown; basal seven pairs of costal strigulae green, distal two pairs white; inner margin of wing and area between fold and dorsum green, with tiny, dark brown spots along dorsum; markings indistinguishable, indicated by a few fragmented, ferruginous spots edged with indistinct, blackish lines on central area of wing; apical 1 / 3 of wing (from R 3 to tornus) with white ground color, bearing a narrow, crescent-shaped subapical mark extending from middle of R 4 to distal 2 / 5 of CuA 1 and from 1 / 3 length of M 1 to CuA 1 on termen, dark brown suffused with ferruginous, with inner side surrounded by brown, curving lines, and scattered, pale brown scales between crescent mark and apex; cilia pale brown, with a brown baseline; underside pale brown, except for grayish-white costal strigulae and a white area overlapped by hindwing. Hindwing upperside brown except for white area overlapped by forewing; cilia pale brown, with a brown baseline; underside pale brown, with an elongate-ovoid patch of dense, blackish androconial scales on lower angle of cell (Fig. 8). Abdomen : Terga 3–7 with tufts of long bristles on posterolateral margins in males. Male genitalia (Fig. 10): Tegumen narrow, subtriangular; uncus small and obtuse; socius slender, pendant, r

summary: Data and R code that reproduce the results of "Divergence Between Absolute Emissions Benchmarks and Output-Adjusted Assessments: Evidence from Korea" (manuscript version 7.7.1, submitted to Energy Economics).   A single command, Rscript reproduce.R, runs 14 analysis scripts (about 15 seconds on a 32-core computer) and lists the 146 numbers reported in the paper in the order in which they appear, each next to the value the package computes or provides. Of the 146 numbers, 121 are recomputed from the distributed data; the other 25 rest on site-level records, coding records of business reports, a page-by-page reading of overseas reports and licensed revenue data, which cannot be distributed, and are provided as computed.   The package requires only R with the jsonlite and ggplot2 packages (versions fixed in renv.lock). The random draws of the original computation are included as files; an included Python script (draws/make_draws.py, numpy) regenerates them byte for byte.   The package of 101 files contains truncated salted hash codes, log changes and ratios for the Korean firm pairs, the overseas pair files, the producer price indices and the boundary audit of the 80 firms in the multi-industry frame. It contains no firm names, business identifiers or levels of emissions, energy, output or revenue for Korean firms. See README.md for the folder layout, the fixed inputs and the results that are provided as computed.   Licences: code under MIT; data produced by the author under CC BY 4.0. Producer price indices and source data remain under their publishers' terms. The README inside the archive is labelled manuscript version 7.7; its data and code are identical to those of version 7.7.1.
tags: replication package; absolute emissions benchmarks; physical output; emissions intensity; R; Korea
title: Replication package for "Divergence Between Absolute Emissions Benchmarks and Output-Adjusted Assessments: Evidence from Korea"

summary: This dataset was produced by iGEM Team Al-Nahrain-IRAQ 2026 (AL-Nahrain University, Iraq) as a part of SYNOVA  project , which aim to  predict, optimize and  detect yeast activity . iGEM wiki : https://2026.igem.wiki/al-nahrain-iraq CONTENTS    Metadata.zip ethanol_yield.csv : Experimental metadata for 8 experiments: strain, genetic modification, target gene, growth medium, temperature, carbon source, time, pH and ethanol yield, manually extracted from published studies, with DOI and BioProject for each experiment. R64.csv : S. cerevisiae S288C reference gene annotation (assembly R64-1-1), exported from Ensembl BioMart (accessed August 2026). Columns: RefSeq DNA ID, Gene stable ID, gene description, chromosome, gene start/end (bp), strand (1 = forward, -1 = reverse), gene name, GC content (%), gene type and SGD ID. Empty cells indicate no identifier available in Ensembl. The Gene stable ID (e.g. YPL071C) links this table to the count and SNP files Gene_Expression_ counts.zip : 7 gene-level RNA-seq count files, used as input for differential expression analysis. RNA_ SNPs.zip : 7 SNP files called from the RNA-seq data, with SNP positions mapped to genes using the R64 annotation. DESeq2_Experimental_ model.zip : differential expression analyses for 2 models/comparisons using DESeq2. One model will be selected as the reference workflow for the project's AI component to analyse count data in the same way.   METHODS   RNA-seq / gene expression (Galaxy): FastQC (quality control) → Trimmomatic (adapter and quality trimming) → HISAT2 (alignment to S288C R64) → featureCounts (gene-level counts). DESeq2 differential expression analysis was run in Google Colab, using code written with AI assistance.  SNP analysis (Galaxy): FastQC → Trimmomatic → HISAT2 → MarkDuplicates → AddOrReplaceReadGroups → bcftools mpileup → bcftools call → bcftools filter → bcftools +setGT → bcftools query. SNP annotation: chromosome/position of each SNP → R64 gene annotation → corresponding gene.  CONTRIBUTIONS  H. R. Abdulateef performed all RNA-seq, SNP and DESeq2 analyses and curated the dataset. H. R .Abdulateef ,T. W. AL-FATAl  , T. N. Taher ,and A. N. Aliyamin collected the data from the literature.
title: AL-Nahrain-IRAQ: RNA-seq gene counts, SNPs and DESeq2 models of ethanol-producing Saccharomyces cerevisiae strains (SYNOVA)

summary: Premessa   Leonardo’s Score non è una ricerca isolata. È un pannello del trittico Leonardo’s Spatial Grammar, insieme a Leonardo’s Rulers e a Leonardo’s CAD: tre indagini nate separate, una sola grammatica metrico-modulare dello spazio. Quella utilizzata da Leonardo da Vinci per costruire i suoi spazi prospettici. Il corpus, depositato su Zenodo, contesta l’idea di una prospettiva albertiana a scacchiera applicata in modo uniforme. Dall’Annunciazione all’Adorazione fino al Cenacolo, Leonardo lascia nel quadro i moduli con cui ha misurato: bugne e mattonelle (geometria inserita), la maglia 4:3 (geometria svelata), i ritmi degli arazzi e dei cassettoni (geometria intonata).   Metodo La ricerca adotta un approccio di retroingegneria: parte da ciò che è visibile e misurabile nelle opere per ricostruire i principi metrici e modulari che ne organizzano lo spazio.   Ricerca: 10.5281/zenodo.20334160     Funzione dell’app L’app è uno strumento di supporto alla ricerca accademica: non la sostituisce, ma la integra, rendendone più accessibili e immediatamente comprensibili i risultati più significativi. È tuttora in fase di sviluppo e viene progressivamente aggiornata con l’avanzamento degli studi.   App: https://comet-zinc-crane-monarch.grok.me     Preface   Leonardo’s Score is not an isolated inquiry. It is one panel of the triptych Leonardo’s Spatial Grammar, with Leonardo’s Rulers and Leonardo’s CAD: three inquiries born apart, one metric-modular grammar of space. The grammar Leonardo da Vinci used to construct his perspectival spaces. The corpus, deposited on Zenodo, challenges the idea of an Albertian checkerboard perspective applied uniformly. From the Annunciation through the Adoration to the Last Supper, Leonardo leaves in the picture the modules he measured with: ashlars and tiles (inserted geometry), the 4:3 mesh (revealed geometry), the rhythms of the tapestries and coffers (tuned geometry). The method is reverse engineering, starting from what can be seen and measured. This app was developed to highlight the most significant findings of the research.         Method The research adopts a reverse-engineering approach: it begins with what is visible and measurable in the works to reconstruct the metric and modular principles that organize their space.   Research: 10.5281/zenodo.20334160   Purpose of the App The app is designed to support academic research: it does not replace it but complements it by making its most significant findings more accessible and easier to understand. It is still under development and is progressively updated as the research advances.   App: https://comet-zinc-crane-monarch.grok.me       Giancarlo De Leo 20 ottobre 2026

summary: CRA-SME is an open-source Python toolkit for research on evidence-based software release decisions under the EU Cyber Resilience Act (CRA, Regulation (EU) 2024/2847), with a focus on small and medium-sized enterprises. Its release-decision engine evaluates a bundle of build-bound evidence and returns PASS, REVIEW_REQUIRED or FAIL with machine-readable reasons. Missing, stale or tampered evidence never passes, and the tool never asserts legal conformity. Research modules replay historical releases using only the knowledge available on each release date, seed evidence faults, check inventory completeness and support blinded manual validation. Main components Release-decision engine (crasme-gate command and Python API). It has 65 reason codes and is fail-safe on missing, failed, invalid, stale or tampered evidence. Each decision is bound to the build by digest and validated against a JSON Schema. PASS means only “eligible for human conformity review”, and risk scores are never inputs to the gate. Evidence and inventory modules. These cover scan-status records, provenance manifests and traceability units. They include CycloneDX SBOM and lockfile parsers (npm, pnpm, yarn, Go, Cargo, pip, rebar3) and ecosystem-aware version ordering. They evaluate OSV affected ranges and filter the CISA KEV catalogue as of a given date, and apply inventory-completeness rules. Research instruments. These are a time-correct release replay with fail-safe data fetching, a seeded-fault suite of 69 evidence faults, and a validation kit with blinded rater sheets, Cohen’s κ and Wilson intervals. Supporting material. This includes a 46-row CRA obligation catalogue (legally unverified by design), a risk and evidence workbook, SHA-pinned GitHub Actions workflows, protocols for nine experiments (E1–E9), eight executed Jupyter notebooks and 285 tests. New in version 1.3.0 Results of the pre-registered E9 retrospective release replay (pre-registration: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23438234 ; registered run 39047161461). The replay covered 144 releases of 20 open-source IoT and network products (2024Q4–2026Q3). – No assessable release shipped a vulnerability that was already KEV-listed (0/119), whereas 58% shipped a version-matched high or critical vulnerability. – The fail-safe engine passed no release with an empty or invalid inventory, but it passed 19 of 20 releases whose inventories were present yet declared incomplete. Exploratory re-analyses: time to first observed absence with Kaplan–Meier bounds, and product-cluster confidence intervals. The post-hoc E9-G completeness-aware gating experiment. It passed none of 24 known-incomplete releases and reduced false passes on seeded faults from 80/130 to 12/130. Resilient OSV retrieval and fail-safe handling of unfetched records (deviations D1–D3, documented in experiments/e9_release_replay/REGISTRATION.md), the validation kit and reproducible figure scripts. Data status. The real data are the E1 pilot outputs and the E9 release sample, inventories and results. The E9 data cache and raw outputs are archived separately at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23441593 . All other example data are synthetic and labelled as such: the demo release bundle, the mutation suite and the synthetic replay cache. E9 findings are version matches, not confirmed exposures. The registered manual validation is in progress. Limits. These are research instruments only: not legal advice and not a conformity assessment. The open-source projects are used as proxies; no claim is made that they fall under the CRA. Licensing. The code is licensed under Apache-2.0. Documentation, templates, the obligation catalogue, workbooks and notebook text are licensed under CC BY 4.0 (see LICENSES/ and NOTICE). AI assistance. Parts of the code, documentation and protocols were developed with the assistance of an AI system (Claude, Anthropic). The authors reviewed all outputs and are responsible for

summary: This dataset accompanies the Perspective “Coupling, Not Mirroring: Complementarity and Credibility in Microphysiological System–Digital Twin Integration” (Bertani et al., NAM Journal, submitted 2026). It contains the evidence behind the article’s map of published integrations between microphysiological systems (MPS) and computational models. Forty-two studies were read in full text. Each was classified by the direction of information flow between experiment and model, using six regimes: R0 data extraction, R1 calibration only, R2 calibration and external projection, R3 model-guided design, R4 offline reciprocal cycle and R5 continuous closed loop. The rubric was fixed before the corpus was read. Every classification is supported by locators to the source article (section, page, figure). The script build/build.py regenerates Figure 2, Supplementary Table S1 and every count reported in the article from the records: 8 / 7 / 17 / 5 / 5 / 0 studies across the six regimes; 25 studies evaluate a model output against evidence not used to build the model; 6 project beyond the calibration conditions without evaluating that projection; 11 do neither. Contents: records/: one extraction record per study (Markdown with YAML frontmatter). Each record gives the classification, its provenance, a paraphrased summary and open questions. One further record covers an adjacent experimental system discussed in the article. skills/: the classification rubric (version 1.1), the nine documented readings that settle boundary cases, and the ratification protocol. build/: Python scripts (standard library only) that check consistency across records and build the outputs. out/: the evidence table, Table S1 rows, counts and Figure 2. search/: the Scopus query strings and a recall check against 25 reference studies. provenance/: DOI, Crossref metadata and licence for every classified article. No full text, PDF, figure or bulk extract of the classified articles is included. Verbatim quotations are kept only for articles that Crossref lists under a Creative Commons licence. For the 13 articles without an open licence they have been replaced by placeholders, and the locators are kept. The Scopus exports are not included. The extraction records were drafted by Claude models (Anthropic), one isolated run per article, under the rubric. They were then checked for consistency, and ratified or decided by the authors where flagged; the record shows who made each decision. Some documentation files are in Italian. Licence: CC BY 4.0 for data and documentation, MIT for the code in build/. Quoted passages remain under the licence of their source article.

summary: Wheeler proposed that acts of registration constitute classical reality through the formation of records. Taking the proposal literally requires a structure that turns what a finite observer can distinguish into persistent classical facts, and a condition that makes many local facts one spacetime. Such a structure is proposed on the observer's causal diamond. Quantum field theory and general relativity are unchanged. A record is a settled classical fact, formed when which-outcome information leaves the diamond. A central postulate is the record rule, which fills unrecorded content from the vacuum, conditioned on the existing records. Constitutive descent, the compatibility of nesting in time with gluing across space, is then proposed to join local records into one shared world. A framework is presented together with its consequences. First, gravity responds only to what has been recorded. Two masses that have been recorded, but whose positions remain in superposition, still attract, yet classically mediated gravity cannot entangle them, a prediction testable by tabletop experiments. Second, records are irreversible and only accumulate, and their accumulation carries an arrow, proposed here as the arrow of time. Third, the structure yields candidate values for quantities usually taken as inputs, including three generations, four spacetime dimensions (d = 4), the rate λ = 3/(16π²) at which recording resolution fails per logarithmic scale, the transfer g = 1/d and the Higgs bare quartic λ₀ = 1/8. Companion papers apply the same recording geometry to cosmological observables and to Standard Model mass ratios. No-go results show that local recording cannot fix absolute amplitudes or favour one allowed branch over another. Absolute scales must therefore be set by measured values, and amplitudes and branch selection are proposed to close through Wheeler's self-excited circuit, in which records fix the geometry that defines the observer. Shared reality is thus built from the records settled on each observer's causal diamond, joined by constitutive descent.
title: Constitutive descent from the observer's causal diamond

summary: The island of St. Vincent and the other Windward Islands in the southeastern Caribbean were chosen as a field site for the study of weak mountain wakes. By the authorsメ definition, a モweak wakeヤ forms when the potential vorticity generated by a mountain is not strong enough to advect itself into eddies; rather, it is simply advocated downstream by the ambient flow. GOES-8 and Landsat sunlit images unambiguously revealed that the mountainous Windward Islands have remarkably long straight wakes. The length of St. Vincentメs wake exceeds 300 km although its width is only 20 km. Near the islands, the wake structures reflect the details of the island topography. These wakes do not exhibit any obvious diurnal effect. Boat surveys in the lee of St. Vincent confirmed the existence of features seen in the images: the sharp wake boundary, the small valley-induced jet embedded in the near wake, and the absence of any reverse flow. Aircraft surveys gave evidence of descent over the island and showed that the wake air is relatively warm and dry. The length of the wake (L) agrees with the formula L = H/2CD (where H is the wake depth and CD is the surface drag coefficient), implying that the reacceleration of the wake air is caused by the ambient streamwise pressure gradient rather than by lateral entrainment of momentum or geostrophic adjustment. Two numerical models were used to simulate St. Vincentメs wake, a single-layer hydrostatic model and a 3D nonhydrostatic model. Both models indicated that air descent, acceleration, wave breaking, and weak potential vorticity generation occur over the island, causing a long straight wake. Deposited content: descriptive metadata only; underlying research data are not included.
title: The Wake of St. Vincent - FGDC XML metadata artifact

summary: This paper demonstrates an objective method of computing monthly mean 700-mb height anomalies (H) at 108 grid points in the Western Hemisphere for a 40-yr period as a function of concurrent anomalies of monthly mean sea level pressure (P), at the same 108 points used for H, and monthly mean surface air temperature (T) averaged over 112 areas in North America. The authors applied a forward stepwise program to derive linear multiple regression equations that explained 81% of the variance of H by means of only 3.5 variables, averaged over all months and grid points. The stability of these equations held up well on 6 yr of independent data in terms of explained variance, root-mean-square error, and the spatial anomaly correlation coefficient. Therefore, it seems feasible to reconstruct maps of H for the first half of the twentieth century as a function of data on P and T only. Deposited content: descriptive metadata only; underlying research data are not included.
title: Reconstruction of Monthly Mean 700-mb Heights from Surface Data by Reverse Specification - FGDC XML metadata artifact

summary: The studies and the guidelines built on them answer for groups. The decision is for one patient, and the gap between the two is bridged by the clinician’s intuition, which practice does not train and almost nobody measures. This note describes a short session that does both: a lecture, a demonstration, then real cases with immediate, sourced feedback and a private report. The examples are obstetric and from early breast cancer; the problem and the method are the same in every field of medicine, because every clinical decision is made for one patient from evidence about groups.
title: Deciding for one patient: training clinical intuition

summary: The NOAA/NASA Pathfinder Program SSM/I Level 3 EASE-Grid Brightness Temperatures will consist of three series produced on CD-ROM, one series each for the EASE-Grid Northern Hemisphere, Southern Hemisphere and Cylindrical (global) projections. Grids represent spatially interpolated data. The interpolation technique maximizes the radiometric integrity of original brightness temperature values, maintain high spatial and temporal precision, and involve no averaging of original swath data. Coverage is global and spans the Pathfinder SSM/I Benchmark period, from 1 August 1987 through 30 November 1988. Resolution is 25 km for all channels and 12.5 km for the 85 GHz channels. There are 18 brightness temperature files per day for a given projection (nine each for ascending and descending passes), and two (ascending and descending) corresponding time files. Data are contained in flat binary files, either one image per file consisting of two-dimensional 2-byte integer arrays of brightness temperatures in tenths of Kelvins, or in the case of time files, two-dimensional 1-byte integer arrays consisting of GMT in tenths of hours. Data are available as processing is completed, with completion of the data set projected for the end of 1995. Data are available via ftp, on CD-ROM and through the Internet. Contact NSIDC User Services for information. Deposited content: descriptive metadata only; underlying research data are not included.
title: Ease-Grid Brightness Temperatures - FGDC XML metadata artifact

summary: Welcome to WARP WARP (WDL Analysis Research Pipelines) repository is a collection of cloud-optimized pipelines for processing biological data from the Broad Institute Data Sciences Platform and collaborators. The contents of this repository are open source and released under the BSD 3-Clause license . Table of Contents WARP Overview Navigating WARP Using WARP WARP Versioning and Releasing Testing in WARP Feedback Acknowledgements WARP Overview WARP pipelines provide robust, standardized data analysis for the Broad Institute Genomics Platform and large consortia like the Human Cell Atlas and the BRAIN Initiative. You can count on WARP for rigorously scientifically validated, high scale, reproducible and open source pipelines. Our pipelines are written as "workflows" using the Workflow Description Language (WDL) and they process a broad spectrum of "omic" and array-related datasets (see the overview table below). | Pipeline Category | Data Types | | --- | --- | | Germline Variant Discovery | Genomes, Exomes | | Genotyping Arrays | Variant discovery, Chip validation, Joint array analysis | | Single-cell/nuclei Transcriptomics | Droplet based (10x Genomics), Smartseq2 | | Single-cell Epigenomics | Single nuclei ATAC-seq, Single nuclei MethylC-seq | | Joint Genotyping | Genomes, Exomes | | Somatic Alignment (beta) | Exomes | Try our pipelines in Terra , a platform for collaborative cloud analysis! Learn how in the Using WARP section. Navigating WARP All versioned and released pipelines are in one of the three pipelines subdirectories: broad (pipelines for the Broad Institute's Genomics Platform), cemba (pipelines for the BRAIN Initiative) or skylab (pipelines for the Human Cell Atlas Project). Each pipeline directory hosts a main workflow WDL that includes a pipeline version number and a corresponding changelog file. Workflows may call additional WDLs, referred to as tasks, that are located in the tasks directory. Pipelines that are in progress or have not yet been validated are in the beta-pipelines folder. Using WARP There are three ways to use WARP pipelines: 1. Download the workflow and run on a WDL-compatible execution engine WDL workflows run on multiple systems, including Cromwell , miniWDL , and dxWDL (see the openwdl documentation ). To run a pipeline's latest release, first navigate to WARP Releases , search for your pipeline's tag, and download the pipeline's assets (the WDL workflow, the JSON, and the ZIP with accompanying dependencies; see Optimus example below). You can also access a pipeline's release page by selecting the pipeline version number at the top of the pipeline's README. After downloading the pipeline's assets, launch the workflow following your execution engine's instructions. 2. Run the pipeline in Terra Several WARP pipelines are available in public workspaces on the Terra cloud platform. These workspaces include both the WDL workflow and downsampled data so that you can test the pipeline at low-cost. If you are new to Terra, you can get started by registering with your Google account and visiting Terra Support . After registration, search for WARP-related workspaces with the "warp-pipelines" tag. To test the pipeline, clone (make a copy of) the workspace following the instructions in this Terra Support guide . 3. Run or export the pipeline from Dockstore Dockstore is a GA4GH compliant open platform for sharing Docker-based tools like WDL workflows. You can find WARP pipelines in Dockstore and run them on the Dockstore platform or export them to other platforms (including Terra). To view all available pipelines, just search "warp" in the Dockstore search and browse the workflow list. See Dockstore documentation for details on launching the workflow. WARP Versioning and Releasing Pipelines in WARP are versioned semantically to support reproducibility in scientific analysis and provide clearer analysis provenance. Version numbers allow researchers to confirm their data has all been processed in a compati

summary: This repository provides the reproducibility package supporting the study “Self-Diagnosing Reliability of Neutron–Gamma Pulse-Shape Discrimination under Operational Drift.” The study experimentally evaluates a reliability framework for neutron–gamma pulse-shape discrimination (PSD) under controlled operational drift. Rather than proposing a new PSD observable or classifier, the framework distinguishes PSD separability, calibration validity, and decision reliability through controlled perturbation experiments, label-free waveform-health monitoring, identifiability assessment, conditional adaptive recalibration, verification, and fail-safe refusal when the available unlabeled evidence is insufficient to support trusted autonomous correction. The package contains the final analysis and figure-generation scripts, derived numerical tables, and six final manuscript figures. The analyses include independent reconstruction and validation of a frequency-domain classification index (FCI), controlled baseline, gain, additive-noise, timing, and clipping perturbations, label-free degradation diagnosis, identifiability-based recalibration, class-prior robustness testing, and an independent NE213A PSD-domain audit. The primary experimental CLYC–SiPM waveform data are publicly available from Zenodo record 8037239 (DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.8037239) . The independent NE213A experimental dataset is publicly available from Zenodo record 14305929 (DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.14305929) . Raw experimental data are not redistributed in this package. The NE213A dataset is used as an independent detector- and PSD-domain audit. Waveform-level drift and recovery are deliberately not claimed for NE213A because the acquisition-specific QDC quantities could not be reconstructed from the released waveforms with sufficient held-out fidelity. The repository includes documentation describing data provenance, analysis order, software dependencies, and the scope and limitations of the reproducibility workflow.
title: Reproducibility Package for Self-Diagnosing Reliability of Neutron–Gamma Pulse-Shape Discrimination under Operational Drift

summary: Wheeler proposed that acts of registration constitute classical reality through the formation of records. Taking the proposal literally requires a structure that turns what a finite observer can distinguish into persistent classical facts, and a condition that makes many local facts one spacetime. Such a structure is proposed on the observer's causal diamond. Quantum field theory and general relativity are unchanged. A record is a settled classical fact, formed when which-outcome information leaves the diamond. A central postulate is the record rule, which fills unrecorded content from the vacuum, conditioned on the existing records. Constitutive descent, the compatibility of nesting in time with gluing across space, is then proposed to join local records into one shared world. A framework is presented together with its consequences. First, gravity responds only to what has been recorded. Two masses that have been recorded, but whose positions remain in superposition, still attract, yet classically mediated gravity cannot entangle them, a prediction testable by tabletop experiments. Second, records are irreversible and only accumulate, and their accumulation carries an arrow, proposed here as the arrow of time. Third, the structure yields candidate values for quantities usually taken as inputs, including three generations, four spacetime dimensions (d = 4), the rate λ = 3/(16π²) at which recording resolution fails per logarithmic scale, the transfer g = 1/d and the Higgs bare quartic λ₀ = 1/8. Companion papers apply the same recording geometry to cosmological observables and to Standard Model mass ratios. No-go results show that local recording cannot fix absolute amplitudes or favour one allowed branch over another. Absolute scales must therefore be set by measured values, and amplitudes and branch selection are proposed to close through Wheeler's self-excited circuit, in which records fix the geometry that defines the observer. Shared reality is thus built from the records settled on each observer's causal diamond, joined by constitutive descent.
title: Constitutive descent from the observer's causal diamond

summary: On 25 April 1992, a magnitude-7.1 Ms earthquake occurred near Cape Mendocino, California, at the southern end of the Cascadia Subduction Zone. Seismological analyses suggest an almost pure dip-slip reverse fault, with subduction of the Gorda Plate beneath the North American Plate. Modeling and observations of crustal deformation due to this fault mechanism produces uplift of the ocean bottom in relatively shallow water just offshore. A tsunami was generated that was measured by the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration sea level gauges along the California, southern Oregon, and Hawaii coastlines and in the deep ocean in the Gulf of Alaska. Several records are characterized by two distinct packets of tsunami energy, the first representing propagation along a minimum time path traversing deep offshore water, the second an apparent edge wave mode trapped along the coast. The largest peak-to-trough amplitude of 1.1 m was recorded at Crescent City in the second packet, approximately 3-4 hours after arrival of the first tsunami wave. Observations of this tsunami will be discussed along with some numerical model results to explain the source area and propagation characteristics. [Reference: Gonz£lez, F.I., E.N. Bernard, and K. Satake. The Cape Mendocino tsunami, 25 April 1992. In Tsunami: Progress in Prediction, Disaster Prevention and Warning, Y. Tsuchiya and N. Shuto (eds.), Series of Advances in Natural and Technological Hazards Research, Kluwer Academic Publishers, 151-158 (1995).] Deposited content: descriptive metadata only; underlying research data are not included.
title: The Cape Mendocino Tsunami, 25 April 1992 - FGDC XML metadata artifact

summary: Seawater concentrations of dimethylsulfide (DMS) and atmospheric concentrations of DMS, sulfur dioxide, methanesulfonate (MSA), and non-sea-salt (nss) sulfate were measured over the eastern Pacific Ocean between 105° and 110°W from 20°N to 60°S during February and March 1989. Although the samples collected in the southern hemisphere appear to be of marine origin, no significant correlation was found between the latitudinal distributions of DMS, SO, MSA, and nss SO. However, an inverse correlation (r = 0.87) was found between atmospheric temperature and the MSA to nss SO molar ratio in submicrometer aerosol particles with a decrease in temperature corresponding to an increase in the molar ratio. Although this trend is consistent with laboratory results indicating the favored production of MSA at lower temperatures, it is contrary to southern hemisphere baseline station data. This suggests either a decrease in the supply of DMS relative to nonmarine sources of nss SO at the baseline stations in winter or additional mechanisms that affect the relative production of MSA and nss SO. Deposited content: descriptive metadata only; underlying research data are not included.
title: Variations in the Methanesulfonate to Sulfate Molar Ratio in Submicrometer Marine Aerosol Particles over the South Pacific Ocean - FGDC XML metadata artifact

summary: Acoustic extensometer instruments capable of making precise daily measurements of horizontal distance were deployed across the north rift zone of Axial Volcano in June 1996 and were in place when a submarine eruption began on Axialメs south rift zone in January 1998. The instruments recorded a gradual 9-cm extension over a 405-m baseline leading up to the eruption, and then an abrupt, 4-cm contraction at the time of the eruption. An elastic point-source deformation model shows that deflation of Axialメs summit can explain both the 4-cm distance decrease at the extensometer array and a 3.2-m subsidence measured by another instrument in the caldera, if the pressure source is located at a depth of 3.8 km below the center of the caldera. The 9-cm distance increase may represent pre-eruption spreading across the rift zone. Deposited content: descriptive metadata only; underlying research data are not included.
title: Evidence for Deformation Associated with the 1998 Eruption of Axial Volcano, Juan de Fuca Ridge, from Acoustic Extensometer Measurements - FGDC XML metadata artifact

summary: The fact that vigorous hydrothermal discharge occurs on ridge segments with a variety of spreading rates and morphological characteristics makes it difficult to discern the large-scale geological controls on the distribution of hydrothermal venting along the mid-ocean ridge. We undertook to simplify this problem by mapping the distribution of hydrothermally produced thermal and light attenuation anomalies along the crest of the Juan de Fuca Ridge, a medium-rate spreading center with segments of markedly differing morphology. Hydrothermal anomalies were detected by towing a high-precision conductivity-temperature-depth- transmissometer (CTDT) package in a sawtooth pattern through the lowermost 1000 m of the water column above each segment. These surveys, conducted between 1985 and 1989, have produced the first quantitative and continuous visualizations of hydrothermal plumes along a multisegment portion of the mid-ocean ridge. Hydrothermal discharge is strongest on those segments, or portions of segments, where the apparent magmatic budget is highest, as indicated by the degree of along-axis inflation and other morphological characteristics. This correspondence implies that magma is episodically delivered in small and spatially discontinuous bodies of melt rather than by the constant resupply of a steady state magma chamber. We propose that the probability of discharge occurring at any point on the mid-ocean ridge is proportional to the spreading rate. This probability, scaled by the observation that significant plumes presently emanate from ~20% of the Juan de Fuca Ridge, is expected to range from ~5% on the slowest-spreading ridge to ~50% on the fastest-spreading ridge. Deposited content: descriptive metadata only; underlying research data are not included.
title: Hydrothermal Venting and the Apparent Magmatic Budget of the Juan de Fuca Ridge - FGDC XML metadata artifact

summary: Tetrahedral head models of 100 Human Connectome Project (HCP) Young Adult subjects, built for finite-element simulation of transcranial magnetic stimulation, with a series of remeshed versions of one subject for mesh-convergence studies. The files are the data used by the cuNIBS manuscripts and benchmark suite. The subjects are the 100 HCP S1200 subjects selected by Berger et al. (2025). We segmented each subject's T1-weighted and T2-weighted scans, taken from the scans Berger et al. distribute, with SimNIBS 4.6 CHARM at default settings, without manual correction. The one non-default setting is --forceqform, which the HCP scans need because their qform and sform orientations disagree. The meshes have 3.94 to 5.53 million tetrahedra (median 4.79 million) and carry all nine CHARM tissue tags. Contents: subjects/<id>.h5: one head mesh per subject, with its EEG cap positions. The ID is the HCP subject ID. ladder/<id>_s<NNN>.h5: one subject remeshed at eight resolutions from 1.71 to 21.2 million tetrahedra. Every element length is scaled by NNN/100. Format: HDF5 files written by HeadMesh.save in cuNIBS, uncompressed. The tissue tags follow CHARM and are stored with the mesh. The meshes are derived from HCP data and carry no names or other identifying information beyond the HCP subject ID. Use is subject to the HCP Open Access Data Use Terms, in addition to the CC BY 4.0 license. Software: cuNIBS ( https://github.com/vcubiomag/cunibs ). The code release that reproduces the manuscripts' results is v0.5.0 (DOI to be added). Acknowledgement: Data were provided by the Human Connectome Project, WU-Minn Consortium (Principal Investigators: David Van Essen and Kamil Ugurbil; 1U54MH091657), funded by the 16 NIH Institutes and Centers that support the NIH Blueprint for Neuroscience Research, and by the McDonnell Center for Systems Neuroscience at Washington University. Those awards funded the acquisition of the data and not this work.
title: CHARM head models of 100 Human Connectome Project subjects with a mesh-resolution ladder, as HDF5 files for cuNIBS

summary: Adaptive Biohybrid Interfaces and Self Repairing Prostheses at the Limit English Publication Description STARLI Flagship 23   30 Physicalized Models   82 Chapters   200 Research Gates Adaptive Biohybrid Interfaces and Self Repairing Prostheses at the Limit is a high-density research monograph on whether prosthetic and implant interfaces can detect wear and tissue change, repair locally, and then independently re-prove mechanical, sensing, and biological function. The book separates surface closure, electrical signal return, and controller compensation from durable recovery. Every intervention may change material composition, residual stress, impedance, sensor calibration, debris production, and tissue exposure; repair therefore creates a new qualification event rather than restoring an assumed past state. Thirty physicalized models connect fracture and delamination, viscoelasticity, continuum damage, reaction-diffusion healing, reservoir depletion, dynamic covalent rebonding, tribocorrosion, wear debris, micromotion, residual stress, Bayesian remaining life, electrochemical impedance, conductive percolation, charge injection, neural-signal drift, recalibration, foreign-body dynamics, fibrosis transport, mechanoinflammation, tissue remodeling, osseointegration, biofilm risk, thermal safety, inverse defect localization, barrier-constrained control, material accountability, accelerated aging, repeated repair, and joint biohybrid requalification. Eighty-two chapters each open with a governing gold equation and develop five one-page research sections. Two hundred Research Gates challenge the system with hidden cracks, delamination, drift, debris, tissue shift, repeated repair, uncertain defect identity, and accelerated aging performed by an independent laboratory. The work is a preclinical research framework rather than a clinical repair procedure or deployment authorization. Unknown defects, unsafe heat or charge, rising immune burden, lost calibration ancestry, changing accelerated-aging mechanisms, and inadequate remaining life are noncompensable vetoes. Its Phoenix Answer Embryo, the Biohybrid Repair Passport, binds the defect, loading history, materials, repair authority and action, retrieved and shed matter, immune state, recalibration, aging evidence, remaining-life interval, and independent verdict into one auditable interface record.
