It includes the prompts collected analyzed from the DevGPT and GitHub repositories, and the prompts used in the controlled experiment. The excel file named "Prompt_Categorization" contains the full annotation of both the DevGPT dataset and the GitHub repository dataset, including all relevant metadata for each prompt/conversation. The markdown files contain conversation with Gemini 2.5 Pro and GPT 5 mini for two prompt techniques: zero-shot and few-shot, respectively.
title: Who Let the Prompt Out?

summary: This is a simulated photoacoustic data set based on the Monte Carlo Method using the simulation framework SIMPA. The simulations use a literature-based forearm model (see Appendix D of Schellenberg et al., Photoacoustics 28, 2022 ) and a digital twin of the MSOT Acuity Echo (iThera Medical). The generating script performs volume generation and optical forward simulation in 3D with MCX using 10⁸ photons and a spacing of 0.1 mm for 16 wavelengths (700 - 850nm in steps of 10nm). Acoustic simulations were performed on the central slice using k-Wave. Images were reconstructed with SIMPA’s delay-and-sum reconstruction algorithm (1540 m/s speed of sound, Tukey windowed bandpass filtering (0.1 - 8 MHz), and Hilbert transform envelope detection.  It comprises 1243 multispectral images in total, each of size 200 x 400 px containing these eight channels: oxygen saturation segmentation with classes: muscle, heavy water, blood vessel, epidermis, US gel, mediprene absorption coefficient scattering coefficient scattering anisotropy fluence initial pressure distribution delay-and-sum reconstruction
title: Simulated multispectral photoacoustic forearm dataset with reference initial pressure, segmentation, and vessel oxygenation maps

summary: Act No. 328/2025 Coll., on Research, Development, Innovation and Knowledge Transfer, represents the most significant recodification of the Czech RDI system in more than two decades. It replaces Act No. 130/2002 Coll., whose repeated amendments gradually reduced the clarity of the original framework and weakened its ability to respond to the changing needs of the research and innovation system. The Act constitutes a comprehensive reconstruction of the legal framework, complemented by Amending Act No. 329/2025 Coll. and implementing regulations. This article interprets the Act as a framework for a more investment-oriented governance of public support for RDI: in other words, as a basis for deciding how the state supports the creation, development and use of knowledge and innovation. Its key principle is the connection between excellence and impact. Excellent research is no longer treated as a value in itself, but as a precondition whose contribution must be demonstrable in terms of the country’s prosperity, security and international credibility. The Act therefore not only strengthens the capacity of research organisations to translate results into practice, but also opens space for instruments that may increase demand for knowledge, technologies and innovation. The text is not a legal commentary on the new legislation. Rather, it offers a sociological, historical and economic analysis that places the new legal framework within the broader context of the Czech RDI system. It is structured as a coherent arc: context – changes – implementation conditions – discussion – recommendations – conclusion.
title: Act No. 328/2025 Coll., on Research, Development, Innovation, and Knowledge Transfer: Recodification of the R&D&I legal framework in the Czech Republic

summary: Third-party pretrained checkpoints are now the default starting point for computer-vision disease detectors in digital agriculture, yet the poisoning rate at which a backdoor trigger survives fine-tuning on clean crop imagery has not been characterised as a design quantity. the present analysis treats the backdoor trigger as a property of the checkpoint supply chain rather than of the attacker, and asks what poisoning rate a defender must assume when the provenance of the pretrained weights is unknown. A formal model of trigger persistence is developed in which the backdoor is represented as a parameter-space displacement whose survival under gradient fine-tuning depends on the ratio of trigger-aligned to task-aligned curvature. From this model a persistence bound is derived, and the bound is then embedded in a before-after-control-impact design that treats the poisoned checkpoint as the intervention and the clean checkpoint as the control. Operating characteristics were evaluated across 2000 replications per design cell for cluster counts of 8, 16, 24 and 32 and effect sizes of 3, 5 and 8 percentage points, under a declared variance structure with between-cluster SD of 6.0, residual SD of 4.5 and intraclass correlation of 0.64. The design required 54 clusters to detect a 5 percentage-point difference at 80% power.
tags: backdoor triggers; poisoning rate; pretrained checkpoints; crop disease detection; before-after-control-impact; intraclass correlation; AI supply chain
title: Backdoor-Trigger Evaluation for Computer Agriculture Disease-Detection Models Under Third-Party Pretrained Checkpoints: An Artificial Intelligence Poisoning-Rate Audit

summary: Differentiable logic-gate networks (DLGNs) are attractive for irrigation controllers because their learned Boolean structure can be verified exhaustively, yet the safety case for deploying them under actuator-failure cascades has not been formalised. The work is a design-and-power analysis of a before-after-control-impact (BACI) evaluation protocol, not an observational study: no field data are used or claimed. Operating characteristics were characterised under a declared variance structure with between-cluster SD = 6.0, residual SD = 4.5 and intraclass correlation = 0.64, across 2000 replications per design cell for cluster counts of 8, 16, 24 and 32 and effect sizes of 3, 5 and 8 percentage points.52 clusters are required to detect a 5-percentage-point compliance effect at 80% power under this variance structure, and that the intraclass correlation of 0.64 dominates the design's sensitivity. A formal-safety audit of DLGN controllers is then specified as a finite-state reachability problem over the actuator-failure cascade, with water-rights compliance encoded as an invariant. The contribution is a benchmark protocol that couples a verifiable controller class to a statistically defensible evaluation design, and a demonstration that the evaluation design, not the controller, is the binding constraint on regulatory acceptance.
tags: differentiable logic-gate networks; irrigation controllers; actuator-failure cascades; water-rights compliance; formal-safety audit; before-after-control-impact; benchmarking evaluation
title: Benchmarking Evaluation of Differentiable Logic-Gate Networks for Computer Agriculture Irrigation Controllers Under Actuator-Failure Cascades: An Artificial Intelligence Formal-Safety Audit for Water-Rights Compliance

summary: Yield anomaly detectors in computer agriculture routinely attribute harvest shortfalls to a single dominant stressor, yet drought and pest outbreaks frequently co-occur and confound one another's signatures in remotely sensed and agronomic covariates. The framework is methodological and theoretical: it defines the attribution game, states the confounding conditions under which Shapley values are point-identified, and derives upper and lower bounds when concurrent drought and pest outbreak render the attribution non-identified. A worked illustration uses NASA POWER monthly reanalysis air temperature at 2 m for Accra, Ghana (5.6, -0.19) over 2000-2023, comprising 312 monthly observations with a mean of 26.521 C, a standard deviation of 1.24 C and a warming trend of 0.1622 C per decade, to show how a single covariate channel can be bounded before attribution is attempted. The contribution is a bound-based audit protocol that replaces point attribution with interval attribution and specifies the evidence required to narrow those intervals in operational detector pipelines.
tags: causal attribution; Shapley decomposition; yield anomaly detection; drought-pest confounding; computer agriculture; partial identification; benchmarking audit
title: Evaluation of Causal-Attribution Bounds for Computer Agriculture Yield Anomaly Detectors Under Concurrent Drought and Pest Outbreak Confounding: An Artificial Intelligence Shapley-Decomposition Audit

summary: Satellite-cloud gaps corrupt the reflectance time series on which computer-agriculture crop-yield estimators depend, and the resulting coverage error propagates into famine early-warning reliability. The framework is evaluated through a replication-based benchmark in which 600 data sets of N = 500 were drawn from a declared data-generating process (intercept 12.0, exposure 0.42, group -3.1, severity 1.35, error SD 4.2) and the ordinary least squares estimator was characterised under the stated process. The benchmark produced an estimated bias of -0.07173 for the intercept and 0.00147 for the exposure coefficient, with RMSE values of 0.89562 and 0.0157 respectively, and empirical coverage of the nominal 95% confidence intervals of 1.0 for both parameters. The coverage-error bound formalises the conditions under which CDA-supported estimators preserve nominal coverage and therefore early-warning reliability, and it identifies the augmentation regimes in which coverage degrades. The contribution is a benchmark protocol and a bound that make the reliability consequences of cloud-gap augmentation auditable rather than assumed.
tags: counterfactual data augmentation; crop-yield estimation; satellite-cloud gaps; coverage-error bound; famine early warning; benchmarking evaluation
title: Benchmarking Evaluation of Counterfactual Data Augmentation for Computer Agriculture Crop-Yield Estimators Under Satellite-Cloud Gaps: An Artificial Intelligence Coverage-Error Bound for Famine Early-Warning Reliability

summary: Artificial intelligence systems that rank farmers for agricultural input subsidies are increasingly evaluated by comparing enrolled cooperative members with non-members, a design that conflates programme effect with the self-selection of farmers into cooperatives. The design is characterised analytically and by replication: between-cluster standard deviation 6.0, residual standard deviation 4.5, intraclass correlation 0.64, with 2000 replications per design cell across 8, 16, 24 and 32 clusters and effects of 3, 5 and 8 percentage points. The bound identifies the conditions under which an audit can separate algorithmic misranking from enrollment-driven selection, and it specifies the cluster count at which the equity contrast becomes estimable. Fifty-four clusters are required for 80 per cent power at a 5 percentage point effect. The contribution is a design-level audit instrument rather than a new estimator: it tells evaluators what a targeting audit can and cannot attribute, and it converts an unverifiable causal claim into a bounded, reportable quantity.
tags: subsidy targeting; instrumental variable; equity audit; cooperative enrollment; before-after-control-impact; intraclass correlation; algorithmic fairness
title: Causal-Attribution Evaluation for Artificial Intelligence Agriculture Subsidy Targeting Under Endogenous Cooperative Enrollment: A Computer Instrumental-Variable Bound for Equity Audits

summary: Tensor-network compression promises to fit convolutional disease classifiers into the memory ceilings of field-deployable diagnostic devices, but the accuracy cost of compression is usually reported as a single post-hoc number rather than as a bounded retention guarantee. the present analysis treats compression as a design problem with an auditable operating characteristic: given a declared memory ceiling, what fraction of the uncompressed diagnostic accuracy survives, and with what uncertainty? We formalise tensor-train decomposition of convolutional kernels as a rank-constrained projection, derive a retention bound that links bond dimension, kernel spectrum and the resulting classification margin, and then characterise the operating characteristics of a benchmarking protocol that estimates retention under a declared variance structure. The protocol is a before-after-control-impact design with between-cluster SD 6.0, residual SD 4.5 and intraclass correlation 0.64, evaluated across 2000 replications per design cell at cluster counts of 8, 16, 24 and 32 and effect sizes of 3, 5 and 8 percentage points. Power reaches conventional levels only at 56 clusters for a 5-percentage-point retention effect, which exceeds every cluster count in the declared grid; the minimum detectable effect at 80% power therefore remains above the 5-percentage-point threshold throughout the grid. The contribution is a retention bound plus a power-calibrated audit protocol that tells practitioners when a compression benchmark is informative and when it is underpowered, and that reframes field diagnostic safety as a property of the evaluation design rather than of the compressor alone.
tags: tensor-train decomposition; model compression; plant disease classification; on-device inference; accuracy retention; benchmark power; diagnostic safety
title: Benchmarking Evaluation of Tensor-Network Compression for Computer Agriculture Disease Classifiers Under On-Device Memory Ceilings: An Artificial Intelligence Accuracy-Retention Audit for Field Diagnostic Safety

summary: Federated learning for crop-disease classification across heterogeneous farm clients is vulnerable to Byzantine participants who submit corrupted model updates, yet the aggregation literature reports robustness without a design-level account of how many adversarial clients a given federation can tolerate before diagnostic integrity collapses. The analysis treats the aggregation rule as a statistical estimator of the honest update direction and characterises the breakdown point of coordinate-wise median and trimmed-mean aggregation under a declared contamination model. A before-after-control-impact design is used to benchmark power across cluster counts of 8, 16, 24 and 32 and effect sizes of 3, 5 and 8 percentage points, with 2000 replications per design cell and an intraclass correlation of 0.640. The contamination bound predicts that coordinate-wise median aggregation tolerates up to 50% adversarial clients in the limit but loses diagnostic integrity at a threshold that depends on the between-cluster standard deviation of 6.0 and the residual standard deviation of 4.5. The benchmarking results indicate that 54 clusters are required to detect a 5 percentage point degradation at 80% power. The contribution is a formal contamination bound that links aggregation-rule choice to the minimum federation size needed to certify diagnostic integrity, together with a benchmarking protocol that makes that link auditable.
tags: federated learning; Byzantine robustness; crop disease classification; contamination bound; benchmarking evaluation; diagnostic integrity
title: Benchmarking Evaluation of Byzantine-Robust Federated Aggregation for Computer Agriculture Disease Classifiers Under Adversarial Client Participation: An Artificial Intelligence Contamination Bound for Diagnostic Integrity

summary: Flood-risk mapping for agricultural insurance in vegetated terrain depends on computed-aperture radar interferometric coherence, yet canopy decoherence attenuates the signal that classifiers must detect. the present analysis formalises the detection problem as a before-after-control-impact design and derives the operating characteristics of a coherence-based flood detector under a declared variance structure with intraclass correlation 0.64, between-cluster standard deviation 6.0 and residual standard deviation 4.5. Power was estimated across 2000 replications per design cell for cluster counts of 8, 16, 24 and 32 and effect sizes of 3, 5 and 8 percentage points. The design required 56 clusters to detect a 5 percentage-point effect at 80% power. The analysis characterises the detection-power bound that canopy decoherence imposes on payout-equity claims, showing that the cluster counts typical of agricultural insurance portfolios are insufficient to separate genuine flood signal from decoherence noise. The contribution is a benchmark-derived bound that links remote-sensing detection power to the actuarial fairness of index-based insurance payouts.
tags: SAR interferometry; coherence; flood-risk mapping; detection power; insurance equity; canopy decoherence; benchmarking
title: Benchmarking Evaluation of computed-Aperture Radar Interferometric Coherence for Computer Agriculture Flood-Risk Mapping Under Vegetation Canopy Decoherence: An Artificial Intelligence Detection-Power Bound for Insurance Payout Equity

summary: Edge pest detection in computer agriculture is constrained less by classifier accuracy than by the thermal power budget of the sensing node. Spiking neural networks (SNNs) promise order-of-magnitude energy reductions on neuromorphic hardware, but the field lacks a design-level account of how that promise translates into deployable detection performance when the thermal sensor itself is the dominant load. The framework formalises a thermal-power budget, defines an energy-normalised detection rate, and derives a power-accuracy frontier for leaky integrate-and-fire classifiers operating on low-resolution thermal frames. A replication-based evaluation of the before-after-control-impact estimator was conducted under a declared variance structure (between-cluster SD = 6.0, residual SD = 4.5, intraclass correlation = 0.64), with power estimated across 2000 design cells. The analysis indicates that 54 clusters are required to detect a 5-percentage-point effect at 80% power. The contribution is a reproducible audit protocol that makes the energy-accuracy trade-off explicit and falsifiable before field deployment, and that identifies the sensor duty cycle, not the network, as the binding constraint in most edge configurations.
tags: spiking neural networks; edge pest detection; thermal sensing; energy-accuracy trade-off; computer agriculture; benchmarking; field-deployment safety
title: Benchmarking Evaluation of Spiking Neural Networks for Computer Agriculture Edge Pest-Detection Under Thermal-Sensor Power Constraints: An Artificial Intelligence Energy-Accuracy Trade-off Audit for Field-Deployment Safety

summary: Vision-language foundation models adapted to weed identification in computer agriculture are typically evaluated by top-1 accuracy on held-out images, a metric that does not bound the agronomic consequence of a misclassification. The framework formalises the adaptation problem as risk minimisation over a hypothesis class of vision-language prompts, derives a PAC-Bayes bound that links few-shot sample size, prompt-space complexity and the divergence between source and target weed floras to an upper bound on the probability of herbicide misapplication, and specifies a benchmarking protocol that reports this bound alongside conventional accuracy. The bound is decomposed into a transfer term, a few-shot estimation term and a distribution-shift term, each of which corresponds to a distinct benchmarking condition that current evaluation practice omits. A worked instantiation for a four-class weed/non-weed decision problem shows how the bound responds to shot count, prompt complexity and shift magnitude, and identifies the shot count below which the bound exceeds a declared safety threshold. The contribution is a shift from accuracy benchmarking to risk-bounded benchmarking for safety-critical agricultural vision, with implications for how few-shot extension deployments should be evaluated before herbicide recommendations are issued.
tags: vision-language models; few-shot adaptation; weed identification; herbicide safety; generalization bounds; benchmarking; computer agriculture
title: Benchmarking Evaluation of Vision-Language Foundation Model Adaptation for Computer Agriculture Weed Identification Under Few-Shot Extension Conditions: An Artificial Intelligence Generalization Bound for Herbicide Misapplication Safety

summary: The lack of interoperable data standards among reference genome data-sharing platforms inhibits cross-platform analysis while increasing the risk of data provenance loss. Here, we describe the FAIR-bioHeaders Reference genome (FHR), a metadata standard guided by the principles of Findability, Accessibility, Interoperability, and Reuse (FAIR) in addition to the principles of Transparency, Responsibility, User focus, Sustainability, and Technology (TRUST). The objective of FHR is to provide an extensive set of data serialisation methods and minimum data field requirements while still maintaining extensibility, flexibility, and expressivity in an increasingly decentralised genomic data ecosystem. The effort needed to implement FHR is low; FHR's design philosophy ensures easy implementation while retaining the benefits gained from recording both machine and human-readable provenance.
title: FAIR-bioHeaders Specification

summary: This archive contains the code, prepared data, results, figures, and Supplemental Material S1 for A Continuous Two-Gamma Formulation for Design Hydrographs Using SCS-CN Runoff Generation and Huff Rainfall Temporal Distributions . Calculate a hydrograph for a new design case. Open supplemental_code/ . The Python and MATLAB functions take total rainfall, drainage area, curve number, storm duration, time of concentration, and a Huff quartile. They return the hydrograph, the sensitivity to curve number, and a plot. Understand the calculation. Read supplement/supplemental_quartile_equations.pdf . It contains the numerical equations, coefficient tables, a worked Brazilian case, the curve number derivative, and a guide to the supplied code. Reproduce the analyses in the paper. Install the packages in requirements.txt , then run the scripts listed below from the extracted archive folder. Contents of the archive To calculate a hydrograph supplement/ : Supplemental Material S1 in PDF format. supplemental_code/ : standalone Python and MATLAB functions, plus a short Python example. src/ : the continuous SCS-CN/Huff reference calculation, the two-gamma hydrograph, and the unit hydrograph comparison routines. To reproduce the study scripts/ : scripts that fit and test the design equation, calculate the Brazilian headwater application, compare alternative hydrograph procedures, and examine the first quartile boundary case. Version v3 adds the scripts that build the headwater inputs, repeat the Brazilian test for return periods of 2 to 100 years, and test the initial abstraction ratio of the reference calculation. data/ : prepared inputs for 11,519 HydroBASINS level 12 headwater catchments in the Cerrado, Caatinga, Atlantic Forest, and Pampa. idf/ : instructions for the GRIDF-BR version 2 Sherman IDF coefficient rasters. They are published under CC BY-NC 4.0 at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23405248 and are not redistributed. scripts/fetch_gridf_v2_idf.py downloads them. To inspect the outputs results/ : numerical outputs for the design grid, curve number and time of concentration sensitivity analyses, Brazilian catchment application, and four catchment method comparison. Version v3 adds the return period results, the runtime and initial abstraction ratio tables, and a comparison of the v1 and v2 IDF inputs. figures/ : figures in PDF, PNG, and SVG formats. SVG files can be edited in vector-graphics software. Run the analyses Install the Python dependencies once: python3 -m pip install -r requirements.txt Run the main design-grid and Brazilian headwater analysis: python3 scripts/run_huff_design_study.py Run the comparison with tabular SCS-CN procedures, the NRCS 484 unit hydrograph, and Guo's General Unit Hydrograph: python3 scripts/run_four_catchment_method_comparison.py Run the direct-use Python example: python3 supplemental_code/example_two_gamma_usage.py How the data are used The prepared catchment table contains the inputs used in the Brazilian application: catchment identifier and location, drainage area, flow length, channel slope, Kirpich time of concentration, GCN250 AMC-II curve number, local intensity-duration-frequency coefficients, and derived 25-year rainfall depth. The results files document the headwater selection, excluded cases, curve number checks, catchment coverage, and hydrograph ordinates used in the comparisons. The archive contains prepared catchment inputs and final figures. It does not redistribute the manuscript, submission documents, or the national boundary, biome, elevation, and GCN250 source layers used only to prepare map context. The manuscript identifies those external sources. README.md gives the full directory guide, data provenance, and software requirements.
title: Two-Gamma Reduced Analytical Hydrograph for SCS-CN Huff Design Storms

summary: Active Microrobotic Sampling for Embodied Biological Digital Twins at the Limit STARLI Research Works  Institute XXVIII  Extension 06 English Description This high-density research monograph turns the biological digital twin from a passive recipient of measurements into an embodied experimental partner. Competing twins use uncertainty, expected information gain, physical reachability, safety, authorization, assay burden and traceability to propose the next microrobotic sampling location, time and analyte. The twin remains a versioned scientific belief rather than a replica of a patient, tissue or living system. Central Contribution The Active Sampling Evidence Charter binds twin ancestry, candidate and rejected actions, expected information gain, safety calculations, authorization state, robot trajectory, quantum and classical raw measurements, structured residuals, model forks, resets, abstentions and human overrides into one replayable evidence object. A quantum measurement qualifies only when it reduces biological sampling burden or improves mechanism discrimination against the best classical readout. summary: Anaxia, the BLLM engine, with the source, the Lean development and the checks of the paper BLLM: Beyond the LLM with Deep Human-Mind-AI by D. Bhattacharjee and U. Bhattacharya. The engine is the Python package eBLLM (command anaxia ), a Lean 4 library and the container image ghcr.io/creelie/bllm-engine, which carries no model weights. The paper proves, in a model with independent runs, that certifying self-modifications costs an entropy (the entropy law), that a sound infinite self-improvement of finite cost exists exactly when one series converges, that a proposer needs a number of proposals set by a Rényi entropy of order one half, and that n verified layers sharing one budget cost at least n log(n/θ). Sixty-five of its theorems are proved in Lean 4 with Mathlib, each depending only on the three standard axioms. The engine combines known constructions in a typed crossing network with a program check and a refuter for every candidate, a shared memory and five target agents, and builds new objects in construction mode. Version 3.1.0 passes its mathematical-physics benchmark: every reflexive descent of each of the 473,800,776 reflexive 4-polytopes of the Kreuzer–Skarke list reaches a seed within 348 steps, so the Calabi–Yau seed conjecture holds; the sharp constants are 5 in dimension two and 11 in dimension three, and in dimension four the sharp constant lies between 22 and 348. The engine also learns from its failures: every failed attempt writes a record with its diagnosis and the one rule of the engine it changed, the loop is proved in Lean to stop, and a skill memory credits each change by the whole run it belonged to. The log holds 10 runs, 73 attempts and 57 rule changes, from the engine's own runs and from the attacks on simple zeros of the zeta function, the Erdős–Straus equation, union-closed families, lonely runners, the Dwork quintic, lattice Yang–Mills and points in convex position. On the Hodge conjecture, every convolution with at most seven line bundles on E 0 6 fails the polarised criterion at every discriminant, and so does every object supported on the 32 Weil threefolds. Version 3.2.0 adds the attack package for the four targets (barrier atlas, bypass search, superstring chain, the audit of a quantum-gravity manuscript, triage and the figure critic), the bridge index of 243 thirteen-crossing knots by transvection representations, and the constructions of the proof that gravity with the form factor of a scale-invariant brane gas has no ultraviolet divergence at any order of perturbation theory for n ≥ 4 (the brane response and its resonant refuter, the power counting, the one-loop tuning, the vacuum energy and the reflection-positivity refuter), each recorded as a CANDIDATE control until refereed. Version 3.3.0 adds the attempts of 21 October 2026 on the Hodge inputs (F2) and (F3') (three results and five construction rounds, all stopped on named walls), the proof that the mirror-fixed clause of the Geometric Selection Conjecture is empty, so that the conjecture is equivalent to a viable vacuum on a component carrying no standard embedding (control gsc-mirror-clause, CANDIDATE), two exact constructions from the TheoPhysEval benchmark, the final passes on Lehmer's totient problem and the brane gas, and a third pass on the knot tables that settles the nonorientable four-genus of 2,093 of the 3,525 open knots with 11 to 13 crossings (control crosscap4d-13, CANDIDATE). Of the six benchmarks only the seed conjecture is passed; the lattice Yang–Mills mass gap, the Hodge conjecture, the standard conjecture of Lefschetz type, Chowla's conjecture and Erdős problem 1183 stay open. The registry of the systems, methods and collections the engine draws on, with what it takes from each and what it leaves, is src/ebllm/bllm/data/sources.json and Appendix D of the paper.
title: BLLM: Beyond the LLM with Deep Human-Mind-AI

summary: The Decolonial Intelligence Algorithmic (DIA) Framework™: Twenty-First Edition Christian ZacaTechO Ortiz DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.23547322 15 September 2026 | Revised 21 October 2026 Abstract Bias in artificial intelligence is not a technical accident. It emerges from choices about what knowledge is collected, whose language is centered, which categories are treated as universal, how populations are represented, what objectives models are trained to optimize, and who holds authority over the systems that result. The Decolonial Intelligence Algorithmic (DIA) Framework™ is an operational decolonial architecture for identifying, interrupting, and replacing the epistemological and governance conditions through which Racial Empire Logic is reproduced in artificial intelligence. Rather than treating bias as a defect that can be corrected solely through post hoc fairness metrics, the Framework moves the site of intervention upstream into data formation, classification, model development, evaluation, deployment, and governance. Xam-Xam bu Gore: The Framework of Liberated Knowledge is the epistemological root of the DIA Framework. Authored by Christian ZacaTechO Ortiz and rooted in Wolof, Afro-Indigenous, and decolonial lineage, Xam-Xam bu Gore establishes that knowledge must exist in a state of liberation from colonial capture, epistemicide, institutional gatekeeping, extraction, and imposed hierarchies of intelligence. Its commitments to epistemological sovereignty, relational knowledge production, living knowledge, and liberation as the governing standard shape the Framework’s treatment of artificial intelligence as a knowledge system rather than a neutral technical instrument. The DIA Framework operationalizes these commitments through Four Pillars: Decolonizing Data Collection, Algorithmic Transparency and Accountability, Intersectional Impact Assessment, and Decolonial AI Governance and Accountability Mechanisms. Together, these pillars locate technical decisions inside their political, historical, cultural, and material conditions. The Framework requires attention to intersecting structures of race, gender, sexuality, disability, neurotype, class, caste, citizenship, language, migration, and colonial status, while rejecting the assumption that Western institutional categories constitute the universal baseline against which all other epistemologies must be measured. This Twenty-First Edition extends the Framework from governance-at-inference toward governance-at-formation through Decolonizing Large-Scale Self-Supervised Pretraining on Heterogeneous Corpora . The protocol identifies corpus construction, provenance, language representation, weighting, training objectives, and corpus revision as sites of epistemic governance. It advances accountable reclamation rather than archival purity, recognizing that knowledge survives through occupation, displacement, translation, institutional capture, resistance, and recovery. Its pluriversal approach seeks meaningful engagement across knowledge systems without requiring those systems to surrender their distinct epistemological structures to a dominant Western frame. Global participation is therefore positioned as decision-making authority over how knowledge enters, shapes, evaluates, and may be revised within an AI system. The edition also provides a corrected mathematical foundation for examining categorical incompleteness and intersectional disparity. Its formal results are deliberately bounded. They show, under stated assumptions, how aggregate parity across coarse categories can conceal disparities among finer community-defined groups and why any fixed category system may require continued refinement and governance. The mathematics does not establish universal elimination of bias, clinical validity, legal validity, ontological completeness, or the effectiveness of any specific deployment. Mathematical guarantees apply only to the quantities, populations, partitions, assump
title: The Decolonial Intelligence Algorithmic (DIA) Framework™: Twenty-First Edition Official Version

summary: Open county-by-year panel of U.S. fatal motor vehicle crashes and deaths, 2015-2024, built from NHTSA's Fatality Analysis Reporting System (FARS). Deaths are split by rural and urban location (2020 Census urban areas, held fixed across years, and the FARS RUR_URB label), road class, road owner, and person type (driver, passenger, pedestrian, cyclist). Includes Census population, 2020 rural population, 2024 FHWA HPMS public road miles by functional class and ownership, a crash-level crosswalk to 2020 Census places and county subdivisions with match flags, a codebook, join rules, a provenance log with SHA-256 fingerprints, a QA report, and validation tables comparing the FARS rural label with Census urban areas. FARS 2015-2023 are Final Files; 2024 is the Annual Report File.
title: U.S. Rural Road Fatality County Panel, 2015-2024

summary: This reproducible code and data documents substantial errors in the Science paper " The air pollution benefits of low-severity fire " (Higuera-Mendieta & Burke 2026), that, when corrected, reverse the core conclusions of the paper. You can find their code here: https://zenodo.org/records/20944436   Their paper uses low-severity wildfire as a proxy for prescribed fire to estimate the tradeoff between the smoke generated by treatment (the costs) and the smoke it avoids in future wildfires (the benefit). However, the analysis contains errors that 1) substantially overestimate benefits and 2) underestimate costs. Correcting these issues reverse the paper's reported air pollution benefits.  The analysis relies on two contradictory definitions of low-severity treatment that artificially inflate the benefit-cost tradeoff. The paper argues that low-severity wildfire (dNBR 100-270) is a valid proxy for prescribed fire when estimating treatment benefits, but then assumes that prescribed fire emits only ~15% as much smoke when estimating treatment costs (it assumes a much lower prescribed fire severity range of dNBR 10-40). Actual empirical ranges of MBTS-mapped prescribed fire in their focal landscapes have a mean fire severity of 133 dNBR. Correcting this issue (either using empirical MTBS dNBR ranges, or more appropriately, using an equivalent 100-270 dNBR low-severity fire range) reverses the findings of net air pollution benefits (their Figure 4 and Figure 5c).  The analysis of the benefit-cost ratio (their Figure 4) also demonstrably overestimates benefits by counting emissions reductions that are not physically possible. For example, their analysis often counts modeled reductions in dNBR that exceed the the observed dNBR in the grid cell (e.g., counting a reduction of 169 dNBR units of emissions when there are only 79 dNBR units of observed wildfire), and counts reductions in dNBR when there was no observable wildfire in the first place (e.g., observed dNBR < 0). Together, this error artificially inflates actual emissions reduction benefits of treatments.
title: Code and data to document substantial errors in "The air pollution benefits of low-severity fire" by Higuera-Mendieta & Burke (2026)

summary: Sequential Monte Carlo (SMC) algorithms for fitting a generalised additive mixed model (GAMM) to surface-enhanced resonance Raman spectroscopy (SERRS), using the method of Moores et al. (2026). Multivariate observations of SERRS are highly collinear and lend themselves to a reduced-rank representation. The GAMM separates the SERRS signal into three components: a sequence of Lorentzian, Gaussian, or pseudo-Voigt peaks; a smoothly-varying baseline; and additive white noise. The parameters of each component of the model are estimated iteratively using SMC. The posterior distributions of the parameters given the observed spectra are represented as a population of weighted particles.
title: serrsBayes: Bayesian Modelling of Raman Spectroscopy

summary: This repository contains the anonymised aggregated data, Python analysis code, and supporting documentation for the Bayesian hierarchical analysis of time to antibiotic administration in the PALOH-UK study. PALOH-UK was a prospective, multicentre implementation study evaluating the introduction of rapid point-of-care MT-RNR1 genotyping into routine neonatal care across 14 neonatal units in England, Scotland, Wales, and Northern Ireland between March 2025 and June 2026. The study assessed whether incorporating pharmacogenetic testing into neonatal admission pathways affected the timely administration of antibiotics. The repository provides the data and code used to estimate changes in time to antibiotic administration following implementation, accounting for differences between neonatal units, uncertainty in baseline measurements, and repeated post-implementation audits. The primary analysis included 863 admissions with antibiotic administration times greater than zero and up to 120 minutes. Sensitivity analyses extended the upper threshold to 180 minutes (948 admissions) and removed the upper threshold entirely (990 admissions). The repository includes the analysis scripts, input datasets, model specifications, reproducibility instructions, and outputs from the primary and sensitivity analyses, including convergence diagnostics. Associated manuscript: McDermott JH et al. National implementation of point-of-care MT-RNR1 testing to prevent aminoglycoside-induced ototoxicity in newborn infants: a prospective multicentre study.   Study registration: ISRCTN10216938. Funding: National Institute for Health and Care Research (NIHR), Invention for Innovation (i4i) Programme (NIHR208090).
title: PALOH-UK: Data and code for Bayesian analysis of time to antibiotic administration following implementation of point-of-care MT-RNR1 testing

summary: Open data on how Baton Rouge, Louisiana weather stresses automotive paint (UV, heat, humidity and rain), and on how often it allows a ceramic coating to be applied and cured. It includes a 12-city U.S. comparison and the 1950–2025 record of 90°F days at Baton Rouge Metro Airport. Headline findings: Baton Rouge averaged 111 days at or above 90°F and 117 days with a peak UV index of 8 or more each year from 2016 to 2025. 59% of all hours were at 80% relative humidity or higher, and 21 "hot-sun rain days" a year brought rain on a 90°F, very-high-UV day. Days at 90°F+ have risen about 2.9 per decade since 1950 (Sen's slope; Mann-Kendall p = 0.014). Airport hourly observations show 165 days a year (2016–2024) when a coating could be applied at 50–86°F and 80% humidity or less with no rain for the next 24 hours. That falls to about 2 days in July and 2 in August, against about 21 in October. On a combined paint-stress score, Baton Rouge ranks 3rd of 12 U.S. metros, after Tampa and Miami. Files: daily Baton Rouge records 2006–2025 (station and NASA POWER model values, with cure-window flags), the 12-metro benchmark, monthly and annual profiles, the 1950–2025 heat record, a threshold sensitivity table, EPA AQI context, stats.json with every headline figure and validation result, a methods PDF with the data dictionary, charts, and the Python code that rebuilds everything from public sources. Sources: NOAA NCEI GHCN-Daily and ISD-Lite; NASA LaRC POWER Project (hourly API); U.S. EPA AirData. Report: https://www.immaculatecarwash.com/guides/ceramic-coating-weather-study-baton-rouge
title: Baton Rouge Car Paint and Ceramic Coating Weather Dataset, 2006–2025
Replication Materials: When Machine Speed Stops Mattering

summary: In this article, we propose ContactFlowFilter, a novel approach for contact estimation that determines the number of active contacts, their locations, and the associated force vectors. We consider a robot manipulator equipped with joint torque sensors and a base force/torque sensor; such a proprioceptive-only setup presents a challenging inverse problem characterized by (i) multi-modality from non-unique solutions, (ii) temporal dependencies in state evolution, and (iii) discrete contact events involving contact addition/removal. Existing approaches, such as particle filters (PFs) and learning-based methods, often struggle to address these challenges simultaneously. To overcome this, ContactFlowFilter integrates a generative model into the PF framework. The recursive structure of the PF captures temporal dependencies, while the flow matching model serves as an auxiliary proposal distribution to track multi-modal beliefs and detect contact events. Extensive validation in both simulation and real-world experiments confirms the effectiveness of the proposed method. In real-world settings, ContactFlowFilter achieves the lowest dissimilarity from the target distribution, with errors of only 0.36 cm and 0.88 cm for single- and dual-contact scenarios, respectively, while operating at 0.69 ms and 2.69 ms.
title: Mixture of Flow Matching and Particle Filter for Proprioception-Based Online Contact Estimation

summary: Malicious actors frequently obfuscate their code to hinder investigative reverse engineering efforts. Among the most formidable techniques is virtual machine (VM) obfuscation: programs are translated into bytecode for a custom VM, often with a randomized virtual instruction set and distributed alongside a corresponding interpreter. Manual analysis and deobfuscation scale poorly due to the complexity of VM obfuscation and the diversification techniques that render each VM and interpreter unique. Existing methods primarily focus on simplifying execution traces and identifying virtual execution boundaries. However, comparatively little attention has been given to recovering higher-level program semantics from VM-obfuscated code. To address this gap, we propose VMSpec, a novel decompiler-based approach that automates the construction of VM processor specifications, enabling existing, well-known decompilers to analyze the VM-obfuscated code. We evaluate our prototype of VMSpec on 147 programs from an established obfuscation benchmark, comprising hash functions, standard algorithms, and randomized functions, obfuscated with different configurations of the Tigress and Code Virtualizer obfuscators. To demonstrate real-world applicability, we additionally include six domain generation algorithms stemming from real-world malware. VMSpec completely strips VM-obfuscation from nearly all obfuscated samples, producing output comparable to Ghidra's decompilation of the original code. Furthermore, it is the first method capable of reconstructing the complete program behavior of VM-obfuscated programs with infinite, input-dependent paths and recursive calls.
title: VMSpec: A Decompiler-based Approach against Virtual Machine Obfuscation

summary: Quantum mechanics has been extraordinarily successful, yet fundamental problems remain, including the measurement problem, nonlocality, and the absence of a complete theory of quantum gravity. This paper proposes a measurement-centric framework in which spacetime is not fundamental. Instead, reality emerges from measurements occurring within a universal probability space composed of interconnected packets of information. Each measurement updates this structure while preserving its underlying symmetry. This framework offers a natural explanation for nonlocality, clarifies the role of observers, and connects general relativity to the conservation of symmetry.
title: Quantum Measurement Evolution: A Framework for Resolving Quantum Gravity and Other Conundrums

summary: Despite the success of foundation models in image synthesis, achieving fine-grained spatial control remains a significant challenge, typically requiring auxiliary structural adapters or complex inference-time steering. While modern vision-language (VLM) text encoders possess the latent capacity to represent spatial coordinates, generative models often fail to leverage this information. We demonstrate that the signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) distribution is a critical determinant of spatial grounding in flow-matching models. Using a novel synthetic benchmark of geometric primitives, we isolate structural mechanics from textural complexity inherent in natural imagery and introduce a rigorous color-aware layout metric to quantify spatial fidelity. We show that training on a centered SNR distribution results in poor layout adherence (25.9%). Instead, we identify high-noise regimes as a "critical learning phase" for spatial grounding. Shifting the training focus toward these stages increases layout adherence to 80.8%, effectively reaching the 83.6% reconstruction ceiling of the underlying variational autoencoder. We find that the necessity for this shift scales with resolution and aspect ratio variance, and that the conservative noise schedules employed by models like FLUX.1 are insufficient for precise layout adherence. Finally, we show that these findings translate to real-world imagery via the COCO dataset (1.0 vs. 57.3 Average Precision), where state-of-the-art layout adherence is unlocked through distribution tuning alone, without architectural modifications.
title: Unlocking Spatial Grounding in Flow-Matching Models via SNR Tuning

summary: We consider the problem of Bayesian estimation associated to inverse problems governed by partial differential equations (PDEs). In most cases of practical interest, one must use numerical solvers to implement computational methods based on Monte Carlo methods. This inevitably leads to an adaptation of multilevel Monte Carlo (MLMC) methods to reduce computational efforts to achieve a pre-specified mean square error (MSE). MLMC is based on sampling coupled versions of Bayesian posteriors associated to increasingly precise numerical solves of the PDE. In this article we present a novel method to implement MLMC based upon sequential entropic optimal transport couplings learned with light Schrödinger bridges, and correct the transport with Metropolis--Hastings steps that preserve the pairing. We bound the mean square error associated to a version of our new estimation method and show, for an elliptic inverse problem, that to achieve a MSE of $\mathcal{O}(δ^2)$ ($δ>0$) one can have an optimal cost of $\mathcal{O}(δ^{-2})$. The results feature explicit bounds on the effect of the fitted transport and of the Metropolis--Hastings correction. From a numerical perspective, on elliptic, Darcy-flow and Navier-Stokes problems, the method reduces the variance of the most precise solver by a factor of five to ten and is faster than multilevel sequential Monte Carlo [arXiv:1503.07259] at tight accuracies.
title: Sequential Entropic Optimal Transport for Bayesian Inverse Problems via Multilevel Monte Carlo

summary: Reliable evaluation of LLM-based alpha mining requires more than positive backtest summaries. We audit a preserved project at three levels: historical run counters, outcome retention, and a separately scoped public reanalysis. Three historical runs report 67, 20, and 11 keep decisions, but the comparison mixes metric populations: a mean over kept candidates is compared with a mean of per-round maxima, and successful evaluations with all returned outcomes. These artifacts cannot identify an architecture advantage. A released 1,837-expression catalog also excludes non-positive OOS outcomes, making its zero-reversal rate non-informative. We then account for all 1,047 unique expressions in a frozen, IS-screened preserved pool using forty A-shares and 2024-2025 rank associations. A versioned public-operator correction yields 923 scorable records, 99 with insufficient valid dates, and 25 unsupported, without modifying the other 990 prior diagnostics. Among scorable records, 671 have positive and 252 negative signed mean rank-IC. Simple untrained references also show positive associations, so this distribution does not establish incremental agent skill or profitability. The case study motivates explicit metric grains, immutable cohort accounting, and provenance-aware interpretation rather than architectural rankings from incomplete records.
title: Auditing LLM Alpha-Factor Mining: Metric Provenance and Full-Cohort Reanalysis

summary: Nanoscale nonreciprocal elements are needed to control signal flow in scalable quantum technologies, but existing nonreciprocal components are often bulky. Here, we show that a strongly nonreciprocal current-voltage relation can arise entirely from coherent elastic scattering in a mesoscopic Rashba nanowire with gate-defined scatterers. We first identify the symmetry constraints that enforce reciprocal transmission in a phase coherent conductor even when inversion and time-reversal symmetry are broken. We then show how gates that are capacitively coupled to the leads, together with a magnetic scatterer or transverse subband mixing, can remove these constraints. In the weak-scattering regime, nonreciprocal conductance originates from interference between distinct backscattering paths. In the strong-scattering regime, nonreciprocity can be resonantly enhanced by the hybridization of the transmitting channel with bound states that arise from a higher transverse subband or spin-split band. In this regime, we find that a bias-induced change in the gate potentials of about one percent can produce an order-unity diode response, i.e., electrons are transmitted almost as in a clean wire for one bias polarity, whereas for the other polarity the current is strongly suppressed.
title: Quantum Interference Enhanced Rectification in Mesoscopic Nanowires

summary: Outcome-predictive signals are often treated as promising optimization targets in reinforcement learning, but predictive validity and optimization utility are different claims. We expose this distinction in GuanDan, a multi-round imperfect-information game in which the implication of a round outcome depends on the public match state. Held-out analysis shows that state--gain interactions provide incremental predictive value beyond a constant signed-gain effect, establishing that match progress is predictively meaningful. We then use changes in a frozen match-win predictor, $ΔΦ$, as a controlled round-level supervision intervention in a matched DanZero-style Monte Carlo self-play protocol. The intervention can succeed in an individual lineage: a selected progress-augmented checkpoint substantially outperforms its matched Baseline on a locked evaluation. Yet the method-level result reverses this impression: none of five preregistered replication seeds is positive, the pooled ten-seed interval includes zero, and across-iteration effects repeatedly change sign without a common late-stage advantage. These results identify a predictive--optimization gap: under the studied learner, a signal can describe outcome-relevant progress while failing to provide a reliably beneficial optimization direction.
title: The Predictive--Optimization Gap in GuanDan Self-Play

summary: Magneto-mechanical resonators (MMRs) are a recently introduced sensor technology for tracking and sensing applications that enables effective miniaturization down to the millimeter regime. However, estimating sensor parameters such as position from raw signals remains computationally challenging, because it requires solving a nonlinear inverse problem with computationally demanding objective function evaluations. In this work, we show how a deep learning method can accelerate this process by directly learning the inverse mapping from the measured signals. We consider the localization problem as an example and show that a convolutional-transformer regressor trained on simulated data with recorded noise can generalize to experimental data. The method achieves a median Euclidean distance error of 7 mm, which is comparable to the size of the sensor and corresponds to 6% of the size of a single coil. These results suggest that deep learning is a promising approach for rapid estimation of MMR parameters.
title: Data-Driven Localization of Magneto-Mechanical Resonators from Time Signals

summary: Quantization-aware training (QAT) aims to recover reasoning capabilities in low-bit large language models (LLMs). Existing recipes typically supervise the quantized student with the original full-precision model on fixed response sequences. However, the resulting low-bit quantized models still struggle on long-horizon reasoning tasks and often fail to terminate within a token budget that suffices for the full-precision model. We identify two challenges in closing this gap. First, fixed-response supervision leaves a mismatch between training prefixes and those encountered during student generation, and this trajectory divergence grows as responses lengthen. Second, on its own prefixes, the student underpredicts some next-token candidates and overpredicts others, and this distributional misalignment becomes more frequent at high-entropy prefixes. We present OnQ, a low-bit recovery pipeline that combines on-policy distillation and candidate-wise Dynamic KL. Starting from block-wise calibration, the quantized student generates responses and receives full-precision teacher supervision on its own prefixes. Dynamic KL weights forward and reverse KL by each candidate's teacher-student probability ratio to balance correction of under- and overprediction. Across Qwen3-1.7B, 4B, and 8B at 2- and 3-bit precision, OnQ achieves the highest nine-benchmark average, with the largest gains on long-horizon reasoning benchmarks. At 2 bits, it outperforms every baseline on every benchmark at every model size, improving the Qwen3-8B average by 10.26 points over the strongest baseline. It also produces shorter responses with fewer truncations and repetitive errors.
title: Right On Q: Recovering Reasoning under Quantization via Self-Generated Trajectories

summary: X-ray and neutron scattering are indispensable for structural characterization across condensed-matter physics and materials science. Yet, because scattering experiments generally record intensities without phase information, distinct structures can yield similar scattering patterns, rendering the corresponding inverse problems non-unique. This ambiguity can be reduced by combining complementary measurements, but their integration into machine-learning frameworks remains challenging. Here we introduce a modular framework for probabilistic multi-measurement analysis based on prior-amortized flow matching. Single-observation posterior estimators are trained separately for individual observation types or physical probes and combined only at inference time through a compositional sampler. This late fusion approach allows pretrained single-observation models to be reused without dedicated joint retraining. As a case in point, we consider reflectometry, which provides depth-resolved, nanometer-scale information about thin films and interfaces. Our single-observation demonstrations span X-ray, time-of-flight neutron and polarized neutron reflectometry. In separate co-refinement studies, task-matched estimators enable homogeneous composition across multiple neutron contrasts and heterogeneous multimodal composition of X-ray and neutron measurements. Together, these results establish compositional flow matching as a modular approach to uncertainty-aware inversion and co-refinement, with potential applicability to other scattering problems in which multiple observations constrain a common physical structure while retaining measurement-specific parameters.
title: Compositional neural networks for multimodal X-ray and neutron scattering inversion

summary: Soliton pumping enables controlled transport of localized wave packets through the interplay between nonlinearity and band topology. Interactions between such wave packets provide an additional means to manipulate their localization and subsequent motion. Here, we investigate collisions of solitons in a driven bichromatic lattice, where solitons associated with bands of opposite Chern numbers are pumped toward one another. For intracomponent collisions, the soliton that dominates the collision survives as a localized outgoing wave packet, while the weaker one can lose its distinct localized identity. For intercomponent collisions, attractive interaction produces spatial locking, whereas repulsive interaction induces redistribution toward the lowest band and reverses the motion of the initially excited-band wave packet. Remarkably, for collisions between vector solitons with comparable initial intensities, the difference between their internal relative phases controls the collision outcome, favoring capture for in-phase preparation and re-separation for out-of-phase preparation. These results connect nonlinear scattering with subsequent topological pumping and identify initial intensity, intercomponent interaction, and relative phase as control parameters for manipulating localized transport within the same pumping protocol.
title: Collision Dynamics of Topologically Pumped Solitons

summary: Pyralysis (PYthon Radio Astronomy anaLYSis and Image Synthesis) is an open-source Python library for radio-interferometric simulation, gridding, and image reconstruction. Imaging is stated as an explicit optimization problem — chi-squared (and closure / bispectrum terms) plus regularizers you choose — solved with modern first-order methods (e.g. FISTA, L-BFGS, SDMM). It is not a black-box CLEAN imager.
title: Pyralysis
Reconstruction of the Neutrino Nature Based on the Great Tao Model and a Unified Explanation of Related Puzzles

summary: We study inhomogeneous random graphs on $n$ vertices with independent Pareto weights of parameter $α>0$ and connection probabilities $\min(\varepsilon_n W_iW_j, 1)$. Our main focus is the infinite-mean regime $0<α<1$. Under the scaling $n\varepsilon_n^α=λ$, with $λ>0$ fixed, the global architecture of the graph is entirely governed by the Poisson point process $Π$ of rescaled extreme weights. In particular, the size of the largest component, divided by $n$, converges to a non-degenerate random variable expressed as an explicit functional of $Π$. Through the point process $Π$, we also characterize the exact limiting connectivity probability, uncovering a non-sharp connectivity threshold. The second largest component and the diameter of the largest component are bounded with high probability. The distance between two uniformly chosen vertices in the largest component is at most three with high probability. We also prove convergence of the point process of rescaled degrees and identify the limiting distribution of the maximum degree. For completeness, we obtain expected degree asymptotics, typical degree limits and connectivity regimes for all $α>0$. Due to the failure of classical branching process approximations in the infinite-mean regime, our approach relies fundamentally on analyzing the extreme weight environment $Π$.
title: Inhomogeneous random graphs: how heavy tails reshape connectivity

summary: World models are increasingly used for planning, where a planner ranks candidate actions by returns imagined by the model. However, these models are judged mainly by how well they render frames, even though a visually faithful rollout can still assign the wrong return. To identify where this mismatch arises, we introduce a transition-level diagnostic that replaces imagined transitions with real ones and measures the reduction in return error against a budget-matched random control. Our analysis yields two findings. (1) Event transitions, the few steps where a reward is earned or an episode ends, are rendered as well as other steps (median pixel-error ratio 0.85), yet restoring them removes a median of 70% of the return error. In contrast, restoring transitions with the largest MSE, SSIM or LPIPS error removes less than a random choice. Across the 44 Atari-100k model--collection pairs that pass our reliability checks, including three released families, event patches outperform random patches in 39 (sign test p=1.4 x 10^{-7}), with a median gain of +44 percentage points. (2) The remaining error is structured: a complementary patch separates errors at true events from those elsewhere, while an eight-step timing tolerance recovers few events missed by our deterministic models. This structure also guides repair: a rule recorded before four repair outcomes were known predicts when a diffusion model repairs these failures. Event patches improve plan ranking, and the same concentration appears on control tasks with rare reward events.
title: Events, Not Pixels: Where World Models Get the Return Wrong

summary: Generative recommenders replace the retrieve-then-rank cascade with a single model: beam search over semantic item identifiers performs retrieval, and the same likelihood performs ranking. We show that this shared score makes them forget long-tail items twice. In retrieval, beam search keeps identifier prefixes by the probability mass of their subtrees, so tail items are pruned early, and a wider beam admits few more of them. In ranking, the likelihood places tail items below head items even when they are admitted, so expanding retrieval alone brings little or no gain. Both failures reflect missing item-level memorization (i.e., direct recall of which items co-occur), which collaborative filtering provides and shared-prefix generation lacks. To this end, we propose CAPE (Co-occurrence-Aware Pool Expansion), a training-free plug-in that restores memorization at both stages: (i) a memorization channel retrieves co-occurrence-supported tail items outside the beam and scores them with the frozen generator, and (ii) memorization-calibrated ranking fuses the generator likelihood with co-occurrence evidence while keeping the generator's first item. Experiments with two generative backbones on product and music domains show that CAPE significantly improves long-tail accuracy over the backbones and over re-ranking baselines that share its candidates, preserves or improves overall accuracy, and adds a small fraction of the latency.
title: Generative Recommenders Forget the Long Tail: Restoring Memorization in Retrieval and Ranking

summary: Thermal cameras enable robots to perceive human activities in darkness while revealing less personally identifiable appearance information and fewer details of the surrounding environment than RGB cameras. As vision-language models (VLMs), originally developed for RGB imagery, are increasingly integrated into embodied systems for scene understanding and high-level planning, thermal sensing offers a promising way to extend activity perception to low-light and privacy-sensitive settings. However, the failure modes of VLMs in thermal human activity understanding for human-robot interaction (HRI) remain underexplored. We fill this gap by evaluating seven locally deployable VLMs, including models developed for physical AI and robotics, on two person-centric thermal datasets. Our diagnostic tasks examine fine-grained action recognition, activity timeline reconstruction, and the ability to withhold unsupported answers. Paired RGB recordings serve as a performance reference, while controlled variations in frame sampling, thermal input presentation, and reasoning are used to assess whether the observed errors can be mitigated. Our results show that models can recognize broad activity categories but struggle with fine-grained actions such as coughing, sneezing, and yawning. They also produce inaccurate event timelines and hallucinate actions involving objects. Simple thermal input preprocessing and additional reasoning offer only limited, model-dependent gains. Abstention behavior also varies across models even under explicit instructions, limiting their reliability for practical robotic use.
title: Failure Modes of Vision-Language Models for Human Activity Understanding in Thermal HRI

summary: In this paper, we investigate why vision-language models (VLMs) produce errors by decomposing them into two sources: visual-representation failures, in which the visual evidence required for the correct answer is not encoded, and visual-utilization failures, in which this evidence is encoded but not successfully used. We propose to estimate the visual-utilization failure rate using lightweight probes and derive theoretical bounds on the true rate that account for probe imperfections. We introduce VELens (Visual Evidence Lens), a rank-based probe that traces visual evidence for both a target object and its ground-truth attribute, such as color, material, or shape, across VLM layers. We evaluate VELens on over 6,000 images using LLaVA-1.6-7B and Qwen2.5-VL-7B. Our method achieves ROC-AUC scores of 0.95 and 0.91, respectively, and outperforms alternative probes in both low-resource and unseen-attribute settings. Using it to diagnose errors, we estimate that visual-utilization failures account for 84.4% of LLaVA errors and 70.0% of Qwen errors, with conservative lower bounds of 77.5% and 61.0%, respectively. Overall, our study identifies visual utilization as the dominant bottleneck in VLMs and suggests that a central opportunity for improvement lies in developing better mechanisms to locate, route, and use the visual information they already encode.
title: Encoded but Unused: Bounding the Sources of VLM Errors

summary: Root cause analysis (RCA) and mitigation prediction are essential for incident management, enabling the identification of underlying causes of failures and ensuring the reliability of complex cloud-based systems. With rising incident volume and system complexity, incident reports have become a valuable resource for these tasks. Recent studies have shown promising results using Large Language Models (LLMs) to predict root causes and mitigation actions from textual descriptions in incident reports. Despite these advances, further progress is hindered by the lack of publicly available datasets; existing work relies on private data, which limits transparency, reproducibility, and generalization. To address this gap, we introduce CloudIR-Bench, the first publicly available benchmark providing a dataset and evaluation framework for incident report-based RCA and mitigation prediction. Curated from incident reports across five leading cloud-based systems, CloudIR-Bench captures a diverse range of real-world production scenarios representing authentic failures and engineers' reasoning. We also release an open-source evaluation framework that includes eight recent LLM-based approaches. Our comprehensive evaluation includes zero-shot and in-context learning experiments, along with a qualitative analysis to identify where and why LLMs fail. Benchmarking results reveal the capabilities and limitations of existing LLMs in this domain. The benchmark, including the dataset, framework and supplementary materials, is available at https://github.com/hoangtnm/CloudIR-Bench.
title: CloudIR-Bench: A Benchmark for Root Cause Analysis and Mitigation of Cloud Incidents

summary: Verifier stacks increasingly sit inside post-training and test-time compute loops. We study a specific control loop: a component verifier is evaluated on fresh policy outputs against the full success label and refreshed when that aggregate score falls. For a conjunctive target $y = F \wedge M$, its on-policy AUC is $(1-q)A_{\mathrm{own}} + qA_{\mathrm{cross}}$, where $q = \Pr[F=1 \mid y=0]$. As the policy masters $F$, $q$ can rise toward one, removing weight from $F$-failures and rewarding information about $M$. We call this on-policy audit collapse. We derive a sharp identified set, a complete-erasure threshold, and the exact point at which the audit can prefer a worse component verifier; its population optimum is the full-outcome predictor, not the component oracle. An exact oracle exhibits the collapse, a natural multi-label text control shows inversion can select a head with lower canonical $F$-AUC at the observed failure mixture, and a prediction-registered ECG study shows that acting on the audit can reduce off-policy $F$-AUC, transfer the damage to an unseen generator, and increase downstream constraint violations. Preserving own-failure support prevents the damage. Matching label-complexity bounds and a controlled-mixture audit give the corresponding repair: audit the component on its own failures, and keep those failures in the refresh distribution.
title: Better Policies, Worse Verifier Audits

summary: Coding agents are rapidly advancing from single-file generation to long-horizon repository-scale engineering, yet the evaluation of their capabilities to author interactive extended reality (XR) applications remains an open challenge. Unlike traditional software, XR applications operate within dynamic 3D physical environments where runtime robustness depends jointly on continuous user motion, spatial input, and environmental sensing. We introduce GenXR-Bench, the first benchmark for the end-to-end evaluation of coding agents in XR software development. GenXR-Bench contains 112 expert-authored tasks spanning 24 feature implementations, 21 bug repairs, and 67 application generation tasks. Held-out tests combine scripted and adaptive interactions with programmatic and visual assertions to evaluate core functionality and runtime behavior. GenXR-Bench's testing suite achieves 96.5% accuracy against blinded expert judgments of 124 candidate applications executed on consumer XR hardware. Evaluating 10 models on GenXR-Bench, we find that the strongest configuration achieves only 50.9% overall Pass@1. Failure analysis identifies recurring misunderstandings in asynchronous sensor lifecycles, physical grounding, and embodied interaction semantics. GenXR-Bench establishes a reproducible testbed for evaluating coding agents in the interactive and physically situated conditions of spatial computing.
title: GenXR-Bench: Benchmarking Coding Agents for Interactive XR Development

summary: While large language models are increasingly deployed as tool-calling agents, their safety evaluations still focus primarily on their ability to refuse harmful requests in text. We investigate whether the refusal behavior in text transfers to tool use. We construct a benchmark of 2,304 prompts across four domains, consisting of matched triplets that present the same harmful or benign request in text-only, standard tool-enabled, and adversarially framed tool-enabled settings. We then assess tool-call safety using 20 predefined forbidden actions. Testing five models of varying sizes and families, we find that requests refused in text frequently result in unsafe tool calls. Under standard tool-enabled prompting, this divergence occurs for 10-52 percent of harmful requests refused in chat. To mechanistically investigate this gap, we identify a refusal-associated direction in the residual stream of each of the five models. We find that in tool-enabled contexts, the activations along this direction decrease in four of five models. Furthermore, lower activation predicts unsafe tool calls across all five models (AUC 0.76-0.86). However, restoring the signal to the respective text-only value through activation patching only prevents a subset of unsafe calls, primarily by suppressing tool use rather than by producing safer calls. Steering along the refusal direction nearly eliminates unsafe calls only at strengths that also suppress benign tool use or degrade the output quality. Our findings indicate that the identified refusal direction contributes to whether a model acts, but only partially explains the refusal divergence. Therefore, evaluating the safety of tool-calling agents requires directly examining their actions along with their textual responses.
title: Behavior Beyond Text: Evaluating Refusal Transfer Failure in LLM Agents

summary: Agentic harness evolution optimizes an agent's instructions, tools, and control flow by using its task execution experiences as evolving evidence. While more evolution tasks should intuitively improve performance, our preliminary study reveals a paradoxical failure mode: the performance of existing methods degrades as the task pool expands. Our further analysis demonstrates that this degradation stems from suboptimal evidence selection during optimization, as different evidence combinations lead to substantially different evolution outcomes. To address this issue, we propose Successive Scale Racing (SSR), a framework that adaptively searches for optimal evidence combinations in each evolution round. SSR constructs diverse evidence combinations based on the corresponding task quality and coverage, and efficiently races the resulting candidate harnesses under a small compute budget. Empirically, across three distinct benchmarks, SSR achieves state-of-the-art results in all six configurations. Notably, as the task pool grows from 40 to 200, SSR steadily improves the pass rate from 64.3% to 68.3%, while the baselines' performances all drop. Furthermore, its racing mechanism identifies near-optimal candidates while reducing validation executions by 60%.
title: Forging More Tasks into Better Harnesses: Agentic Harness Evolution via Successive Scale Racing

summary: Agentic systems have demonstrated strong capabilities on complex tasks by enabling multiple interacting large language model (LLM)-based agents to collaborate and execute subtasks in parallel. However, this collaborative structure introduces new challenges for reliably evaluating and diagnosing system failures, particularly failure attribution: tracing a system's execution to identify the agent step responsible for an incorrect final outcome. Because manually performing this task is time- and labor-intensive, recent work has turned to LLMs as judges to automate the process, referred to as automated failure attribution (AFA). These approaches assume that a sufficiently capable model can infer the failing step directly from an interaction transcript. In practice, however, direct prompting often performs poorly, which motivates follow-up work that explores various ways to improve AFA performance, including alternative prompting strategies and inference-time interventions. In this paper, we examine a more fundamental question: whether this weak behavioral performance reflects a genuine capability limitation. Using linear probes applied to internal activations, we uncover a significant \emph{knows-but-won't-say gap:} models encode sufficient information to attribute a failure correctly but fail to explicitly output the responsible step. Building on this finding, we propose \emph{grafting}, a simple manual intervention that exploits knowledge already encoded in the model to improve AFA performance without requiring ground-truth labels at inference time. Extensive evaluations across multiple LLMs and benchmark settings demonstrate that grafting consistently outperforms direct-prompting approaches, underscoring the potential of leveraging latent model knowledge for more reliable failure attribution. Our code is available at https://github.com/wendyzheng22/mi4afa.
title: A Mechanistic Study of Automated Failure Attribution in LLM-based Agentic Systems

summary: A hardening release from the 2026-10-21 full review ( docs/reviews/2026-10-21-full-review.md ): untrusted bundles and archives can no longer read or write outside themselves or exhaust memory, arkiv convert no longer destroys records, and malformed archives, bundles, and JSONL files report a clean error instead of a traceback (for crafted databases, only colliding asset rows are covered so far; see Known issues). No on-disk structure changes; arkiv_format stays "0.2" . Security S1: README contents entries (and schema.yaml , nested README files, and the archive's own README.md ) that are absolute, contain .. or a backslash, or resolve outside the archive are refused, so a crafted archive can no longer import arbitrary .jsonl files, or the text of any host file, from the host. S2: symlinks under media/ (including a symlinked media/ itself) are never followed or imported, so host files cannot land in the database and then in exported bundles. Directory import, the source fingerprint, and pack_bundle now share one walk ( iter_source_files ). S3: tar bundles are read with bounded headers: GNU long-name and pax headers over 1 MiB, or chained deeper than 8, are refused before they are read into memory, and sparse members are refused. A 65 KB archive no longer needs hundreds of MiB, and unpack_bundle is bounded too. S4: a database path containing # , ? , or % (or non-ASCII characters, or spaces) opens the file it names when opened read-only, instead of opening, and creating, a different file. S5: duplicate tar and zip members are refused on unpack, as are tar hard and symbolic links, FIFOs, and devices, so iter_jsonl and convert can no longer disagree about an archive's content. Names that differ only in case or Unicode normalization ( records.jsonl and Records.jsonl ) count as duplicates, since a case-insensitive filesystem (APFS, NTFS) stores them as one file. S6: MCP sql_query aborts after 10 seconds (an infinite recursive CTE no longer hangs the server) and cuts any text or blob cell over 100000 characters. S7: asset rows in a crafted database can no longer overwrite README.md , *.jsonl , or other non-media files on export; only canonical paths under media/ are written, checked on the resolved path. Fixed L1: arkiv convert <dir> after MCP write_record no longer silently deletes the written records; it refuses and names the export command. L2: reconverting a directory into its existing database rebuilds it from scratch, so collections, README text, and schema descriptions removed from the directory are gone from the database too, and status no longer reports in_sync over stale content.
