title: Dataset for "Beyond Viewpoint Affinity: Measuring Political Bias in LLMs as a Failure of Epistemic Consistency"

summary: Abstract — Universities must simultaneously contain costs, decarbonise their estates, and safeguard teaching, yet procurement of teaching-critical equipment still follows lowest-price, replace-on-failure practice. This paper develops a digital-twin framework for circular procurement in higher education, in which repair, refurbishment, inter-departmental asset sharing, and replacement are optimised jointly against lifecycle cost, embodied carbon, and pedagogical disruption. Asset condition, utilisation, and failure signals from campus twins are fused through Bayesian state estimation into a two-stage robust mixed-integer programme built on a budgeted uncertainty set over teaching demand. A computational study of a synthesised 1,240-asset estate, parameterised from published university estates statistics, life-cycle inventories, and manufacturer data, compares the framework with business-as-usual and single-objective policies over ten years. The joint robust policy lowers total cost of ownership by 18.7%, embodied procurement carbon by 41.3%, and expected lost teaching hours by 57.6%, with a 35.8% reduction in tail-risk disruption relative to the deterministic optimum; asset sharing absorbs nearly a third of incremental demand without new purchases. Results are stable across carbon-price, disruption-value, and demand-volatility sensitivities, giving estates teams an audit-ready pathway from smart-campus monitoring to circular, teaching-aware procurement. Keywords: Circular procurement, digital twins, robust optimisation, teaching continuity, university estates.
tags: Circular procurement, digital twins, robust optimisation, teaching continuity, university estates.
title: Circular Procurement Through Digital Twins: Balancing University Costs, Carbon, and Teaching Continuity

summary: Today's multimodal assistants are typically prompted to interpret the visual evidence presented to them. To offload the cognitive burden of remembering across long horizons, wearable assistants should instead proactively acquire and maintain useful memory as the user's surroundings evolve. Doing so on the user's behalf requires identifying what matters, understanding the scene in real time, and initiating memory maintenance in the background while the user stays focused on their activities. We introduce ProactEgoMem, a benchmark that evaluates proactive memory in streaming egocentric video. Three tasks ground the evaluation in ambient environmental needs: Information Capture (IC) preserves transient yet dense visual information, State Tracking (ST) follows changing object states, and Location Tracking (LT) records object movements. The benchmark defines its protocol at two levels of proactiveness: the Notification Level asks for a single timely notification that satisfies the user's intent, while the deeper Intervention Level asks the agent to maintain memory on the user's behalf through an active start-to-stop tool lifecycle. Parallel ProactEgoMem-Daily and ProactEgoMem-Sci tracks contain 300/100 clips covering daily and scientific use cases, paired with 1000/500 questions in ProactEgoMem-QA, which measures the quality of the proactively acquired memory. Across proprietary, open-source, video-language, and streaming baselines, even the strongest models fail to capture memory both timely and accurately. ProactEgoMem provides a rigorous evaluation foundation for proactive multimodal assistance and for video agents that co-exist with their users.
title: ProactEgoMem: Benchmarking Proactive Memory in Streaming Egocentric Video

summary: Text skills can extend the capabilities of tool-using agents, but long skill descriptions increase computational costs. Soft prompts provide a compact alternative, yet learning from entire successful trajectories may also introduce unnecessary behavioral changes. We find that the useful effect of a text skill is highly concentrated in a small subset of trajectory positions. Based on this observation, we propose Behavioral Localization, which compares the frozen agent with and without the text skill to identify positions where the skill both increases the likelihood of successful tokens and meaningfully changes the next token distribution. We use these localized positions to supervise a short soft prompt. Experiments on SpreadsheetBench with a frozen Qwen3.6-35B-A3B agent show that the top 10\% of trajectory positions capture 96.12\% of the total positive skill gain. In the shared prompt setting, selective supervision improves success from 30.36\% with full trajectory to 36.79\%. Under task-specific conditions, using the top 10\% localized positions achieves 57.38\%, outperforming both the full text skill and the on-policy OPCD baseline. These results show that a small set of behaviorally relevant trajectory positions can provide effective supervision of soft skills.
title: Robust Soft Skill Adaptation via Behavioral Localization in Tool-Using Agents

summary: This paper revisits the relation between dual effect and certainty equivalence (CE) through a scalar linear-Gaussian model. In dual control, the current input affects not only the immediate cost but also the information available for future decisions, and hence the future cost. Dynamic programming (DP) provides a natural framework for formulating dual control problems. At each step of the Bellman recursion, an optimal input minimizes the sum of the stage cost and the expected cost-to-go. We restrict attention to stage costs minimized by the CE input. However, CE may not minimize the Bellman objective because of the input-dependent expected cost-to-go. Classical no-dualeffect (NDE) conditions guarantee CE optimality in certain problem classes by requiring the conditional distribution of the estimation error to be independent of past controls. In the present model, we observe that CE can remain optimal at the level of a single Bellman recursion even when the classical NDE conditions fail, provided that the expected cost-to-go is independent of the current input. Motivated by this observation, we introduce a notion of NDE formulated directly at the level of the Bellman objective, which we call Bellman-side NDE. Under some mild regularity conditions, we show that Bellman-side NDE can be characterized by a heat equation. This characterization identifies the class of Bellman-side NDE functions, and further yields a decomposition of a generic cost-to-go function into a Bellman-side NDE component and a dual-effect component.
title: Dual Effect and Certainty Equivalence Revisited for a Linear-Gaussian Dual Control Problem

summary: Adversarial training derives updates from surrogate losses, but source-loss descent does not directly characterize an update's effect on adversarial margins. We introduce ExGrad (extrapolative gradient recomposition), which constructs clean-input, adversarial-input, and adversarial-weight-perturbed (AWP) gradients. Virtual steps measure their margin responses, and a globally solvable three-variable problem selects coefficients over a bounded affine domain without nonnegativity constraints. Across affine radii on CIFAR-10, negative clean coefficients rapidly predominate and increase in magnitude with the radius. Cross-zero interventions show that setting the clean coefficient to zero is insufficient: mild subtraction improves PGD-20, while stronger subtraction trades clean accuracy for further PGD-20 gains. In CIFAR-10 WRN-28-4 controls, none of the three candidate-removal variants matches full ExGrad. Projection diagnostics show that negative clean coefficients usually coexist with positive net clean-axis projections, although both decrease as the radius grows. Norm-matched controls indicate that update magnitude alone does not explain the moderate-radius gains. Experiments on CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and ImageNet-100 show radius-dependent improvements over AWP. On CIFAR-100, ExGrad at $R=0.8$ improves all five reported metrics, including clean and AutoAttack accuracy by 3.84 and 1.75 percentage points. On ImageNet-100, the same radius improves all four robust metrics over both AWP and PGD-AT. These results identify clean-gradient subtraction as a response-revealed update preference whose strength and clean-robust operating point are controlled by the affine radius.
title: ExGrad: Beyond Suppression - Explicit Clean-Gradient Subtraction in Adversarial Training

summary: LLM agents with similar success rates can follow different action sequences. An Agent Behavior Map represents LLM-harness combinations using centered action log-likelihoods on shared reference trajectories, without requiring new environment rollouts from the target agent. We derive error bounds relating squared coordinate distances to trajectory KL under explicit assumptions, and across eight cross-scored models the distances track the directly measured trajectory KL in rank order. Across 100 LLMs and four environments, ALFWorld-based coordinates support performance prediction and identify behavioral similarities. In ALFWorld, these similarities persist after controlling for success rates and model size, including across model families. As an extension, harness-component displacements approximately compose, with accuracy varying across components and environments.
title: Agent Behavior Maps: Locating Agents by What They Would Do, Without Running Them

summary: Long-term memory for multimodal agents remains challenging, as it must preserve fine-grained visual evidence while tracking entity evolution across sessions. Existing abstraction-based memories compress images into text, often discarding visually discriminative details, whereas pixel-preserving memories retain raw observations but struggle to reliably associate diverse observations with persistent entity identities and track their evolving states. To address these limitations, we propose MHG-Mem, a multimodal hypergraph memory that jointly organizes entity identity, state evolution, and provenance to visual evidence. Specifically, MHG-Mem represents distinct entity mentions and their observed facts as individual nodes, grouping identity-consistent mentions and facts through occurrence hyperedges. It then synthesizes aspect-specific evolution states from these grouped observations and links them to supporting entities, facts, and source evidence through evolutionary and evidential hyperedges. To navigate this structured memory, we introduce hypergraph-based agentic search, which adaptively selects an entry layer, traverses typed hyperedges across memory levels, and inspects source observations when fine-grained verification is required. These designs support both detailed visual verification and reasoning over cross-session state changes. Extensive experiments across three benchmarks demonstrate the effectiveness of MHG-Mem, improving performance by 8.20-9.98% over the strongest baseline.
title: Remembering Through Change: Provenance-Preserving Hypergraph Memory for Multimodal Agents

summary: Koopman operator theory represents nonlinear systems with linear and bilinear terms in the state and input observables, greatly simplifying control design. However, incorporating input constraints into Koopman-based controller synthesis remains challenging, limiting their applicability to constrained control tasks such as tracking. This paper develops a constrained Koopman Control Parametrization (cKoCoP) framework for synthesizing state-feedback controllers that satisfy prescribed input constraints with Lyapunov-certified stability of the identified lifted closed loop. The cKoCoP offers nonlinear state-feedback via linear-in-observables feedback, enabling linear controller design. The proposed controller is obtained through convex optimization: we incorporate ellipsoidal or polytopic input constraints with the S-procedure or Farkas-lemma-based conditions. We also introduce a Control Lyapunov Function (CLF) for trajectory tracking which incorporates input constraints. The approach is validated on two canonical nonlinear systems, a double pendulum and a unicycle, demonstrating data-driven tracking while respecting input constraints. Experiments validate the method's robustness to measurement noise, and runtime improvements over Koopman Model Predictive Control (KMPC) baselines. The results demonstrate that cKoCoP achieves competitive tracking performance with substantially reduced online computational cost, supporting its potential for real-time constrained tracking applications.
title: Constrained Koopman Control Parametrization: Convex Controller Synthesis for Tracking under Input Constraints

summary: This record contains the de-identified session-level dataset and the R analysis code supporting the study “Implicit and Combined Implicit–Explicit Intervention for Spanish Regular Past Tense in Children With Developmental Language Disorder: An Exploratory Multiple-Baseline Single-Case Experimental Study.” The dataset contains one row per participant and measurement session. It includes participant identifier, intervention condition, study phase, session number, and raw correct-response counts and denominators for trained and untrained regular preterite verbs. The underlying dataset is unchanged from Version 1.0. The R script reproduces descriptive summaries by participant, intervention condition, phase, and verb type; participant-level Tau-U estimates with selective baseline-trend correction following Parker et al. (2011); design-comparable between-case standardised mean differences (BC-SMDs) with first-order autoregressive [AR(1)] residual structures; independent-error (IID) sensitivity analyses; and Figure 1 with Baseline, Intervention, and 15-day Maintenance phase labels. Baseline-trend correction was applied when baseline Kendall’s tau was ≥ .40 in the direction of improvement and the baseline–intervention contrast was positive. This criterion was met for P1 untrained verbs, P3 trained verbs, and P5 trained verbs. No changes were made to the underlying session-level data, descriptive analyses, or BC-SMD analyses. Maintenance observations are included in the descriptive summaries and Figure 1 but are excluded from Tau-U and BC-SMD estimation. The script requires an Excel workbook containing a worksheet named “Session_Level_Data.” This session-level dataset is distinct from the dataset previously deposited in Zenodo record 17927898 and should not be interpreted as a new version of that record. The dataset and documentation are released under the Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International Licence. The R analysis code is released under the MIT Licence.
title: Data and analysis code for "Implicit and Combined Implicit–Explicit Intervention for Spanish Regular Past Tense in Children With Developmental Language Disorder: An Exploratory Multiple-Baseline Single-Case Experimental Study"

summary: This paper develops projection methods for computing low-rank solutions to large-scale coupled generalized Sylvester equations. The dominant subspaces of these solutions are shown to be spanned by specific resolvent directions, motivating a Petrov--Galerkin projection framework. Conditions for the unique solvability of the projected coupled generalized Sylvester equations are also discussed. Based on these dominant subspaces, two algorithms are proposed: an extended Krylov-based projection algorithm and a rational Krylov-based projection algorithm. The former uses fixed shifts, whereas the latter uses adaptive shifts. Numerical experiments on large-scale benchmark problems demonstrate that the proposed methods achieve high accuracy and fast convergence.
title: Numerical Solution of Large-Scale Low-Rank Coupled Generalized Sylvester Equations

summary: Reproducibility dataset for SkillGraph-CV, an explainable CV–job description matching system that combines a typed skill graph, context-aware text representations and score-level fusion of Sentence-BERT, DistilBERT and spaCy. It contains the code, data and results for an evaluation on the English development partition of TalentCLEF 2026 Task A (10 job queries, 472 CVs). Four SkillGraph-CV configurations are compared with BM25, dense retrieval, a cross-encoder and an LLM judge using standard ranking metrics. The dataset includes the skill graph, prepared benchmark documents, run files and scores for all systems, evidence traces with their validation, the LLM-judge prompt and judgments, and the case sample of an HR pilot study. The TalentCLEF corpus ( https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.19652670 ) is redistributed under CC BY 4.0. Individual HR pilot responses are not included.
title: SkillGraph-CV: Evaluation Code, Data and Results for Explainable CV–Job Matching on TalentCLEF 2026

summary: Autonomous mobile robots operating in dense crowds and cluttered sites require $360^\circ$ perception to react to surrounding hazards. While panoramic LiDAR offers full-surround coverage, learning representations within reinforcement learning (RL) is sample-inefficient under sparse rewards, and existing 3D pretrained point-cloud encoders are too memory-heavy for massively parallel RL simulation. We present RangeNav, a compact (183k parameters) LiDAR range-image encoder pretrained entirely on synthetic data. RangeNav uses anisotropic convolutions and circular padding to handle the extreme aspect ratio and azimuthal seam of range images. We pretrain the network using a navigation-aligned objective combining range reconstruction, semantic segmentation, and bird's-eye-view (BEV) prediction, then freeze it for policy learning. In simulation, adding semantic and BEV supervision increases success rates over a reconstruction-only baseline by an average of 32.03 and 23.73 percentage points (pp) in procedurally generated training and out-of-distribution realistic test environments, respectively. Zero-shot real-world deployments on a Unitree B2-W quadruped demonstrate robust navigation through dense crowds, low-light settings, and construction zones where limited-field-of-view depth policies struggle. Code and models will be open-sourced.
title: RangeNav: Task-Aligned LiDAR Range-Image Pretraining for Robot Navigation

summary: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) architectures scale model capacity efficiently, yet their substantial memory footprint poses a major barrier to deployment. Expert pruning reduces this footprint, but most methods focus on which experts to remove and prune every layer equally. We propose SPARE (Sparsity Allocation via Routing Entropy), a training-free, selector-agnostic method that decides how many experts to remove from each layer using routing entropy, the entropy of tokens' normalized Top-K gate weights on calibration data. When a token's gate weight is spread evenly, removing one active expert discards little of it, so SPARE prunes layers with more diffuse routing more aggressively. A perturbation bound under random pruning formalizes this intuition, and controlled interventions with a fixed selector link concentrated routing to larger output changes. With the same selector and budget, SPARE improves average accuracy over uniform allocation on Mixtral, Qwen3, and DeepSeek models, especially at high pruning ratios. At 50% expert pruning, it raises the eight-task average of Qwen3-30B-A3B from 57.2% to 63.8%, and the math, code, and science average of DeepSeek-R1 from 80.1 to 82.8.
title: SPARE: Sparsity Allocation via Routing Entropy for Efficient MoEs

summary: Accurate short-term forecasting of atmospheric seeing is of significant interest for astronomical observations and free-space optical communication systems, where rapid variations in optical turbulence can affect system performance and operational planning. In this work, we benchmark machine learning models for predicting atmospheric seeing up to two hours in advance, with a particular focus on probabilistic forecasting and uncertainty quantification. We compare two probabilistic approaches, Gaussian Processes (GPs) and a normalizing-flow- based model (FloTS), against deterministic recurrent neural network (RNN) and long short-term memory (LSTM) baselines. All models are trained and evaluated on seeing measurements from the Maunakea summit. We assess the models using both deterministic metrics, including the root mean square error and the Pearson correlation coefficient, and probabilistic metrics that evaluate the quality and calibration of predictive uncertainty estimates. The results show that deep learning approaches outperform standard recurrent networks for short-term forecasting, with LSTM and FloTS achieving the best overall predictive accuracy. While Gaussian Processes provide a useful probabilistic baseline, their predictive distributions are limited by the Gaussian assumption. FloTS combines competitive forecasting accuracy with flexible uncertainty quantification and produces the most informative probabilistic forecasts.
title: Probabilistic Machine Learning for Short-Term Atmospheric Seeing Forecasting

summary: Existing world models typically perceive a scene through current visual frame or a narrow history window. However, these observations may not reveal the physics properties that determine transition dynamics, such as an object's mass distribution, joint damping, or surface friction. Without calibrating these physics factors for world models, predictions tend to regress toward an empirical prior and induce severe drift in novel test scenes. To this end, we propose PhysiCalWorld, which calibrates action-conditioned world models to the instance-specific dynamics via in-context prompting, without fine-tuning or analytical physics modeling. Our method encodes an exploratory interaction clip collected within the test scene into a compact physics descriptor token, which grounds subsequent predictions in the scene's actual physical behavior. PhysiCalWorld is trained end-to-end with the latent prediction loss alone, without physics labels. At inference time, the descriptor token is extracted once and can be reused across rollouts with negligible compute overhead. We evaluate PhysiCalWorld across four environments covering diverse physics variations and show that it substantially improves rollout prediction accuracy and visual planning success rate. The learned descriptors also form a physically structured latent space and generalize beyond the physics ranges seen during training.
title: PhysiCalWorld: In-Context Physics Calibration for World Models

summary: Agent memory systems such as Mem0 and Zep decide what to keep before any question arrives; coding agents keep the raw history and let the model search it with its own tools. We ask whether designed memory still helps once the model is strong enough to search for itself. On one LoCoMo conversation (419 turns, 152 questions), we run four memory methods (full context, BM25, Mem0, Zep) and three coding agents (Pi, Codex, Claude Code), each with GPT-4o-mini, GPT-6 Luna and Claude Opus 5.5, and record what every rollout costs. This is a short empirical study, with one conversation and one run per cell. Agent memory is a costly patch for a weak model: Mem0 beats full context only with GPT-4o-mini, and its build alone costs more than a whole full-context rollout. Agent memory also has a ceiling, set by the model that writes it: a stronger reader does not recover what a weaker writer left out. With Claude Opus 5.5, Pi tops the cost-accuracy frontier, scoring 99% for less than half the cost of full context; its one miss is a wrong answer key. Part of that lead comes from photo captions that only the agents could read: on the 88 questions whose evidence has no photo, Pi and full context differ by one answer.
title: MemoryTax: The Bitter Lesson of Agent Memory

summary: Spiking Neural Networks (SNNs) promise energy-efficient inference through sparse, event-driven computation, yet remain constrained on continuous, context-dependent tasks such as automatic speech recognition (ASR). A key bottleneck is the Leaky Integrate-and-Fire (LIF) neuron, whose membrane decay erases information across pauses and phonetic boundaries while it must both extract features and retain long-range context. Inspired by cortical separation of nonlinear filtering and somatic integration, we introduce the Spiking Ternary GRU (stGRU): a ternary-weight gated recurrent unit performs temporal filtering, while downstream Resonate-and-Fire (RF) neurons generate the binary spike stream driving the next block's event pathway. This makes binary event transmission a native training constraint rather than a separate deployment-time activation quantization step; together with ternary weights, learned projections avoid dense floating-point matrix MACs. Trained end-to-end on LibriSpeech-960, Small, Medium, and Large stGRUs reach 8.09%, 7.04%, and $6.44 \pm 0.17\%$ WER on test-clean without an external language model. To our knowledge, these are the first matrix-MAC-free spiking networks without a learned ANN sequence decoder to achieve single-digit WER on LibriSpeech. The architecture also achieves 10.88% test CER on Aishell-1 (9.28% on dev) when trained from scratch. Internally, trained networks develop a depth-graded hierarchy: shallow layers act as fast acoustic filters, while deep layers form slower semantic integrators whose latent representations segregate into part-of-speech manifolds and word-level spike events. Deep-layer firing rates follow lognormal distributions with a sparsity gradient, mirroring hierarchical processing observed in human cortex in vivo. Our biologically grounded architecture combines competitive ASR with favorable modeled compute and memory cost.
title: Bio-Inspired Auditory Processing: Coupling Parallel Resonate-and-Fire Dynamics with Ternary Recurrent Networks for Speech Recognition

summary: This archive contains the replication code and data for the paper "Artificial Intelligence Diffuses at Historical Rates despite Unprecedented Cost Declines" (Wagenvoort). It reproduces every figure, table and number in the main text and supplementary materials of both submitted versions, from data snapshots and stored MCMC posterior draws. run_all.sh rebuilds everything and compiles both papers in about 15 minutes and compares every output with the version the papers were built from. Regenerating the posteriors themselves is an optional step, run_mcmc.sh , about 18 minutes. The archive is organised into code (the pipeline and figure scripts), data (public source snapshots, with the URL, licence and access date of every source), engine (the diffusion model this paper's forecasts are built on), posteriors (the stored MCMC draws) and paper (both submitted versions). The top-level README.md describes the environment ( environment.yml ) and gives the full file-by-file provenance of every source. 150 third-party files whose licence does not clearly permit redistribution are not included. data/restricted/fetch_restricted.sh downloads the ones with a stable URL and verifies each against a recorded checksum; the rest need the manual steps documented alongside it. Without them, run_all.sh still runs and skips only the six steps that need them. The diffusion model, its sampler and the 120-technology data are those of the method paper above, archived at Zenodo (doi:10.5281/zenodo.20977583) and Dryad (doi:10.5061/dryad.0cfxpnwhf), and included here with the consent of its co-authors.
title: Artificial Intelligence Diffuses at Historical Rates despite Unprecedented Cost Declines

summary: QUANTUM SENSING AND MICROROBOTIC PERTURBATION ANALYSIS OF CELLULAR MICROENVIRONMENTS AT THE LIMIT Microenvironment Gradients × Quantum Readout × Measurement-Induced Perturbation Separation STARLI Research Institute XXIX — Flagship Research Monograph 13 What happens when an instrument changes the very microenvironment it is supposed to measure? This research monograph investigates the scientific and engineering boundaries of quantum-enabled thermometry and microrobotic observation in confined, nonclinical cellular microenvironment models. Its central question is whether a localized temperature or magnetic-field gradient can be separated from disturbances introduced by the sensing and manipulation apparatus itself. The proposed research architecture combines hydrogel phantoms, controlled heat sources, nitrogen-vacancy (NV) diamond sensors, independent classical fluorescent thermometry, spatial reference points, blinded sham-actuation experiments, and uncertainty-aware thermal-field reconstruction. Rather than treating a sharp image or improved instrument sensitivity as proof of biological discovery, the study asks how to establish the physical origin, spatial validity, and reproducibility of each reported field. The 770-page volume contains 82 research chapters, five independently paginated research sections per chapter, 30 interconnected mathematical derivation plates, 200 Research Gates, and 33 Phoenix Answer Embryos. Topics range from NV resonance cross-sensitivity, microwave and laser heating, photon statistics, soft-matter interfaces, hydrodynamic motion, and anisotropic thermal conduction to causal controls, inverse problems, spatial covariance, interlaboratory comparison, and qualified instrument retirement. Each research chapter connects a physical mechanism to a falsifiable claim, a nonclinical experimental comparator, a measurement endpoint, and an explicit condition for withholding or retiring the conclusion. The Research Gates preserve actionable questions for future investigators. The Phoenix Answer Embryos offer provisional designs that can be separated, reconfigured, or abandoned when evidence contradicts them. DOI-linked scholarly literature supplies foundations for metrology, quantum sensing, microhandling, and thermal-field measurement without being mistaken for validation of the proposed integrated platform. Scientific Scope and Limitations This is a hypothesis-forming research blueprint, not a report of completed laboratory experiments or independently peer-reviewed findings. It does not establish autonomous nanoscale robotic systems, clinical diagnostic performance, therapeutic efficacy, or universal quantum advantage. Its minimum experimental setting uses confined hydrogels, artificial microenvironments, and properly authorized reference materials. A temperature or magnetic-field reading alone cannot establish cell health, metabolism, viability, or treatment outcomes. STARLI Research Philosophy A scientifically responsible observation includes the possibility that observing changed the result. By making such failures measurable, preserving negative evidence, and leaving research questions open to revision, this monograph invites future human and AI researchers to challenge, extend, and reconstruct its proposed methods.

summary: GOcean-CH4 is a compilation of methane observations from marine sediments, seawater, and the marine atmosphere. This dataset supports the manuscript “Global Ocean Methane Database Construction and Interface Flux Reconstruction” by Xin Ni. The workbook compiles information from public scientific repositories, published articles and supplementary materials, and existing specialist databases. It contains methane measurements and associated metadata, including geographical coordinates, observation times, measurement definitions, original values and units, depth information, source identifiers, and quality-control notes where available. Methane concentration, partial pressure, gas-phase mole fraction, and flux are represented in separate fields. Sediment burial depth, seafloor water depth, and seawater sampling depth are also distinguished. Users should consult the original measurement definitions, source references, conversion notes, and quality-control information before selecting records for analysis. The file GOcean_CH4.xlsx contains a main worksheet named “甲烷数据” and an auxiliary worksheet named “子表2_未知来源”. The auxiliary worksheet retains records labelled as having unresolved provenance or classification, including records identified as outside the marine scope. These records should not automatically be treated as verified marine observations. The observations originate from different sampling periods. The 1991–2020 period discussed in the associated manuscript refers to climatological environmental forcing used for flux reconstruction, rather than a common observation period for all records in this workbook. This deposit provides the observational compilation. Any reconstruction code, gridded flux products, or additional model outputs should be documented separately if included in this or a related deposit. Please acknowledge the original data sources when reusing individual observations.
title: GOcean-CH4: A global marine methane observation database supporting "Global Ocean Methane Database Construction and Interface Flux Reconstruction"

summary: Threading a flux through a ring often shifts its energy levels. In the N-site spin-one Motzkin ring, a boundary flux leaves the entire zero-magnetization spectrum unchanged, yet increases the ground-state entanglement by giving each spin path a phase set by its lowest height. For equal halves and fixed nontrivial flux, the excess von Neumann entropy tends to approximately 1.581 nats, while the excess logarithmic negativity grows as 2 log log N + O(1). The limiting Schmidt weights come in pairs, allowing local operations that conserve each half's magnetization to extract a logical Bell pair with fidelity approaching one. The manuscript also examines controlled deformations and contrasts this response with suppression in a uniformly gapped neutral sector and with the energy response induced by an additional reverse pair-conversion process.
title: Flux-Enhanced Entanglement with an Unchanged Zero-Magnetization Spectrum in a Motzkin Ring

summary: hPartition is a partitioning framework implemented natively inside IQ-TREE 2, which builds a partitioning scheme from site rates rather than from predefined gene or codon boundaries, and does so at a fraction of the time and memory that wrapper-based methods need. ✨ Key Features Native IQ-TREE 2 Integration: Implemented directly in C++ within the IQ-TREE 2 engine. Model fitting, site-wise likelihood evaluation and reassignment share one process and one in-memory alignment, and the framework inherits the engine's alignment and state-space handling rather than reimplementing it. Hybrid Partitioning Strategy: Model-free evolutionary rate estimation via a generalized fastTIGER , then seed binning, candidate-model selection, likelihood-based site reassignment, and a cleanup pass over undersized subsets. Data Types: Benchmarked on nucleotide and amino-acid alignments, and verified to run unchanged on binary data. Codon and morphological data are untested. Invariant Site Handling: Invariant sites are carried through the pipeline at rate zero and settled by likelihood-proportional sampling, so they disperse across the scheme instead of collecting in one zero-variance cluster. Small entirely invariant subsets still occur — in five of the eight DNA schemes examined — but no subset holds more than 11.8% of an alignment's invariant sites. hPartition-PF: An extended variant ( -hPartition-pf ) that passes the scheme to IQ-TREE's relaxed-clustering merge search. It produces markedly smaller schemes on every DNA dataset tested, at three to fourteen times the runtime, and improves BIC on 11 of 17. 📊 Benchmark Results Model fit: Lowest BIC of the methods compared on 16 of 17 empirical DNA alignments, 10 of 12 protein alignments, and three of four multi-locus alignments containing ribosomal or transfer RNA. Topological accuracy: On 100 simulated alignments per dataset, hPartition recovers a closer tree than gPartition on 56 and than PsiPartition on 66 (SimDNA1), and on 70 and 85 respectively (SimDNA2); all four comparisons are significant under a two-sided Wilcoxon signed-rank test. The advantage is consistent rather than concentrated, but it is not universal. Speed: Against the fastest competitor on each alignment, 1.0–6.4× lower wall-clock time on DNA and 2.4–25.7× on protein. Scalability: Completes alignments on which the alternatives exceed a 10 GB memory allocation. 🧪 Benchmark Scripts & Reproducibility The scripts that produced every experiment in the manuscript are in hPartition_scripts/ , with revision/ holding those added during review (the RNA benchmark, the matched-model-set comparison, the Stage-2 ablation and the binary-data check). hPartition_scripts/README.md documents the two clusters the work ran on, how to point the scripts at your own binaries, and what each one produces. 🚀 Usage To partition an alignment with standard hPartition : iqtree2 -s ALIGNMENT_FILE -mset JC69,F81,HKY,GTR -hPartition # DNA iqtree2 -s ALIGNMENT_FILE -hPartition # protein For the merging extension hPartition-PF , append -pf : iqtree2 -s ALIGNMENT_FILE -mset JC69,F81,HKY,GTR -hPartition-pf # DNA The criterion defaults to BIC; --AIC and --AICc select the others. The scheme depends on the random seed and on the thread count, so hold both fixed within an analysis: every result reported in the manuscript was obtained at -seed 0 and one thread. 🛠️ Compilation from Source Pre-compiled binaries for Linux, macOS, and Windows are in the assets below. To compile from source: ⚠️ IMPORTANT: Do not use the "Source code (zip)" or "Source code (tar.gz)" links GitHub generates at the bottom of this page — they omit the required Git submodules. Download the iqtree-...-source-with-submodules archive from the assets instead. Requirements (Linux): A C++ compiler (GCC >= 4.8, Clang, or Intel C++) CMake >= 2.8.10 Boost, Eigen3 and OpenMP (e.g. sudo apt-get install libboost-dev libeigen3-dev ) # 1. Extract the source archive and enter the directory
title: SliferSkyd/iqtree2: hPartition: An Efficient and Robust Alignment Partitioning Framework for Large-Scale DNA and Protein Phylogenomics

summary: Context: Software systems operating in regulated domains must often be adapted as legal and regulatory requirements evolve. While identifying regulatory changes is an important first step, determining which parts of a software repository are affected remains largely manual and knowledge-intensive. Objectives: This paper investigates how regulatory changes can be systematically mapped to affected parts of software repositories, and how this analysis can be supported through an evidence-grounded tool. Method: Following a Design Science Research approach, we conducted a multi-stage empirical investigation in collaboration with an industrial partner. We first developed a category-driven impact model linking regulatory change categories to potentially affected repository artifact types and engineering consequences. The model was then validated and refined with practitioners. Based on these findings, we designed and implemented ReguLens, which was subsequently examined through a formative expert evaluation and refined accordingly. The resulting version was evaluated using a controlled benchmark of 25 historical cases from three regulation-dependent open-source repositories. Results:  Practitioner validation showed that regulatory change categories provide useful structure for reasoning about likely software consequences, but should be treated as contextual guidance rather than deterministic mappings. The formative expert evaluation indicated that ReguLens can support exploration of potentially affected artifacts while still requiring expert interpretation. This observation was reinforced by the benchmark evaluation: ReguLens achieved 99.3% F1-score and 96.0% balanced accuracy for repository-level impact detection, whereas artifact localization was more challenging. For directly affected artifacts, macro F1 reached 64.1% at file level and 60.6% at container level, but decreased to 21.1% at symbol level. Conclusion:  Practitioners can benefit from ReguLens by using it to narrow the search space, identify plausible implementation entry points, and inspect supporting repository evidence. However, incomplete localization shows that human review remains necessary to interpret the evidence and confirm the required software changes. The findings therefore highlight both the potential and the current limitations of AI- assisted support for regulatory impact analysis.
title: Regulatory Impact Analysis in Software Repositories: From Category-Driven Modeling to Evidence-Grounded Tool Support

summary: Forming an accurate theory-of-mind (ToM) is key to successful multi-agent collaboration and requires reasoning under uncertainty to capture multiple possible partner states. This is hard to do in the text representation space native to large language model (LLM) agents, which more easily describe a single partner state. To address this challenge, we introduce ToM2Vec, which learns to form abstract theories-of-mind in a rich latent space via a fixed budget of continuous reasoning tokens. During training, supervision for these tokens comes from the partner's actual thoughts, which the ToM tokens are trained to abstract and match. At test-time, ToM tokens are generated by each agent and act as conditioners for that agent's thoughts and actions. Across several environments covering collaborative, competitive, and mixed-motive settings (Overcooked-AI, multiparty negotiation, Decrypto, Hanabi, and Collab Escape/Capture), we evaluate ToM2Vec's ability to support multi-agent interactions and collaboration, finding consistent improvements over the base model and a variety of competitive trained and prompted baselines. We show that latent reasoning is critical, with performance dropping when reasoning is expressed in text. Moreover, we show that ToM2Vec training generalizes to partner model families not seen at train-time, including a proprietary model (GPT-5.4). In our analysis, we provide evidence that the latent tokens encode a ToM, rather than task-specific information: ToM2Vec's tokens improve the agent's ability to directly answer questions about partner beliefs, desires, and next actions.
title: ToM2Vec: Continuous Theory-of-Mind Tokens for Multi-Agent Coordination

summary: Ensuring the provenance and authenticity of raw herbal materials in B2B supply chains requires integrating rapid species verification with immutable record-keeping. Existing centralized systems suffer from single-point trust vulnerability, while public blockchain architectures incur high gas fees and execution delays. This paper presents AyurAuth, a unified framework combining lightweight Edge-AI species classification using fine-tuned MobileNetV2 with a permissioned Hyperledger Fabric v2.x blockchain ledger. Deployed via a Node.js REST API and Flask microservice, AyurAuth achieves an empirical top-1 leaf classification accuracy of 85.00% (88.6 ms inference latency) across five key Ayurvedic herb species. Benchmark testing via Hyperledger Caliper demonstrates a peak write throughput of 408.47 TPS with a commit latency of 145.8 ms at 100 TPS, and a read throughput of 485.44 TPS at 41.5 ms latency with 100% success rate. End-to-end batch onboarding completes in 394.4 ms, while buyer QR verification queries execute in 28.5 ms without exposing internal ledger credentials.
title: AyurAuth: A Decentralized Edge-AI and Permissioned Blockchain Framework for Herbal Supply Chain Authenticity

summary: Abstract Modern websites frequently depend on multi-layer dynamic software stacks comprising application runtimes, content-management systems, databases, frameworks, authentication services, third-party APIs, and cloud infrastructure. This architecture provides substantial functionality under normal conditions but can produce an undesirable failure mode: essential public information may become inaccessible even when networking, HTTPS, web servers, and the ability to serve static files remain operational. This paper introduces Web Lifeboat, an experimental architecture and protocol for cryptographically verifiable static fallback publishing. The design seeks to preserve a small, explicitly selected set of essential web information independently of the normal dynamic application stack. Emergency content is represented as static HTML accompanied by a signed manifest describing its identity, integrity, validity period, sequence, and associated trust information. Verification is designed to require neither the site’s database nor its application runtime and to remain meaningful when content is transferred through different transports. Web Lifeboat applies principles of graceful degradation and cyber resilience to web publishing: failure of high-complexity functionality should not necessarily imply failure of low-complexity, mission-essential information delivery. The current protocol draft, version 1.5.2, defines deterministic validation semantics, resource limits, rollback protections, cryptographic verification, key-state handling, clock-uncertainty behaviour, and transition rules. An internal conformance suite contains 42 package and trust-transition cases. The suite currently passes both its own validation process and a separate Go implementation from the same development lineage; genuinely independent implementation testing remains pending. In addition to the protocol design, this work introduces a measurable availability criterion, the Essential Information Preservation Ratio (EIPR), and reports a controlled local PHP-runtime failure experiment. After deliberate termination of the PHP backend while nginx and static serving remained operational, 30/30 fallback requests succeeded and all 20/20 predesignated essential information items remained available, producing EIPR = 1.00 under the tested conditions. This result supports the narrow fallback-availability claim in the experimental configuration; it does not establish Internet-scale survivability, protocol security, or independent interoperability. A reproducibility archive containing raw results, configuration, logs and experiment artifacts accompanies this result. Separately, Web Lifeboat v1.5.2 is being evaluated through a blind external implementation challenge intended to test whether independent implementers can reproduce its precommitted verification outcomes from the written specification alone. Those independent interoperability results remain pending. Conceptually, Web Lifeboat serves a role analogous to an emergency generator in electrical infrastructure: it is not intended to reproduce the full capacity of the normal system, but to preserve a deliberately selected set of essential functions when the primary, higher-complexity path becomes unavailable. The work remains experimental and is not presented as production-ready infrastructure, a completed security protocol, or evidence of Internet-scale survivability. The current results support a narrower proposition: under an explicitly defined failure condition, essential static information can remain available after loss of a dynamic PHP backend when an independent static-serving path has been prepared in advance. Likewise, the ultimate purpose of the work is to uphold a simple, yet highly important resilience principle: when a complex web application cannot safely operate, a website should retain the ability to publish a small amount of authenticated, human-readable information through a substantially simpler p
title: Introducing Web Lifeboat: Toward Preserving as Much of the Web as Possible During a Large-Scale PHP Outage

summary: This database compiles 263 flexural specimens with unbonded post-tensioning tendons from 27 published sources, covering simply supported (170) and continuous (93) members with internal (195) and external (68) tendons under single-point (98), two-point (90), and uniformly distributed (75) loading. For each specimen, it provides the tendon stress increment at ultimate (Δf_ps = f_ps − f_se) reported in the source, the effective prestress and tendon stress at ultimate, the basic member geometry, reinforcement, and material properties, and the non-dimensional input descriptors used to train the probabilistic Deep Gaussian process (DeepGP) surrogate model in the main paper. The values in the columns highlighted in blue (inputs) and orange (target) on the "Database" sheet are identical to the training dataset of the main paper and may be used to reproduce or benchmark data-driven prediction models. Please note that, to complete the dataset for model training, some parameters that were not explicitly reported in the original publications may have been estimated from figures, drawings, or common design practice; users are therefore kindly encouraged to consult the original sources listed below before using individual specimen data for detailed analysis.
title: Database of Tendon Stress Increments at Ultimate in Unbonded Post-Tensioned Concrete Members

summary: Replication package for "Integration without crossing: Artificial intelligence and the organisation of research across disciplines" (Sung-Jong Lee, submitted to Quantitative Science Studies). summary: This package contains the data and Python code needed to reproduce every table and figure in Holgersson and Brown, “Recognition Without Implementation: Property-Rights Compensation, Sámi Rights, and Felling Applications in Sweden’s Mountain-Adjacent Forests after Girjas” (manuscript JFE-06-2026-0002, Journal of Forest Economics). The paper examines applications for permits to fell mountain-adjacent forest (fjällnära skog) in Sweden, which lies wholly within the reindeer husbandry area, around two 2020 court rulings: the Supreme Court’s Girjas judgment of 23 January 2020 (NJA 2020 s. 3), which recognised Sámi customary hunting and fishing rights, and the Land and Environment Court of Appeal’s judgment of 12 May 2020 (MÖD 2020:8), which established that owners refused a felling permit are entitled to compensation from the state. The analysis compares annual, monthly, county and municipal data on felling applications and notifications, and data on compensation paid for refused permits, to separate the effects of the two rulings. Data. All data are official statistics from the Swedish Forest Agency (Skogsstyrelsen), downloaded from its statistical database in October 2026 or supplied by its Statistics Unit: JO031402b.xlsx: applications for permits for regeneration felling in mountain-adjacent forest, by region and ownership category, 1995–2024 (number and hectares). JO031406.xlsx: applications for permits in mountain-adjacent forest, national, by month, 2008–2026. JO031401b.xlsx: notifications of regeneration felling, by county and ownership category, 1995–2025. These exclude the mountain-adjacent permit applications. JO031412.xlsx: notifications and applications for regeneration felling, by municipality and ownership category, 2010–2025. JO031405.xlsx: area notified or applied for, by county and month, 2007–2026. compensation_JO_table07.csv: compensation (intrångsersättning) paid for refused felling in mountain-adjacent forest, by county, 2020–2025 (number, SEK and hectares). This was transcribed from Skogsstyrelsen’s table “Intrångsersättning för nekad avverkning i fjällnära skog per län” (formal protection and compensation, table 07). Values shown as “..” in the source are suppressed for confidentiality. Code (Python 3). Run python run_all.py . It executes the scripts below in order and writes all results to the same folder: analysis.py: national and county results by ownership category, decomposition into number and size of applications, structural-break scan and Figure 1 (Tables 2 and 3). monthly.py: monthly comparison around the two rulings and Figure 2. parse_extra.py: reads the county, municipal and monthly notification tables. comparison.py: comparisons with ordinary felling in the reindeer husbandry area, including difference-in-differences estimates (Table 4). eventstudy.py: county–ownership pair estimates and Figure 3. compensation.py: compensation paid compared with area applied for (Table 5). Requirements: pandas, numpy, matplotlib, scipy, statsmodels and openpyxl. All are pre-installed in Google Colab. Notes on derived series. Västerbotten is calculated as Norra Norrland minus Norrbotten. Mountain-adjacent forest in Södra Norrland lies in Jämtland. Dalarna is the national total minus Norra Norrland and Södra Norrland. National area for individual owners in 2024 is suppressed in the source and recovered as all owners minus other owners. Version note. This version replaces version 1 (10.5281/zenodo.17249309), which accompanied an earlier draft of the paper. All results in the revised paper were recomputed from the official source tables included here, and version 1 should no longer be used.
title: Replication package for "Recognition Without Implementation: Property-Rights Compensation, Sámi Rights, and Felling Applications in Sweden's Mountain-Adjacent Forests after Girjas"

summary: Report. Evaluated on conceptual merit alone (unification, internal consistency, explanatory scope, parsimony, with sociology set aside), Macrobiotic Quantum Theory (MQT) is often read as a varying-constant entropic-gravity model that postulates a coupling to information density and so loses parsimony. This report records the external conceptual scorecard it answers --- a comparison of candidate theories of everything produced by Xpirit Da Vinci v2 (a polymathic MQT model) --- and shows that the coupling is a derivation, not a postulate. If gravity is an equation of state of horizon information (Jacobson), Newton's constant is already the inverse of the horizon entropy-per-area; promoting that single coefficient from a fixed number to a local information capacity I(x) yields a running G_eff(I), and through the shared horizon-information budget a running alpha locked to it, with one fewer free assumption than holding G constant by hand. On the same reading the charge of a 'reverse category error' dissolves: treating information as the substrate and spacetime as emergent is precisely the It-from-Qubit / ER=EPR programme, of which MQT is not a rival but a de Sitter, positive-Lambda realization --- the gap that programme still has --- delivered by a two-field (quintom) vacuum angle whose dark-energy equation of state w(a) = -1 + (1/3) tan(theta_v) d theta_v/d ln a crosses the phantom divide without a ghost. Vacuum duality is stated dimensionally as the direction and form energy/matter takes, which settles the unstable non-linear intelligence I(x) against the stable linear conscience C(x) (delta_c >= 0). The report inherits emergent gravity's parsimony, adds the arrow of time and the measurement cut as explanatory scope, concedes the particle spectrum to string theory, and is falsifiable at one joint point: a confirmed null in both the dark-energy evolution and the alpha-G drift refutes it. Strictly on the public MQT surface.
title: The Running of G and alpha from Horizon Information: Macrobiotic Quantum Theory as a de Sitter Completion of Emergent Gravity

summary: SlideRule is an open source server-side framework for on-demand processing of science data in the cloud. The SlideRule project offers a new paradigm for NASA archival data management – rapid delivery of customizable on-demand data products, rather than hosting large volumes of standard derivative products, which will inevitably be insufficient for some science applications. The scalable server-side components of SlideRule run in the AWS cloud with optimized functions to read HDF5 data hosted by NASA in S3 cloud object storage. While SlideRule can be accessed by any HTTP client (e.g., curl) through GET and POST requests, the sliderule-python client provides a user-friendly API for synchronous interaction with the SlideRule service. The client library returns standard Python data containers (i.e., Pandas DataFrame) and facilitates serialization with provenance metadata for reproducible science. SlideRule uses a plugin framework to support different NASA missions and data products. The ICESat-2 SlideRule plugin offers customizable algorithms to process the archive of low-level data products from the NASA Ice Cloud and land Elevation Satellite-2 (ICESat-2) laser altimetry mission. The user defines a geographic area of interest and key processing parameters via an interactive web interface or the API, and SlideRule returns high-level surface elevation point cloud products in seconds to minutes, enabling rapid algorithm development, visualization and scientific interpretation.
title: SlideRule

summary: TRUSTWORTHY AUTONOMOUS BIOLABORATORIES THROUGH MICROROBOTICS AND QUANTUM SENSING AT THE LIMIT Replayable Experiments x Permission Governance x External Metrology STARLI Research Institute XXIX - Flagship Research Monograph 20 Can an autonomous biolaboratory become scientifically useful without acquiring the authority to redefine its own permissions, validate its own evidence, or release untraceable measurements? This nonclinical research monograph investigates a bounded laboratory architecture connecting microrobotic sample handling, quantum-enabled and classical sensing, independent metrological reference chains, experiment replay, physical safe stopping, and human authority. Its central proposition is that reliable autonomy is a property of the entire evidence pathway rather than of any single robotic manipulator or AI model. A laboratory result is eligible for release only when sample identity and integrity, authorized execution, traceable references, justified uncertainty limits, and external acceptance are all demonstrated. An apparently successful action is not equivalent to a scientifically accepted sample. Digital replay does not replace physical replication, cryptographic event integrity does not guarantee sensor truth, and a quantum hardware label does not establish a practical sensing advantage. The research design is developed across 82 chapter-level inquiries with five independently paginated investigations per chapter, 30 connected mathematical research plates, 200 distinct Research Gates, and 33 Phoenix Answer Embryos. The chapters address typed authority graphs, specimen provenance, sample exposure, closed-chip physics, covariance-aware sensing, AI planning within finite action spaces, common-cause fault injection, external interlocks, blinded classical benchmarks, evidence DAGs, cross-site replication, data retention, and responsible system retirement. The proposed minimum experimental prototype uses a closed microfluidic chip with interchangeable handling modules, two independently referenced readout channels, simulated or inert-tracer specimens, a separate audit service, and a physically verifiable stop mechanism. Proposed tests include unauthorized-action challenges, hidden calibration drift, interrupted events, sample contamination, unannounced network partitions, and independent laboratory replay or rerun. DOI-linked scientific references establish the relevant literature in automated laboratories, microrobotics, quantum sensing, uncertainty metrology, FAIR data stewardship, and computational reproducibility. They do not independently validate the integrated system proposed here. SCIENTIFIC STATUS AND LIMITATIONS This book is a hypothesis-forming nonclinical research architecture. It reports no completed microrobotic or quantum biosensing experiments, no demonstrated clinical performance, no universal quantum advantage, and no autonomous system capable of authorizing itself. Statistical models, formulas, and decision policies require experimental verification, specialized review, and appropriate boundary conditions. A failed external reference, unavailable provenance chain, or revoked permission requires abstention rather than inference by convenience. STARLI RESEARCH PHILOSOPHY A trustworthy laboratory must remain answerable to evidence outside itself. Autonomy becomes scientifically meaningful when an experiment can be stopped, questioned, reconstructed, and handed to future researchers who retain the right to refuse its original assumptions.

summary: Version 2.0 preserves the original June 2026 Bridge Settlement manuscript and adds a separately dated October 2026 supplement. The addendum introduces Residual Strategic Optionality as an extension of Stakeholder Coherence Theory, examining the incentives of actors capable of disrupting negotiated settlements. It also compares the Bridge Settlement with Jeffrey Sachs's October 2026 peace framework for Ukraine, identifying areas of conceptual convergence and distinguishing the Bridge Settlement's emphasis on reciprocal economic interests, institutional participation, and self-reinforcing peace mechanisms. The original manuscript remains unchanged. This study develops a comparative Bayesian framework for evaluating natural zoonotic and research-associated hypotheses for the proximal origin of SARS-CoV-2 under incomplete evidence. To reduce double counting, correlated observations are consolidated into three causal blocks addressing phenotype and proximal adaptation, the Huanan Seafood Wholesale Market and early epidemic topology, and the Wuhan sarbecovirus research environment. The central calibration yields a likelihood ratio of approximately 1.49 favoring research-associated emergence, while alternative defensible calibrations reverse or strengthen that preference, demonstrating substantial sensitivity to evidentiary weighting. The paper introduces the “Missing Bridge” as the unresolved proximal viral population and transmission history connecting deeper sarbecovirus ancestry to sustained human transmission. It argues that provenance-rich evidence—including authenticated proximal viruses, earliest-human genomic and epidemiological linkage, and upstream ecological or research records—has substantially greater discriminatory value than additional circumstantial observations. The resulting assessment is characterized as  preference without closure .
title: The Missing Bridge

summary: This archive provides the computational methods, structural coordinate files, source data, model outputs, and reproducibility documentation supporting an exploratory investigation of geometric persistence and prediction uncertainty at HIV-1 envelope (Env) glycan sites. The research examines whether local sequence divergence and sparse structural-context observations can improve the identification of unreliable glycan-site geometric predictions. The approach combines sequence-informed error estimation with residual information obtained from six observed glycan-site probes. Held-out evaluations included five BG505-derived Env structures and two JR-FL structures. In the original experiments, the six-probe method improved pooled dangerous-error discrimination relative to sequence-only prediction, with ROC AUC increasing from 0.704 to 0.945 in BG505 and from 0.522 to 0.761 in JR-FL. These results are exploratory. The original evaluations contained only two dangerous underestimates in BG505 and three in JR-FL. Within-structure discrimination did not consistently improve, and training-test construct overlap was identified. Additional construct-family exclusion analyses document the sensitivity of the findings to training composition and failure prevalence. The principal computational outputs were regenerated exactly from archived structural coordinates using the supplied scripts. The archive includes frozen protocols, structural data, prediction tables, provenance audits, family-exclusion analyses, and a companion manuscript draft. The study supports further investigation of sparse structural context for uncertainty assessment but does not establish reliable cross-strain site-level failure detection, glycan occupancy prediction, or protein synthesis prediction. This deposit is intended to support transparency, independent reproduction, methodological evaluation, and future extension of HIV-1 Env structural bioinformatics research. This research extends the author's previously deposited HIV-1 Env glycan-shield investigations by examining the predictive and uncertainty-assessment implications of geometric persistence, local structural constraints, and glycan-site organization.
title: Ensemble Geometric Persistence: HIV-1 Env Glycan-Site Geometry and Sparse Structural-Context Uncertainty Assessment (Reproducibility Archive)

summary: This package contains the code and data needed to reproduce every table, figure, and number in El Akrouchi and Mhada, “When one funder is the field: reporter concentration, voluntary sustainability disclosure, and the measurement of philanthropic development finance” (Frontiers in Sustainability). It shows that a 2017 discontinuity in policy-marker coverage across nineteen subsystems follows the identity of one dominant reporter rather than reporter concentration. Notebook 2 ( 2_disclosure_horizons_crops.ipynb ): the agricultural analyses, including the text-based reconstruction with bootstrap uncertainty, commitment horizons, and crop-system content (Tables 3, 4, S2, S4 to S15, S21 to S25; Figures 1 and 3 to 7). data/ : the agricultural extraction, the public ODA control series, derived all-sector datasets, the hand-coded audit of the crop dictionary, the crop dictionary, and the reporter list. outputs/ : every table and figure, named after the manuscript item it produces, and the fitted reconstruction model (serialized objects and portable coefficients). summary: Geometric Observability and Optimal Design for Vehicle Localization by a Three-Dimensional Beacon Array     https://orcid.org/0009-0007-5661-7332 https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23575194 Abstract This paper develops a geometric analysis of vehicle-position observability when line-of-sight measurements are obtained from a surrounding beacon array. The vehicle is represented by an unknown Cartesian position, while each beacon contributes a unit line-of-sight vector. The associated Jacobian yields the Fisher information matrix, whose inverse supplies the Cramér–Rao bound on position covariance. In the horizontal plane, beacon directions determine the conditioning of the position estimate through their angular spread; in elevation, nonzero vertical separation supplies sensitivity to depth and suppresses the vertical dilution that occurs in a coplanar arrangement. Design implications are stated in terms of angular diversity, range, symmetry, and beacon elevation, and are formalized through the classical D- and E-optimality criteria. The treatment is first-order and analytical: no field calibration, stochastic measurement data, or performance claim beyond the stated linearized model is made. Index Terms —Beacon localization, Observability, Line-of-sight geometry, Fisher information, Cramér–Rao bound, Optimal experimental design, Position covariance, Vehicle navigation.
title: Geometric Observability and Optimal Design for Vehicle Localization by a Three-Dimensional Beacon Array

summary: Unrefereed research candidate. A random walk is robust if an adversary who may change every transition probability by a small relative amount cannot make it much slower to reach its targets. Zuckerman (Markov chain robustness, ITCS 2026, LIPIcs 362, 118) conjectured that the largest safe relative change is at least a constant divided by the graph's diameter (Conjecture 1.16). This package shows the conjecture is false. A graph can have short routes that the walk almost never uses; a small fixed bias away from a target accumulates between rare visits to them and depletes the target's stationary mass, and Kac's formula turns this into a long hitting time. For explicit cubic graphs J_b on N vertices with diameter O(log N), every effective resistance is at most 684 (proof), and a fixed perturbation of size 1/b, with error times diameter tending to zero, multiplies the worst-case hitting time by a factor of order b; the robustness is O(N^(-1/3)). For explicit 3m-regular graphs of diameter exactly three, the mixing time is at most 50(m+1), so with Zuckerman's mixing-time theorem the robustness lies between constant multiples of N^(-1/2) and N^(-1/4) (proof; not matching). An exact computation shows a 5.80-fold slowdown on a 5,995-vertex member with error times diameter 0.74. A diameter-two example, a reversible-perturbation bound and a comparison with Kemeny's constant are included. The archive contains the manuscript (PDF and LaTeX), seven verification scripts with a driver that reproduces the reference JSON results byte for byte under python -B -O, semantic negative controls, figures and SHA-256 sums. Assurance: written proofs; exact checks; producer-side replay including a clean replay in a separate copy; internal AI-assisted review, AI-assisted adversarial reviews (OpenAI gpt-5.6-sol; Anthropic Claude Opus 5.5; OpenAI gpt-6-astra) and a verification re-review. This is not peer review, independent reproduction or formal verification. Creator: Anonymous. Prose, manuscript and data CC0-1.0; code MIT.
title: Small diameter does not control hitting-time robustness

summary: We extend the Deep Hough Transform (DHT), which detects semantic lines by aggregating learned features along candidate lines into a two-dimensional parameter space, to higher-dimensional parametric curve families. The extension is hard because the accumulator for a family with d parameters has O(B^d) cells for B bins per axis. We propose a factorized deep Hough transform, a differentiable feature-space voting cascade that splits the parameter vector into a spatial anchor and a shape. A coarse two-dimensional accumulator votes for anchors, and a dense shape accumulator is built only around the top-k anchors, so memory falls from O(B^d) to O(B^d1 + k B^d2). Lines are the degenerate case with no second stage. We also define a curve agreement score that extends the EA line similarity to parametric curves, and a synthetic benchmark of parabolas, circles and ellipses with noise, occlusion and distractors. We evaluate with thresholds selected on a validation split and the test split scored once, and we give the geometric baselines the same treatment. Under this protocol the choice of Stage-1 pooling over probe shapes matters a great deal: max pooling raises parabola F from 0.51 to 0.70 over log-sum-exp (3 seeds). With it, the cascade ties a tuned RANSAC fit on parabolas (0.706 vs. 0.702) and circles (0.743 vs. 0.742) and is slightly behind it on ellipses (0.382 vs. 0.410), while direct regression and query-based heads reach 0.15 and 0.13 on parabolas. So the cascade is competitive with classical fitting rather than better than it, and its practical advantage is memory: at B=32 a dense d=5 accumulator would need about 4 GB (computed, not instantiated) against a measured 236 KB for the cascade. We locate the remaining error in Stage 1. Running Stage 2 at the ground-truth anchors gives F = 0.938 against 0.706, and curves whose anchors lie within about 8 pixels of each other lose about 0.2 F because their Stage-1 peaks merge. We also report a TuSimple lane-detection stress test, which we treat as a feasibility check rather than a competitive result. Code and the benchmark generator are released.
title: Beyond Lines: A Factorized Deep Hough Transform for Parametric Curve Detection

summary: Absorption and scattering coefficients for the Jerlov optical water types, taken from the primary literature with the provenance of every value recorded. Values that a published table got wrong are flagged rather than silently repaired, and quantities the data do not determine are refused rather than guessed. Twenty-five entries are documented, nine of them confirmed defects in the source literature: duplicated rows in Solonenko & Mobley (2015) Table 7, a transcription error in the small-particle scattering coefficient that propagated into their published coefficients, a Data Availability Statement that gives the DOI of an unrelated dataset, and a reprint whose stated unit is out by a factor of ten. Three further entries were open questions that obtaining the 1968 first edition settled. The same Jerlov water type is in circulation with beam attenuations differing by a factor of five, which is why every coefficient here carries the source it came from. Every shipped table can be regenerated from its primary source by the scripts in tools/ , and each generation step checks the result against the equations of the paper it came from. The package computes the direct and veiling components along a horizontal underwater path, converts spectra to CIE XYZ, sRGB, or the response of an arbitrary camera or set of photoreceptors, gives the Jerlov type that typically applies in each 10 m layer down to 200 m and carries the downwelling irradiance down through those layers, integrates photosynthetically available radiation (PAR), or the photon flux over any other band or weighted by any spectral sensitivity, with depth, gives the spectrum at any depth and the effective Kd between two, and finds the depth at which PAR falls to 1 percent, ranks the Jerlov types by their distance from a measured Kd spectrum, carries Jerlov's measured profiles of quanta irradiance (350-700 nm) by water type and checks the depth profile against them, carries Tyler's (1958) measured radiance distribution in Lake Pend Oreille, carries the wave-induced light fluctuations measured by Darecki et al. (2011) and Gernez & Antoine (2009), read from their figures, carries the Paulson & Simpson (1977) shortwave penetration parameters used by ocean circulation models, converts a backscattering sensor's single-angle reading into the backscattering coefficient, and carries Petzold's (1972) volume scattering functions for eight measured ocean waters.
title: jerlov: inherent optical properties of the Jerlov optical water types, with provenance
